title: CATL advances solid-state battery development to 20 Ah samples - electrive.com
content:
According to Chinese media, CATL has expanded the development of its solid-state battery from a 10-Ah-class validation platform to test runs with 20-Ah samples. The company continues to aim for small-scale production in 2027 and is reportedly targeting an energy density of around 500 Wh/kg.
Image: CATL
According to Chinese media, CATL published an update this week on its solid-state battery development in response to investor queries via the state-regulated online communication platform of the Shenzhen Stock Exchange (“Hudongyi Platform”). According to the update, test runs with 20 Ah samples are now underway, and the start of pilot production
remains planned for 2027
CATL also shared that the development team working on this project comprises more than 1,000 employees and that the programme aims to achieve an energy density of approximately 500 Wh/kg at the cell level. However,
Car News China
notes that CATL has not explicitly confirmed this figure as a specification for mass-produced cells, nor “disclosed expected trial output, automotive customers or a vehicle launch date tied to these cells”. The company is still aiming for large-scale production around 2030.
Solid-state batteries are widely regarded as a promising technology for the next generation of energy storage. Their defining feature is the replacement of the liquid or gel-like electrolyte in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid electrolyte based on sulphide, polymer, or oxide materials. This is expected to improve fire safety, increase energy density, enable faster charging times, extend service life, and enhance the range of EVs.
Little is yet known about CATL’s specific technology approach. Unconfirmed reports suggest the company is primarily focusing on sulphide-based solid-state batteries. However, CATL has not yet disclosed the intended anode configuration.
In addition to CATL, companies like BYD and Toyota, as well as promising startups such as
Factorial
QuantumScape
, are advancing the technology. However, in June,
CATL CEO Robin Zeng noted
that technical and manufacturing challenges mean that the deployment of solid-state batteries in the mass market is still several years away, and he does not expect volume production before 2030. Moreover, Zeng stated that solid-state batteries will likely initially be used only in premium automotive platforms.
CATL also stated in June that its solid-state technology is currently at level four on the nine-point Technology Readiness Level (TRL) scale. This classification means that CATL is still engaged in laboratory validation and prototype development for solid-state batteries this summer.

title: Batteries and the Ballot: Trump's Mixed EV Record in 2026
content:
Industry Outlook
Battery Manufacturing
Automotive & Mobility
New DOE funding, tariff whiplash, and a vanished tax credit — what battery-affiliated voters should know before midterms.
October 29, 2026
7 Min Read
US President Donald Trump delivers remarks at the Department of Energy in 2017.
Kevin Dietsch-Pool/Getty Images
At a Glance
DOE launches BattMan accelerator and national battery strategy six days before the midterms.
EV tax credit expired in 2025; U.S. sales fell nearly 24% in early 2026 as a result.
Graphite tariffs near 220% raise costs even as they aim to boost domestic production.
The US Department of Energy announced on October 28, 2026, the
launch of the Battery Manufacturing Accelerator, or BattMan
— a new national consortium designed to close the long-standing gap between laboratory battery breakthroughs and full-scale domestic manufacturing. Led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, with Argonne National Laboratory, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and the National Laboratory of the Rockies participating, BattMan aims to pair artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing techniques — including digital twins, real-time process monitoring, and closed-loop control — to help battery technologies move faster and more affordably from the bench to the factory floor.
"The advances we make today in battery manufacturing technology will determine America's energy security and economic competitiveness for decades to come," stated Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson in the announcement.
Related:
John Warner Maps Four Trends Transforming Today’s Battery Industry
Illustrative overview of global supply base case by region for 2030. Not all battery supply chain nodes are included. Credit: US Department of Energy
BattMan's launch comes just six days before the November 3 midterm elections — contests in which President Trump's name will not appear on any ballot, but which he has nonetheless framed as a referendum on his administration. Trump has repeatedly urged supporters to "
pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot
". For voters whose livelihoods are tied to the battery, EV, or BESS supply chains, and who take that instruction at face value, 2026 offers a genuinely split record — one of real federal investment in manufacturing capacity, paired with policy choices that have made it harder to sell what that capacity produces.
A steady drumbeat of federal investment
BattMan is not an isolated gesture. It is the latest in a string of DOE funding actions throughout 2026 aimed at building up domestic battery and critical minerals capacity. In March 2026, DOE opened a $500 million
Notice of Funding Opportunity for battery materials processing, manufacturing, and recycling
— the third round of funding under the department's Battery Materials Processing program, with letters of intent due March 27 and full applications due April 24. Later in the year, the administration touted a $3 billion investment in critical minerals and battery projects and highlighted that it had signed or approved roughly 160 minerals-related deals worth nearly $40 billion since January 2025, under a broader banner of "American energy dominance."
That framing — energy security, supply chain resilience, and domestic jobs — runs consistently through nearly every one of these announcements, including BattMan's. And the underlying rationale is sound: DOE's own strategy document acknowledges that while the US pioneered lithium-ion battery science, it never built a complete domestic supply chain. China controls between 60 and 100% of global production capacity across several midstream battery component categories — cathodes, anodes, electrolytes, and separators — making that segment of the chain a genuine point of vulnerability for U.S. manufacturers and, by extension, for national security.
Related:
Peak Energy’s Dr. Lucy Li on Sodium-Ion Battery Innovations
Tariffs that cut both ways
The administration's approach to that Chinese dominance illustrates the double-edged nature of its battery policy. In February 2026, the Department of Commerce issued a final determination in an anti-dumping investigation into Chinese battery-grade graphite, finding that
Chinese active anode material producers had been dumping into the US market
at rates of 93.5%. Layered with additional countervailing duties, the total effective tariff on Chinese graphite — the single largest material by weight in a lithium-ion battery, and a material the US produces almost none of domestically —
reached roughly 220% by mid-2026
US - China trade war illustrationnarvikk / iStock / Getty Images Plus
For battery manufacturers, that tariff cuts in two directions at once. It is designed to protect the kind of domestic midstream investment DOE's national strategy calls for, giving US anode producers room to compete against artificially cheap Chinese material. But in the short term it raises input costs sharply for any manufacturer still reliant on Chinese graphite — which, given the current state of domestic anode capacity, is most of them.
Related:
Battery Show Keynotes Tackle Supply Chains, AI Impact & Manufacturing Scale from Oct. 12-15
Pulling the rug out from under demand
While DOE has spent 2026 building up the supply side of the battery industry, the same administration has worked, through Congress,
to dismantle the demand-side incentives that helped grow the EV market in the first place
. The $7,500 federal tax credit for new EV purchases — along with a $4,000 credit for used EVs — expired on September 30, 2025, after Congress eliminated the incentives as part of the 2025 tax legislation. The credits had previously been authorized through 2032.
The effect was immediate and then lasting. A rush of buyers tried to beat the deadline in August and September 2025, followed by a steep falloff. One year later, U.S.
EV sales were down nearly 24% in the first half of 2026
compared with the prior year. NPR's retrospective coverage, published on the one-year anniversary of the credit's expiration, asked directly
whether the EV market's future was still viable
without federal purchase support.
It’s a strange juxtaposition: The same federal government funding hundreds of millions of dollars in battery manufacturing grants throughout 2026 removed, in that same period, the single most direct lever for growing the vehicle market those batteries are meant to supply.
An inadvertent assist, with a catch
Not all of the administration's actions have cut against the battery and EV industries, even unintentionally. The U.S. military conflict with Iran, which escalated in early 2026, drove global oil and gas prices sharply higher. According to an April 2026 analysis from Yale Climate Connections, the resulting spike in fuel prices
gave a real boost to clean technologies worldwide, with global EV sales surging
as drivers sought alternatives to costlier gasoline.
But that lift was not evenly distributed. The same reporting — along with broader coverage of the global EV market in 2026 — suggests Chinese automakers captured much of the increased international demand, while the US market, still reeling from the loss of its tax credit, did not see a comparable domestic sales bump.
In other words, a geopolitical decision made by Washington ended up helping the EV industry — just largely outside US borders, and to the advantage of exactly the international competitors that the administration's tariff and critical-minerals policies are ostensibly trying to counter.
An industry caught between two policy tracks
For battery manufacturers, suppliers, and BESS developers trying to plan capital investment, the throughline of 2026 is less a coherent industrial strategy than a set of parallel, sometimes contradictory tracks. DOE's funding announcements — from the March NOFO to the August grants to today's BattMan launch — consistently aim to de-risk domestic manufacturing and shore up midstream supply chain gaps that have left the US exposed to Chinese dominance in critical materials. That is a real and durable policy contribution, and BattMan's focus on AI-driven process innovation targets a genuine bottleneck: the
"valley of death" between promising lab discoveries and bankable commercial-scale production
Battery Technology
has previously examined.
At the same time, the removal of EV purchase incentives and the imposition of steep near-term tariffs on essential battery inputs have made the commercial case for scaling that same manufacturing capacity considerably harder. A domestic graphite producer may eventually benefit from tariff protection, but a cell manufacturer paying 220% more for graphite today, while watching EV demand contract, faces a tougher two or three years in between.
That split record is likely to matter beyond the industry trade press in the coming days. With Trump asking voters to treat the midterms as a judgment on his administration, battery- and EV-affiliated workers, suppliers, and investors have, in BattMan and the dueling policy tracks around it, a genuinely mixed data set to weigh — manufacturing investment up, tariffs cutting both ways, demand-side incentives gone, and a geopolitical windfall that mostly bypassed US shores. Whether that record reads as a net positive or a net negative likely depends on which part of the supply chain a given voter sits in. This is the record as it stands in the days before Americans go to the polls.
About the Author
Michael C. Anderson
As editor-in-chief of
Battery Technology
, Michael C. Anderson leads the brand’s coverage of advancements in battery technology as well as associated materials and manufacturing techniques across industries such as automotive/EVs, e-mobility, maritime, aerospace, medtech, and consumer electronics.
Mike is also a member of
The Battery Show North America Advisory Board
, where he contributes his expertise to advising on industry trends and speaker selection for The Battery Show North America while helping to shape discussions on battery technology and electrification.
Mike and
Battery Technology
senior editor Maria Guerra De Egui are joint
2025 Neal Award Winners
in the category of "Best Coverage of the 2024 Election on Your Served Market."
Mike was a recent guest journalist on the popular automotive-industry webcast, Autoline After Hours.
Mike has been covering manufacturing and transportation technology developments for more than 25 years. At SME (
The Society of Manufacturing Engineers
), he served as lead editor of
Aerospace & Defense Manufacturing
, lead editor of
Medical Manufacturing
, senior editor for
Manufacturing Engineering,
and acting lead editor of
Smart Manufacturing
. He has also been senior editor of
Cutting Tool Engineering
, senior technical editor of Gardener Business Media’s
Automotive Design & Production
, PR manager at B2B advertising/PR agency G. Temple Associates, and editor at the SM Wu Manufacturing Research Center at the University of Michigan.
This all followed more than a decade of teaching English, ESL, literature, and argumentation as a lecturer at Eastern Michigan University (Ypsilanti, MI) and, for five years, at Sakura no Seibo Junior College (Fukushima, Japan).
Mike has a bachelor’s degree in English language and literature and a master’s degree in rhetoric and written communication from Eastern Michigan University.

title: People, AI or Both? Exploring the LSG Operating Model
content:
People, AI or Both? Exploring the LSG Operating Model
Prioritise Us
on Google
Lean Solutions Group explores the role of the human in the loop. Credit: Getty
Jack Freker, CEO of Lean Solutions Group explores the necessary role of the human-in-the-loop in long-term supply chain transformation
The supply chain sector is one facing increasing levels of demand - driven by heightened consumer demand, legislative pressures to operate more sustainably and the
growing risk of cyber attacks
requiring new levels of security.
When facing a growing demand, many leaders are turning towards automation – or wanting to, but not knowing where to start.
Lean Solutions Group helps businesses understand where technology and AI can help, offering a model which helps drive immediate cost savings, resilience and growth.
A human-AI workforce
In an era defined by ongoing technological innovation, finding the
balance of adoption
can be a challenge of its own. Many organisations are purchasing AI as the new must-have tool, but are failing to recognise where it may be less helpful in their operations, or updating their framework in order to support the tool.
Lean Solutions Group (LSG) understands that AI can make a significant difference, but it also recognises that there is an added layer of complexity to decision-making that many leaders ignore. LSG is a solutions provider which integrates AI-driven automation, industry expertise and tech-powered talent in its offerings.
Its model aims to help those in the supply chain sector as they navigate the growing demand and increasing complexity in the modern market. It works to help companies with cost savings, efficiency, long-term resilience and business growth.
It embeds into its clients’ business operations and combines human and artificial talent in order to increase efficiency for its clients. It approaches each challenge with an integrated approach, looking at where human insight is critical and where AI agents can do the work.
Organisations need to find the balance of human insight and AI operations. Credit: Getty
At a glance
LSG has more than 13,000 employees across six countries
It has a growing base of more than 600 clients
One of its clients cut turnover rate by 66% in 30 days through using LSG
Employee satisfaction has reached 90% for some clients who are embedding LSG’s industry expertise
Productivity rose by 85% in 90 days for one LSG client
The adoption gap
In October 2026, Lean Solutions Group released its study, conducted with Everest Group, demonstrating where the gap lies in
AI adoption and transformation
. The research found that organisations are adopting the technology at a faster rate than they are redesigning operations.
Due to this, the infrastructure of the company is unable to support transformation, meaning the AI tools are not able to deliver the expected results from the integration. The survey uses insights from US-focused senior decision makers in the transportation, logistics and supply chain industries.
Though the study found that 69% of organisations have moved beyond isolated AI use cases, only 19% have redesigned their workflows to a standard that can
support collaboration between people and AI
– the ‘human-in-the-loop’ approach.
“The challenge is no longer simply getting AI into the business. It is changing how work gets done,” said Jack Freker, CEO of Lean Solutions Group.
Jack Freker, CEO of Lean Solutions Group
“Technology can analyse, recommend and automate at scale, but people remain accountable for the outcome. The organisations that get the most from AI will combine experts in the loop, intelligent technology and redesigned processes in a way that improves performance for customers.”
The report supports LSG’s argument that coordinated changes must take place in order to accurately transform an organisation with AI. There needs to be a collaboration between industry expertise, optimised processes and AI-enabled execution in order to make a difference to business value.
In doing this, businesses can see an improvement in their standardised processes, data visibility capabilities, customer relationships and
complex decision-making
Technology can analyse, recommend and automate at scale, but people remain accountable for the outcome.
Jack Freker, CEO of Lean Solutions Group

The company delivers immediate cost savings and efficiency while building long-term resilience by embedding intelligent technology, optimized processes, and high-performance talent into clients' core business operations.

title: Sphera AI Introduces Agentic AI Supply Chain Risk Tools
content:
Sphera AI Introduces Agentic AI Supply Chain Risk Tools
Prioritise Us
on Google
Sphera has launched new AI capabilities for Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM)
Sphera CEO Paul Marushka outlines AI-powered supply chain risk management for faster supplier, product and operations decisions
Sphera has launched new AI capabilities for Supply Chain Risk Management (SCRM), designed to connect external risk signals with the suppliers, products and operations they could affect.
The new capabilities include agentic AI tools, conversational AI features and a Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows organisations to pull insights directly from SCRM into compatible AI tools.
The Chicago-based company said the technology is intended to help organisations assess disruption impacts and coordinate responses in minutes rather than days.
The announcement follows the publication of Sphera research showing that external events - including supplier failures, port closures, material shortages and trade restrictions - are a major source of operational disruption.
Paul Marushka, CEO at Sphera
External risk is becoming operational risk
Across the US, UK, Germany, France and UAE, 58% of surveyed chief operating officers said their most significant disruptions originated at least as much outside their organisation as within it. The figure rose to 71% among respondents in the UAE.
The research surveyed 750 COOs. It found that the most difficult parts of disruption management were:
Identifying exposed suppliers or products: 33%
Selecting the right mitigation action: 30%
Quantifying potential business impact: 29%
The findings reflect a growing gap between risk detection and operational decision-making. Organisations may identify an external event quickly, but still struggle to determine which sites, products, suppliers or customer commitments are exposed.
“The boundary of the enterprise is no longer the boundary of operational risk. A disruption can begin with a supplier, a critical material or an event on the other side of the world, but its consequences are felt inside the business,” says Paul Marushka, CEO and President of Sphera.
"The challenge is connecting those external signals to the products and operations they affect quickly enough to make a better decision. Sphera AI helps close that gap, while keeping people in control of the decisions that matter most,” adds Paul.
Sphera notes 58% of surveyed chief operating officers said their most significant disruptions originated at least as much outside their organisation as within it.
Sphera AI connects signals to business impact
The new Sphera AI capabilities are designed to link external intelligence to internal business context.
Users can ask questions about supplier and supply chain risk in plain language and identify which suppliers, products and operations may be exposed. The aim is to reduce the need to compare multiple dashboards or manually trace relationships between an external event and the business processes it threatens.
The capabilities include: external risk signals, supplier exposure, product dependencies, operational impact, risk severity, mitigation decisions, response coordination, supply continuity, production protection and revenue protection.
Sphera’s Supply Chain Risk Management platform combines external risk intelligence with suppliers, products, commodities and multi-tier dependencies.
Model Context Protocol extends risk intelligence
Sphera has also added support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
MCP allows organisations to make selected SCRM insights available through compatible artificial intelligence tools. This means risk information can be accessed in the environments where teams already analyse data and make operational decisions.
The potential applications include querying supplier risk through compatible AI assistants, retrieving risk context without switching between systems, connecting external events to internal supplier records, supporting procurement and operations workflows, making trusted risk data available to authorised users and reducing time spent searching across separate applications.
The approach is intended to make risk intelligence more accessible while retaining organisational controls over data, workflows and decision-making.
AI agents support risk triage
Within Sphera’s Risk Response & Resolution Center, the recently introduced AI agents assess risk severity and supplier impact.
The system is designed to help teams distinguish urgent risks from lower-priority signals. By automating aspects of triage, Sphera said users can focus on the events most likely to affect production, supply continuity or revenue.
The Risk Response & Resolution Center provides a central workspace for triaging risks, assigning ownership, executing mitigation plans and tracking outcomes with an audit trail.
Sphera’s broader platform monitors more than 300,000 news sources each day and processes approximately 15 billion data points each month, according to company information.
Human control remains central
Sphera’s announcement positions artificial intelligence as a decision-support capability rather than an autonomous replacement for supply chain and procurement teams.
The company said every one of the 750 COOs surveyed identified at least one risk-management activity they would allow AI to progress automatically, provided appropriate rules and controls were in place.
This creates a governance model in which AI could detect relevant events, classify risk signals, summarise complex information, match events to suppliers, estimate potential exposure, prioritise response activity as well as potentially recommending next steps.
Human teams remain responsible for decisions involving suppliers, production, customer commitments, financial exposure and operational continuity.
Traditional supply chain risk management often stops at the alert. Sphera’s announcement focuses on the next stage: translating an alert into an operational response.
The workflows that follow the identification of such a disruption include: detecting a geopolitical, environmental or logistics event, identifying affected suppliers and sub-tier relationships, mapping impacted products and facilities and estimating operational and commercial consequences. These steps are then followed by the assignment of response ownership, the selection and execution of mitigation actions, and tracking whether an organisation's exposure has reduced.
Sphera describes this connection between risk signals, business impact and response workflows as a way to reduce decision latency across the disruption lifecycle.
Key disruption workflow activities
Detecting a geopolitical, environmental or logistics event
Identifying affected suppliers and sub-tier relationships
Mapping impacted products and facilities
Estimating operational and commercial consequences
Assigning response ownership
Selecting and executing mitigation actions
Tracking whether exposure has reduced

title: DHL Group Strengthens Asia Pacific Healthcare Supply Chains
content:
DHL Group Strengthens Asia Pacific Healthcare Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Did you know?
You can read this and more in the magazine
DHL commits €2bn globally to life sciences and healthcare logistics. Credit: DHL
As demand for reliable healthcare logistics increases, DHL is investing in its Asia Pacific operations to increase compliance and efficiency
DHL Group is strengthening its
Life Sciences and Healthcare (LSHC) capabilities in Singapore
, following the opening of its Pharma Hub in 2025.
As the company continues to
grow its investments
, the region will see expanded capacity across its medical supply chains, driving greater efficiency and security across the industry.
In a critical sector like healthcare, a reliable supply chain saves lives.
Through these investments, DHL is making better healthcare accessible for more people, resulting in patient satisfaction and supply chain resilience.
Demand for logistics
Healthcare supply chains
are incredibly complex, brought into the light during the COVID-19 pandemic when vaccines were being brought out,
was in high demand and non-critical surgeries were being pushed back.
Since this period of disruption, organisations have been examining their supply chain and logistics capabilities, exploring where issues occurred and what demonstrated resilience.
Healthcare supply chains have been seeing greater investments in recent years, driven by a new understanding of their importance.
Key Stats
€2bn – DHL Group announced a €2bn (US$2.29bn) global investment into LSHC
€500m – the amount DHL is investing in the Asia Pacific Health Logistics expansion
US$239bn – Asia Pacific’s pharmaceutical logistics market is expected to grow to US$239bn by 2031
12,000 – DHL Supply Chain’s Singaporean footprint will accommodate 12,000 pallet positions
These supply chains require careful strategies, temperature-controlled carriers and efficient handovers. The smallest error can result in high amounts of monetary and product waste – and put lives at risk.
“In healthcare logistics, precision is non-negotiable. A temperature excursion of just a few degrees can compromise the integrity of high-value medicines, biologics and other critical healthcare products,” explains
Praveen Gregory
DHL Global Forwarding
Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.
“That is why building an end-to-end, unbroken cold chain is essential. Beyond protecting products, it gives healthcare companies the confidence that life-saving therapies can move safely, compliantly and reliably across increasingly complex global supply chains.”
Praveen Gregory, CEO of DHL Global Forwarding Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. Credit: DHL
DHL, therefore, is further developing its LSHC capabilities in Singapore, growing its capabilities across transport, storage and distribution, medical devices and clinical trial materials across Asia Pacific.
The investments prioritise infrastructure, specialist expertise and strategic partnerships.
Temperature-controlled carriers are vital to safe healthcare supply chains Credit: DHL
DHL’s investment
In 2025, the Asia Pacific
pharmaceuticals market
was valued at US$163bn.
Following an ongoing demand for vaccines, biologics and temperature-controlled products, it is expected to reach almost US$239bn by 2031.
DHL has committed a €2bn (US$2.29bn) global investment into LSHC, €500m (US$568.9m) of which is going towards the Asia Pacific Health Logistics expansion.
This will go across infrastructure, technology, storage, fulfilment, distribution, global transportation and last-mile delivery.
DHL’s Global Expansion
1969 - DHL was founded by Adrian Dalsey, Larry Hillblom and Robert Lynn
1979 - The company began to deliver parcels
2002 - Deutsche Post acquired DHL
2007 - The Group opens the DHL Innovation Center
2012 - DHL opens its biggest express hub in Asia
2025 - DHL Group commits to €2bn investment by 2030
DHL Global Forwarding is developing the DHL Singapore Coldchain Hub. It is a €15m (US$17m) facility, which will provide 3,047 sqm of GDP-aligned temperature-controlled infrastructure.
This will correctly store pharmaceuticals, vaccines and biologics, with dedicated handling environments across chilled and ambient temperatures.
It is designed to ensure the cold chain operates unbroken, preserving product integrity end-to-end and is expected to launch in late 2027.
DHL Singapore Coldchain Hub will support vaccines, biologics and medicines. Credit: DHL
Following the success of the Pharma Hub, first launched in Singapore in 2025, a second will be developed in order to support ambient storage capability across
pharmaceuticals
and medical devices.
The €5m (US$5.6m) facility will operate between 15°C and 25°C in temperature controlled environments, with a humidity control below 60%.
“Capacity on its own isn’t the goal. It’s what that capacity allows our customers to do,” adds
Eunis Hew
, Managing Director,

title: Deloitte & Sirion: Providing Visibility for Supply Chains
content:
Deloitte & Sirion: Providing Visibility for Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Deloitte and Sirion are partnering to improve visibility across supply chain operations. Credit: Getty Images
Kanti Prabha, President, Chief Product & Technology Officer at Sirion, explores how a new partnership is helping transform supply chain planning
Deloitte has formed an alliance with Sirion to deploy AI
contract lifecycle management tools
for supply chain operations. The partnership targets supply chain teams working with enterprise resource planning systems.
The collaboration brings together Deloitte's consulting services and Sirion's AI platform to automate contract processes across supplier relationships. Through this, leaders could gain access to contract data that has traditionally remained siloed across departments and systems.
Supply chain organisations increasingly face pressure to demonstrate value through cost reduction and risk mitigation. Contract management represents a significant opportunity in both areas, yet many teams lack the tools to extract insights from existing agreements. The partnership addresses this gap by connecting contract intelligence
directly to supply chain workflows
Contract data remains disconnected
In recent years, supply chain operations have adopted digital tools across multiple functions. Contract management has lagged behind these efforts.
According to Sirion and World Commerce & Contracting, 54% of organisations lack automated data flow between contract management systems. The study launched in May 2026 found that 73% of respondents store contract data across multiple disconnected platforms.
Gaps in contract infrastructure
71% of North American respondents store contract data in shared drives
27% of organisations store all executed contracts exclusively in contract lifecycle management systems
54% have no automated data flow between systems
9% have two way synchronisation to keep contract data updated across platforms
42% are adopting or implementing AI in contracting processes
Teams are managing pricing negotiations, delivery schedules and renewal terms across supplier networks. When contract information sits in separate systems, tracking these commitments becomes difficult.
The fragmentation of contract data creates particular challenges for supply chain resilience. Procurement professionals may struggle to identify which suppliers hold critical commitments or where alternative sourcing arrangements exist. This lack of visibility can delay response times when supply disruptions occur or when organisations need to renegotiate terms quickly.
Supply chain visibility depends on access
"Contract lifecycle management is rapidly evolving from a back office function to a strategic enabler of business transformation," says Mark Ross, Legal Business Services Growth and Markets Leader at Deloitte. Organisations that cannot access contract data could miss supplier commitments or fail to respond to changing commercial conditions.
Supplier relationship management requires structured access to contractual terms. Supply chain teams need this information to
identify potential disruptions
before they affect operations.
AI contract lifecycle management platforms could help companies optimise supplier agreements and reduce costs. According to Sirion, the company has saved clients a combined total of more than US$2.2bn through its platform.
Modern supply chains operate across multiple tiers of suppliers, each with distinct contractual arrangements. Teams must track obligations across this network while maintaining compliance with regulatory requirements and internal policies. Without centralised contract intelligence, organisations risk exposure to supplier failures, price volatility and delivery delays that could have been anticipated through better data access.
Carin Giuliante, chair and CEO, Deloitte Tax
Procurement integration drives adoption
"As organisations accelerate their digital transformation journeys, the ability to manage contracts intelligently has become a strategic imperative, not just for legal teams, but for tax, finance, procurement and the broader enterprise," says Carin Giuliante, chair and CEO, Deloitte Tax. The alliance aims to embed contract intelligence into procurement workflows.
Sirion's platform uses conversational interfaces and AI agents to store,
create and manage contracts
. According to the company, it supports more than seven million contracts across more than 100 languages.
The platform can flag invoice discrepancies and monitor compliance across supplier agreements. It provides tools for each stage of the contract lifecycle from drafting through risk management.
"Sirion's AI first platform was built to handle the complexity of global supply chains and financial relationships," said Ajay Agrawal, CEO of Sirion. Deloitte will integrate contract intelligence into wider business processes using its Legal Business Services experience.
Operational resilience requires contract visibility
"Our partnership with Deloitte is about giving supply chain, procurement, legal, finance and delivery teams something they've rarely had, which is a real view into what their business has actually agreed to," explains Kanti Prabha, President, Chief Product & Technology Officer at Sirion. Supplier contracts often become inaccessible after execution.
Kanti Prabha, Co-Founder and President at Sirion (Credit: Sirion)
Finance teams could miss savings they negotiated. Operations might only learn about supplier problems after they disrupt production.
The partnership brings contract intelligence into finance, supply chain and enterprise resource planning systems. Teams can access this information through the platforms they use daily.
Deloitte serves almost 90% of the Fortune 500 through its finance and procurement network. The firm will apply this reach to help organisations integrate Sirion's platform.
Deloitte expands digital offerings
The Sirion alliance follows Deloitte's February 2026 launch of Enterprise AI Navigator. That solution helps organisations assess business processes and technology readiness for AI investments.
Enterprise AI Navigator supports development of AI agent prototypes and implementation roadmaps. According to Deloitte, the solution can reduce time required for
traditional AI strategy
work by up to 50%.
The firm launched Risk Clarity shortly before the Sirion partnership. The AI platform for risk management could offer efficiency gains of up to 30%, according to Deloitte.
"This alliance is about reimagining contract management as a driver of business value, insight and risk mitigation in an increasingly complex world," says Carin. The contract lifecycle management offering extends Deloitte's digital consultancy portfolio across the implementation process.

title: This $15,000 low-speed EV is now on sale, and it's street-legal
content:
Fiat Topolino
Peter Johnson
| Oct 29 2026 - 8:34 am PT
It may be small, but it’s already drawing a big response. The
2027 Fiat Topolino
is now on sale in the US: a street-legal, low-speed EV that starts under $15,000.
Meet the 2027 Fiat Topolino EV
With many dealers selling out of the first batch of 2026 models, the Fiat Topolino (which we already
had a chance to test out
) is back for 2027, bringing a new Open Air body style and color options.
The Topolino is even smaller than the Fiat 500e, measuring just over 8 feet (8’3″) long. That’s slightly longer than the average golf cart, but it can be driven legally on the street.
Federally classified as a motor vehicle, the Topolino is street-legal and can be driven on most public roads with a speed limit of 35 mph or less. While you won’t be taking it on the highway, it’s perfect for driving around neighborhoods and beach towns, golf communities, campgrounds, and more.
2027 Fiat Topolino Open Air (Source: Stellantis)
Using a 5.4 kWh lithium-ion battery and an 8 hp electric motor, the Topolino can drive up to 46 miles on a single charge with a top speed of 25 mph. A full recharge using a standard outlet takes about five hours.
The 2027 Fiat Topolino is now available at select US dealers, starting at $14,985, including the destination fee.
You can choose from three different body styles: Topolino, Dolce Vita, and a new Open Air model. The new Open Air version has the Dolce Vita’s roll-back soft-top roof and asymmetrical full doors, like the standard Topolino.
Fiat is offering a free LSV conversion kit, which includes a rearview mirror, a backup camera, and a pedestrian alert system to make it street legal.
Unlike the initial batch of
2026 models
, the 2027 Fiat Topolino will arrive at dealers as already street legal. Fiat is also offering complimentary home delivery for those who live within a 50-mile radius of the dealer.
You can learn more about the Topolino or
pre-order yours
on Fiat’s website.

title: The Ford Escape may return as an EV based on the UEV platform [Update]
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 29 2026 - 7:13 am PT
pulled the plug on the Escape last year after a 25-year run, but the crossover SUV could return as an EV on the new UEV platform.
Is Ford launching the Escape EV?
While Ford is preparing to launch the Fathom, its first vehicle based on the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform in 2027, the company is already hinting at what could be its second UEV-based model.
The last gas-powered Escape models rolled off the production line at Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant as it retooled the facility to prepare for the new Fathom electric pickup.
Typically, when Ford retires a model, its landing page says something like “we’re discontinuing” it, or “it’s the end of the road,” such as with the Edge SUV.
Meanwhile, the Escape landing page says the “SUV may be taking a breather for now,” declaring the “Ford Escape is tapping the brakes,” with no mention of it being discontinued. Instead, the site directs you to check out Ford’s other vehicles while it’s on hiatus.
(Source: Ford.com)
According to
Ford Authority
, the Escape will return as an all-electric crossover SUV based on the UEV platform.
Update 10/29/2026:
A Ford spokesperson told
Electrek
that the
Ford Authority
report is pure speculation and the company has not announced the Escape will return as an EV or that it will be based on the UEV platform.
If it does come to life, the Ford Escape EV would likely remain close in size to the outgoing gas model, which measures 180.1″ long, 74.1″ wide (without mirrors), and 66.1″ tall, with a 106.7″ wheelbase. That’s about the size of other compact SUVs like the Toyota RAV4 and Hyundai Tucson.
Covered Ford Fathom prototype at the Louisville Assembly Plant (Source: Ford)
The report claimed the electric Escape is expected to enter production at Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant in 2029, possibly making it the second vehicle based on its UEV platform, following the Fathom pickup.
CEO Jim Farley confirmed on Ford’s Q3 earnings call on Wednesday that the Fathom launch “remains on track for the fourth quarter of next year.”
The Fathom is “a breakthrough product,” Farley said, adding the pickup is highly capable, innovative, and affordable.
Ford Fathom EV pickup prototype (Source: Jim Farley)
Ford will open preorders for the Fathom in early 2027, starting at $28,350 for the standard-range version. With the $1,595 delivery fee, Ford’s electric pickup will still start under $30,000, which the company says will be “right in the heart of the market.”
The Fathom will be the first vehicle to integrate Apple Maps into its navigation system. It will also be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving. Other standard features include Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, plus bidirectional charging capabilities.
CEO Jim Farley presents the Ford Universal EV Platform in Kentucky (Source: Ford)
Ford claims the electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, not including the added bed and frunk (front trunk).
Inside, the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with an easy-to-use navigation system using Apple Maps.
Ford has yet to reveal battery specs or range, but the UEV platform uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries to reduce costs. We also know the Fathom will have an NACS charge port after a few prototypes were spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.
The UEV platform is flexible enough to underpin vehicles ranging from compact crossovers to pickup trucks and vans, so an electric Escape would make sense.
With the Fathom set to launch next year, we should learn more about the potential Ford Escape EV soon. Check back for updates.

title: BYD (BYDDY) Q3 profit jumps 28% on exports, but inventory balloons 60%
content:
Fred Lambert
| Oct 29 2026 - 7:00 am PT
BYD second-generation Seagull EV (Source: Zhang Zhuo)
BYD’s Q3 2026 earnings are out, and net profit jumped 28% year-over-year to ¥10.02 billion as the Chinese automaker shipped more than half a million vehicles out of the country in just three months.
But the rest of the filing is messier. BYD’s inventory is up 60% since January, its cash pile has shrunk by almost half, and profit is still down for the first nine months of the year.
BYD is still operating at a high level, but its business is changing.
BYD Q3 2026 earnings by the numbers
BYD filed its third-quarter report with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on Thursday. Here are the key figures for July through September:
Revenue: ¥221.49 billion, up 13.6% year-over-year
Net profit attributable to shareholders: ¥10.02 billion, up 28.1%
Net profit excluding one-time items: ¥8.63 billion, up 25.3%
Earnings per share: ¥1.10, up 29.4%
BYD’s key financial data for Q3 2026, from its third quarterly report filed with HKEX on Oct. 29, 2026
That’s BYD’s best quarterly profit since the end of 2024, and the first time revenue has grown year-over-year after four straight quarters of declines.
It’s also a big rebound from the start of the year. BYD’s Q1 2026 profit collapsed 55% to ¥4.08 billion, before recovering to ¥8.24 billion in Q2.
Still, it came in under expectations. Brokerages polled by Reuters were looking for ¥11.4 billion to ¥12.95 billion.
And zoom out to the full year so far, and BYD is treading water. Revenue for the first nine months was ¥566.30 billion, up just 0.01%, while net profit fell 4.2% to ¥22.34 billion. That’s on top of 2025, when BYD’s annual profit had already dropped to ¥32.62 billion from ¥40.25 billion in 2024.
Exports are carrying BYD now
The quarterly report doesn’t break out vehicle volumes, but BYD’s monthly sales filings do. The automaker sold 1,323,065 vehicles in Q3, up 18.7% from 1,114,192 a year earlier.
All of that growth, and then some, came from outside China. BYD exported 550,704 vehicles in the quarter, up 137% from 232,806 in Q3 2025. Everything else, which is mostly the Chinese market, fell about 12% to roughly 772,000 units.
Exports now account for 42% of BYD’s sales. In the first half, overseas markets already brought in ¥181.3 billion, or 53% of the company’s revenue.
For perspective, Tesla
delivered 486,532 vehicles worldwide in Q3
. BYD exported more cars than Tesla sold on the entire planet.
At home, it’s a different story. China’s price war hasn’t let up, and BYD is now fighting it with cars like the
new Seagull with 5-minute flash charging, starting under $10,000
. That’s great for buyers. Not so much for margins.
Going global isn’t cheap
BYD doesn’t report gross margin in its quarterly filing, but it can be calculated from the income statement. We get about 18.0% for Q3, slightly better than 17.6% a year ago, but down from roughly 18.9% in Q2.
The bigger hits are further down the income statement.
Finance expenses came in at ¥7.37 billion for the first nine months, compared to a ¥2.94 billion gain in the same period last year. BYD blames exchange losses. That’s a swing of more than ¥10 billion when the company made ¥22.34 billion in profit, which is the price of doing half your business in foreign currencies.
Impairment charges are also climbing. BYD booked ¥2.71 billion in asset impairment losses, up 68%, which it says is mostly inventory write-downs because of “the expanded inventory scale.” Credit losses tripled to ¥944 million, set aside “in line with the increase in trade receivables.”
And then there’s R&D. BYD’s research and development expenses fell 17% to ¥36.28 billion over nine months. A small part of that is accounting, since BYD capitalized more development costs on its balance sheet this year, but it’s still a notable drop for a company that has built its brand on vertical integration and in-house tech.
The balance sheet is where it gets uncomfortable
Here’s how a few key line items moved between Dec. 31, 2025 and Sept. 30, 2026:
Inventories: ¥221.58 billion, up 60% from ¥138.42 billion
Trade receivables: ¥56.47 billion, up 53% from ¥37.00 billion
Bills payable: ¥78.86 billion, up 251% from ¥22.46 billion
Cash plus trading securities: ¥71.72 billion, down 45% from ¥129.96 billion
BYD attributes both the inventory and receivables jumps “mainly” to the growth of its overseas auto business. That makes sense. Cars on ships, in ports and at foreign dealers sit on the books a lot longer than a car sold to a dealer in China.
The bills payable number stands out too. Those are short-term notes BYD hands suppliers instead of cash, and they more than tripled this year, which BYD explains as “the increase in settlement of bills.”
On the financing side, BYD cut its short-term bank borrowings roughly in half to ¥18.67 billion, but tripled its bonds outstanding to ¥14.99 billion and issued super short-term commercial paper.
To be fair, there are healthy signals in there as well. Operating cash flow for the first nine months was ¥54.47 billion, up 33%. Customer prepayments (contract liabilities) rose 81% to ¥92.95 billion, which points to strong orders. And cash spent on new factories and equipment fell 24% to ¥87.38 billion as BYD’s huge buildout slows down.
Electrek’s Take
On the surface, this is a good quarter for BYD. Profit is up 28%, revenue is growing again, and the export strategy is clearly working. BYD exporting more cars in a quarter than Tesla sells worldwide would have sounded absurd just three years ago.
But we don’t think it’s as clean as the headline number suggests.
BYD added over ¥83 billion worth of inventory in nine months while its sales were down 3.9% year-to-date. Receivables are up, supplier IOUs are up, and cash is way down. That’s what it looks like when you push a lot of cars into a long overseas pipeline and wait to get paid for them. It works as long as those cars sell at decent prices. If they don’t, those impairment charges we’re already seeing get a lot bigger.
And the domestic business isn’t getting easier. BYD is selling fewer cars in China than a year ago while it
now employs over 1 million people
. The cuts to R&D spending are a sign the company is looking for savings somewhere.
These are all signs of BYD’s business changing. It is going to take a while for it to settle, but I think they are currently in a great spot with the switch to their Blade battery 2.0 virtually over, and new capacity coming from Hungary, Thailand, and Brazil.

title: New Trek e-bike is first to get Bosch’s new motor with a major power upgrade
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 29 2026 - 5:00 am PT
Trek is getting a head start on the competition with the latest version of its Marlin+ electric mountain bike, becoming the first North American bicycle manufacturer to feature Bosch’s newly upgraded Active Line Plus motor.
brings more power, less weight, and a smaller footprint to Trek’s approachable electric mountain bike platform, helping make the Marlin+ 6 Gen 2 an even more compelling option for riders who want a capable e-bike without necessarily stepping up to a full-blown, high-performance electric mountain bike.
Trek Marlin+
has traditionally occupied an interesting Goldilocks position in the company’s electric mountain bike lineup. It’s designed to offer the versatility of a trail-capable eMTB while remaining practical enough for everyday recreational riding, commuting, and exploring gravel paths.
In other words, it’s the kind of electric mountain bike that doesn’t require you to be an actual mountain biker to enjoy it.
And the new Bosch motor seems particularly well suited to that mission.
More power without more weight
The biggest upgrade comes courtesy of Bosch’s new-generation Active Line Plus motor, which now offers up to 600 watts of power and 60 Nm of torque.
That’s paired with up to 340% pedal assistance, giving riders a substantial boost when accelerating or tackling climbs.
Despite the improved performance, Bosch has actually managed to shrink the motor. A redesigned two-stage gearbox reduces its volume by 17% while shaving approximately 1.1 lb (0.5 kg) from the previous generation.
The new motor weighs just around 6 lb (2.7 kg), helping manufacturers like Trek build lighter, more streamlined electric bicycles.
Bosch has also focused on improving the riding experience, with updated sensors and software designed to provide smoother, more natural-feeling assistance. Specially machined gears help make the motor virtually silent, while improved sealing and bearings are designed to withstand riding in all weather conditions.
The motor provides pedal assistance up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in the US, making it a Class 1 e-bike without a throttle. With a launch price of US $2,999, it’s also one of the more affordable options in Trek’s lineup.
For a bike like the Marlin+, that combination of moderate weight, smooth assistance, and plenty of usable power could be more important than chasing the enormous torque figures found on increasingly powerful premium eMTBs.
Bosch has more upgrades coming, too
The new motor isn’t the only addition to Bosch’s electric bicycle ecosystem this fall.
The company has also unveiled its new Intuvia 200 display, featuring a 2.4-inch grayscale screen designed to remain readable in bright sunlight. It’s joined by a redesigned LED Controller that’s approximately 65% smaller than the previous LED Remote, offering five thumb-operated buttons and a USB-C charging port.
Bosch is also expanding its theft protection technology with an updated ConnectModule that uses Bluetooth Low Energy alongside GPS and cellular connectivity to help locate stolen e-bikes within a few yards, including in areas where GPS reception is poor.
Perhaps most interesting for long-distance riders is the new PowerTube 720 battery, which packs 720 Wh of capacity into a compact package weighing just 8.6 lb (3.9 kg). Bosch claims up to 115 miles (185 km) of range under favorable conditions on compatible touring e-bikes.
Those additional products are part of Bosch’s broader smart system updates, though Trek hasn’t confirmed which, if any, will be included on the updated Marlin+.
With Bosch supplying drive systems to a large number of e-bike makers worldwide, these upgrades will likely find their way onto plenty of other electric bicycles in the coming months.
But for now, Trek gets the distinction of being first in North America to bring the new Active Line Plus motor to riders.

title: US customs frees detained Ethiopian solar cells as duty probe continues - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has released shipments of Toyo’s Ethiopian-made solar cells, while a separate US Department of Commerce inquiry into whether cells from Ethiopia circumvent duties on Chinese solar products continues.
Brian Publicover
29 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Toyo Co. said US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has released shipments of solar cells made at its factory in Ethiopia after reviewing supply chain documentation that included polysilicon and wafer sourcing.
The Japanese manufacturer did not say how many shipments were released, when, or under which authority they had been held. In a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Toyo said CBP issued detention notices on May 27 and May 28 for two cell shipments totaling about 0.094 MW, valued at $13,770, which CBP indicated were suspected of being associated with forced labor. Toyo has not said whether those are the shipments now released.
Toyo said it is pursuing certification under CBP’s Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism program and has expanded the import compliance program that supports its US manufacturing operations in Humble, Texas. Chief Executive Officer Takahiko Onozuka said customers need confidence in where their solar products come from and that the company intends to provide it across its full supply chain.
The US Department of Commerce
opened a country-wide circumvention inquiry
on July 17 into solar cells and modules completed in Ethiopia using Chinese components. It followed a request filed in May by
eight US manufacturers
naming Toyo and Origin Solar Manufacturing. A preliminary determination is due within 150 days of the inquiry’s start, putting it in mid-December unless extended. Toyo has
denied the allegations
, saying its Ethiopian cells use polysilicon from the United States and Malaysia.
Toyo operates 4 GW of tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) cell capacity in Hawassa, Ethiopia, and completed an expansion of its
Humble module plant
to 2 GW in October. It plans a
1.5 GW heterojunction cell line
at the Texas site, with pilot production targeted for the first quarter of 2028.
CBP has previously released detained solar imports after supply chain reviews, including

title: Researchers develop molecular locking strategy for organic solar cells - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Small-area organic solar cells featuring the molecular locking strategy achieved a power conversion efficiency of 20.4%, while larger-area modules reached a record active-area efficiency of 18.8%.
Patrick Jowett
29 Oct 2026
Research & Development
The interface diagram and performance of organic solar cells based on the molecular locking strategy
A group of Chinese scientists have developed a molecular locking strategy for organic solar cells.
The team’s strategy involves using a vacuum-deposited indium chloride (InClx) interlayer to stabilize the interface between the electrode and the hole-transport layer in organic solar cells.
The interlayer works by triggering ligand exchange, forming a robust, multidentate indium-oxygen-phosphorus (In-O-P) coordination network capable of densely and uniformly anchoring self-assembled monolayers (SAMs).
The scientists’ work is presented in the research paper
Chloride-mediated SAM locking via ligand-exchange reaction enables 18.8% active-area efficiency and stable organic solar modules
, available in the journal
The paper explains that while organic solar cells have reached impressive laboratory efficiencies, the difficulty in forming dense and stable SAM contacts on indium tin oxide surfaces is holding the technology back from forming commercially-viable modules. It adds that the In-O-P coordination network “increases the binding energy and promotes near-ideal monolayer coverage, even on large-area substrates with excellent batch-to-batch reproducibility”.
The research team developed small-scale organic solar cells featuring the molecular locking strategy that achieved a power conversion efficiency of 20.4%.
Professor Liu Quan, corresponding author of the study, added the team then scaled the technique to modules with an aperture area of 15.6 square centimeters. These larger-area devices achieved an active-area power conversion efficiency of 18.8%, which Liu said is a record.
Additional findings from the research paper reveal the devices retain more than 85% of their initial efficiency after 2,000 hours of maximum power point tracking under continuous operation at 25 C.
“Our approach provides a generalizable interfacial platform that overcomes the efficiency-stability-scalability trilemma,” the research paper concludes.
The research team consisted of scientists from the
Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology and Engineering
Chinese Academy of Sciences
. The work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the key program of the Ningbo Public Welfare Research Plan.

title: Ground-mounted solar used 2,798 hectares of land in Italy in 2025 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Ground-mounted photovoltaic (PV) installations accounted for 27% of Italy’s land consumption in 2025, according to the National System for Environmental Protection (SNPA).
Massimiliano Tripodo
29 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Ground-mounted solar installations occupied 2,798 hectares in Italy in 2025, up from 1,700 hectares in 2024, according to the new “Land Consumption, Urban Ecosystems and the State of the Territory” report by the Italian Institute for Environmental Protection and Research (ISPRA) and the National System for Environmental Protection (SNPA).
Annual additions have increased sharply over the past five years, from 75 hectares in 2021 to 263 hectares in 2022, 420 hectares in 2023, 1,700 hectares in 2024 and 2,798 hectares in 2025. The area occupied by new ground-mounted solar installations grew from 0.75 square kilometers to 28 square kilometers over that period.
Solar accounted for around 27% of the 10,243 hectares of land consumed in Italy in 2025, as total land consumption increased by 22.4% compared with 2024. After accounting for 746 hectares of restored land, net land consumption reached 9,497 hectares, the highest level since 2012.
Ground-mounted solar installations now occupy a total of 21,368 hectares, corresponding to around 12,570 MW of capacity. The southern region of Puglia has the largest installed area, at 4,764 hectares.
According to ISPRA, ground-mounted solar panels represent a significant share of reversible land consumption, unlike buildings and roads, which are classified as permanent land consumption. The report separately identifies 448.5 hectares of low-density solar installations, including many agrivoltaic projects, where modules cover less than half of the site area. These installations are not counted as consumed land.
Lazio, Sicily lead
In 2025, Lazio recorded 952 hectares of new ground-mounted solar installations out of 1,436 hectares of total land consumption, accounting for about two-thirds of the regional total. In Sicily, solar installations occupied 858.5 hectares out of 1,619 hectares. Together, the two regions accounted for almost 65% of the ground-mounted solar area added in Italy during the year.
They were followed by Piedmont, with 189 hectares; Puglia, with 145 hectares; and Sardinia, with 136 hectares.
The province of Viterbo recorded the largest annual increase in land consumption, at 969 hectares, more than twice the previous year’s figure. The municipalities with the largest increases were Tuscania, at 319 hectares, and Montalto di Castro, at 316 hectares, followed by Catania, at 198 hectares.
Excluding ground-mounted solar, the ranking changes, with Rome recording the largest increase at 74 hectares, followed by Foggia at 72 hectares, Cerignola at 53 hectares and Campagna at 51 hectares. Lazio also recorded Italy’s highest relative increase, equivalent to 1.01% of its existing artificial surface area.
The report states that, in municipalities covered by the European Union’s Nature Restoration Regulation, the loss of natural land in central and southern Italy and the islands is largely driven by large ground-mounted solar installations. In northern Italy, buildings, logistics facilities and construction sites are the main drivers.
Based on grid connection requests submitted to Italian transmission system operator Terna, projects totaling 10,263 MW with signed connection contracts could require more than 10,260 hectares of land over the next 18 to 24 months.
The estimate falls to around 9,750 hectares when 515 MW of advanced agrivoltaic projects funded under Italy’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan are excluded. A further 54,365 MW of projects have already received environmental approval.
According to ISPRA, standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS) could also increase the amount of solar capacity that can be developed, with implications for land consumption. More than 9,600 MW of standalone storage has contracted grid connections, while around 76,000 MW has received connection approval.
Storage could reduce renewable energy curtailment and connection costs in areas where the grid is congested, potentially enabling additional solar development. The report does not provide an estimate of the land area that battery installations themselves would occupy.
The report also references Italian Constitutional Court ruling No. 127/2026, which upheld restrictions on ground-mounted solar installations in agricultural areas and described soil as a scarce resource.
ISPRA estimates that Italy has up to 1,116 square km of potentially usable rooftop space, which could accommodate between 140 GW and 193 GW of solar capacity without consuming additional land.
ISPRA also identifies the expansion of data centers, driven by demand for digital infrastructure and cloud services, as an emerging source of land consumption. Data center development accounted for an additional 13 hectares in 2025, mainly in Lombardy. In the Milan area, 39% of new projects were located on previously undeveloped land.
Wind power installations occupied 118 hectares in 2025. Of this area, 58% consisted of unpaved yards, 41% of unpaved roads and just over 1% of sealed surfaces associated with turbine foundations.

title: Western Australia moves to legalize plug-in solar on German model - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
A draft technical standard out for consultation in Western Australia is based on Germany’s plug-in solar specification and would class balcony systems as ordinary electrical appliances.
Ev Foley
29 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Plug in solar
Residential
Western Australia is consulting on a draft technical standard that would class plug-in solar and battery systems as ordinary electrical appliances, opening them up to renters and apartment dwellers.
In an Australian first, Western Australia is on the path to legalizing plug-in solar panels and batteries based on German standards. The systems plug into a household wall outlet, offering clean energy for homes and apartments unable to benefit from rooftop solar installations, and can be moved when a resident changes address.
Western Australian Energy and Decarbonisation Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the benefits of cheap solar have been out of reach for anyone who doesn’t own their roof.
“I’m proud that our state is leading the nation on this issue – millions of European households already use these systems every day, and WA families should be able to do the same,” said Sanderson.
The state’s Department of Energy and Economic Diversification (DEED) and the Building and Energy Division of the Department of Local Government, Industry Regulation and Safety (LGIRS) are consulting on the proposed legalization pathway and a new technical standard.
The proposal would class plug-in systems as standard electrical appliances through a new Technical Bridging
Standard
(TBS). The draft is based on DIN VDE V 0126-95, the German technical specification for plug-in solar devices, with local changes for Australian plugs and wind loading. It would allow systems with a combined solar and battery output of up to 2 kW (DC) and inverters of up to 800 VA (AC).
The TBS does not propose to set an upper limit on plug-in battery storage capacity, but limits batteries to lithium iron phosphate or sodium-ion chemistries. It also allows only one plug-in system per household and none at homes that already have a fixed installation such as rooftop solar.
Heidi Lee Douglas, chief executive of Australian solar advocacy group Solar Citizens, said the group agrees it isn’t fair that the benefits of cheap solar are out of reach for anyone who doesn’t own their own roof.
“WA’s announcement starts a ‘race to the top’, and puts a rocket up the need for the federal government to announce a nationally coordinated approach for the release of this money-saving technology across Australia by July next year,” Douglas said.
“We support the Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen announcing a date for the legal safe sale of these money saving devices that are already legally and safely available in the United Kingdom, Germany and 10 states of America.”
“Plug-in solar and batteries are an anti-inflationary energy reform. They put downward pressure on household electricity bills, allow more Australians to use cheap solar power, and can reduce demand for expensive electricity during peak periods,” Douglas said.
According to the state’s plug-in solar and batteries consultation website, DEED and LGIRS will continue to work with safety experts, other states and territories, and the Australian government to support nationally consistent requirements for plug-in systems.
“For this reason, the final TBS is likely to have two separate parts, one each for product-specific requirements and another for installation requirements. This would make the TBS more consistent with AS/NZS technical documents,” the site says.
The departments will also work on other changes that might be needed to support renter access to the systems once they are available.

title: Spain solar PPA prices fall to €30.93/MWh as BESS gains ground - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Average prices for standalone solar power purchase agreements (PPAs) in Spain fell 7.7% year on year to €30.93 ($34.46)/MWh in the third quarter of 2026, while hybrid solar-and-storage contracts reached €48/MWh. Rising development costs and renewable energy curtailment are increasing interest in battery storage.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
29 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Average prices for solar power purchase agreements (PPAs) in Europe rose 0.4% between the second and third quarters of 2026, according to the latest data from LevelTen Energy. In the United States, prices increased by 4.9%.
LevelTen attributes the European increase to macroeconomic factors, including higher photovoltaic module prices and interest rates. Rising costs are increasing project development expenses and pushing PPA prices slightly higher to maintain project financial viability.
The consultancy has also changed how it presents its data. Rather than reporting prices directly in euros per megawatt-hour, it now uses an index based on prices eight quarters earlier, assigning the reference period a value of 1.00.
Under this methodology, the European solar PPA price index stood at 0.86 in the third quarter of 2026, equivalent to 86% of the price recorded in the third quarter of 2024, when the average reached €63.64/MWh. The wind PPA index stood at 0.99, indicating a much smaller decline over the same two-year period.
The quarterly increase therefore does not offset the cumulative fall in solar PPA prices since 2024. Instead, the data point to recent stabilization following a more pronounced period of decline.
Hybrid PPAs gain ground
Contracts combining renewable generation with battery energy storage systems (BESS) are gaining traction across Europe. LevelTen reported hybrid PPAs in nine European markets during the third quarter, with Spain and Portugal accounting for almost half of the hybrid contracts recorded across the region.
In Spain, the average price for standalone solar PPAs fell to €30.93/MWh, down 1.2% from the second quarter and 7.7% year on year. LevelTen considers prices to be approaching the lower limit at which projects can still secure financing.
Spanish hybrid PPAs, by contrast, reached an average of €48/MWh. The difference reflects the additional value storage can provide by shifting some generation to other hours, reducing exposure to periods of low electricity prices and limiting the economic impact of renewable energy curtailment.
Hybrid PPA prices did not move uniformly across Europe. In Spain, they rose 6.8% quarter on quarter, while in Germany they fell 12.7%. Adding storage does not, by itself, eliminate PPA price volatility; outcomes depend on the conditions in each market.
In Spain, growing renewable energy curtailment is an important factor. Curtailment reached 2.5 TWh in the first half of 2026, more than three times the volume recorded in the same period of 2025 and 50% above the total for all of 2024.
Against this backdrop, integrating BESS into renewable energy projects and their PPAs is emerging as one way to make generation more flexible and reduce exposure to periods of surplus supply.
Operational assets attract greater interest
For the first time, LevelTen’s report includes data on PPAs linked to operating assets, alongside contracts associated with new projects. Agreements involving operational installations currently account for about 40% of transactions recorded on the platform.
The trend is also reflected in offers, with PPAs linked to operating assets rising from less than 10% of the total to nearly 40% in the third quarter of 2026.
Operating assets carry less development risk because they avoid many of the uncertainties associated with permitting, construction and commissioning delays.
They can also offer buyers a faster route to adding renewable electricity to their portfolios. This may appeal particularly to buyers that prioritize energy availability and price over additionality — the contribution a new project makes to increasing renewable energy supply.
European PPA markets are therefore moving from a period of steep price declines toward one shaped by higher development costs, pressure on standalone projects and greater integration of storage. In Spain, where solar PPA prices are among Europe’s lowest and renewable energy curtailment is increasing, hybridization with BESS is playing a growing role in the economics of new projects.

title: US Navy warship power systems to get zero-trust shield to protect fleet from cyberattacks
content: The US Navy awarded a $23.13 million contract to South Carolina-based Integer Technologies to develop cybersecurity defenses for warship electrical power systems, helping naval platforms withstand cyberattacks without disrupting critical operations. The Department of War announced the contract on October 28, funding research into the Threat Resilient Integrated Defense for Enhanced Naval Technologies (TRIDENT) program. Integer Technologies will work with Florida State University and its Center for Advanced Power Systems to develop zero-trust security frameworks tailored to shipboard power networks. The six-year contract has a 36-month base period and a 36-month option period that begins 12 months after execution, with work expected to finish in October 2030. The Navy has obligated $10.13 million to fund the base period. Why shipboard power systems need cyber defenses Warship electrical networks do more than supply lights and routine onboard equipment. They distribute power to machinery, control systems, sensors, and other mission-critical equipment. On ships with integrated power systems, electricity can also support advanced weapons and high-power sensors. The Navy’s Office of Naval Research identifies secure control methods and resilient electrical distribution as important requirements for future naval power systems. A cyberattack targeting these networks could potentially interfere with monitoring or control functions, making it harder for crews to understand the system’s condition or respond to faults. Defending them requires more than protecting conventional IT networks because the digital systems involved interact directly with physical equipment. The challenge is maintaining cybersecurity without slowing the time-sensitive control processes needed to distribute electricity safely. Zero trust designed for warship power grids TRIDENT will investigate threat-informed zero-trust architecture (ZTA), a security model that does not automatically trust users, devices, or connections simply because they are already inside a network. Instead, access must be verified, permissions restricted, and system behavior monitored. Security controls can also separate connected systems so that a compromised component has fewer opportunities to affect other parts of the network. For shipboard power systems, however, these measures must account for low-latency requirements and the coexistence of legacy equipment with newer technologies. Some older systems may have limited security features or may not support modern authentication methods without substantial modification. The Navy’s research aims to help ships maintain awareness of their cyber and physical operating conditions, dynamically adjust their defenses, and continue functioning during adversarial attacks. In April 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and other federal agencies published guidance on adapting zero trust to operational technology. The guidance emphasizes that security measures must account for the reliability and safety requirements of systems that control physical processes. Research could help keep ships operating under attack Integer Technologies and its research partners will investigate ways to apply these principles to naval electrical networks while preserving system performance. The contract announcement does not identify specific ship classes scheduled to receive the technology or confirm that a deployable system has already been developed. The work is part of a bigger project to make naval systems more resilient to cyber interference. The Office of Naval Research’s cyber-resiliency program also focuses on protecting complex naval systems that combine legacy hardware, software, and interconnected controls. If the TRIDENT research produces effective solutions, the Navy could gain new methods for detecting suspicious activity, restricting unauthorized access, and preserving electrical-system performance during cyber incidents. In a time when warships are increasingly dependent on interconnected electrical and digital systems, the goal is to ensure that a cyberattack does not translate into a loss of critical ship functions.
