title: Audi tests mobile humanoid robots to sort parts in car factories
content: Audi is testing mobile humanoid robots developed by Agile Robots to automate parts sequencing at its facility in Germany. The proof of concept focuses on picking components from containers and arranging them in the correct order for subsequent assembly operations.The project brings together Audi, Agile Robots, Dassault Systèmes, and NVIDIA to explore the use of humanoid robots in automotive manufacturing. The initiative combines physical robot testing with virtual simulation, but it has not disclosed quantified performance results or a timeline for wider factory deployment.Humanoids automate sequencingAudi is testing mobile humanoid robots to automate parts sequencing at its Ingolstadt Production Lab in Germany. The proof of concept combines robotic manipulation, AI and virtual simulation to explore how robots can pick components from containers and arrange them in the correct order for vehicle assembly.Announced on October 21 at NVIDIA GTC Berlin, the project aims to automate a material-handling task that remains challenging for conventional industrial robots because component shapes, packaging, and positions vary.Audi’s material-supply operations involve around one million picks daily, with components required to reach assembly workstations in the correct order. This figure describes the scale of the existing workflow, not the performance achieved by the humanoid robots.The trial uses Agile One humanoids designed to combine human-height reach and dual-arm manipulation with the mobility of a wheeled base. This configuration allows the robots to operate within existing industrial environments without necessarily requiring factories to be redesigned around fixed robotic workstations.The robots are being tested at Audi’s Production Lab, where the company evaluates technologies for future manufacturing and logistics operations. The system is intended to retrieve components from material containers and place them in a predetermined sequence for subsequent assembly.“For decades, picking within the sequencing process has remained one of the toughest automation challenges in automotive logistics. Together with our partners, we are now exploring how AI-powered robotics can help solve this challenge and unlock a new level of productivity in our Audi factories,” said Gerd Walker, Board Member for Production and Logistics at AUDI AG, in a statement. Advances in factory automationHandling unsorted components presents several technical challenges. A robot must identify individual parts, determine how to grasp them, extract them without damaging them, and position them correctly. Flexible or semi-rigid components can be particularly difficult to handle because they may deform during manipulation.AI-powered perception and dual-arm coordination are intended to help Agile Robots’ systems address these challenges. The approach could extend automation to parts-handling tasks that are difficult to perform reliably using conventional systems designed for specific objects and carefully controlled environments. However, the announcement does not provide measured picking rates, error frequencies, or other performance results from the trial.The project also uses virtual simulation to evaluate the robots before deploying them in Audi’s logistics operations. Dassault Systèmes is creating a virtual twin of the logistics environment using its DELMIA application and 3DEXPERIENCE platform. The digital environment will allow engineers to assess whether a proposed robotic task is feasible and evaluate cycle times, ergonomics, and safety. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries provide additional capabilities for simulating physical environments and robot interactions.Testing these factors virtually can help engineers identify potential problems before conducting physical trials on the factory floor. It also provides a way to examine different operating conditions without repeatedly interrupting real production processes. The partners also plan to use AI-powered virtual assistance to support engineering workflows and speed up development and validation.The initiative is part of a broader automotive industry effort to use humanoid robots for logistics and manufacturing tasks. Its practical value will depend on whether the systems can consistently handle varied components, operate at useful production speeds, and work reliably within existing factory infrastructure.For now, the Audi project remains a proof of concept, with no confirmed timetable for factory-wide deployment.

title: Ultrafast imaging shows graphene electrons tunneling with 100% success
content: Scientists in Germany have observed electrons crossing an energy gap in graphene with a probability of up to 100%, revealing how intense electric fields can drive quantum transitions in real time.Researchers from the University of Regensburg, Philipps University of Marburg, and Forschungszentrum Jülich used a new imaging technique combining ultrafast lasers with electron microscopy to track the movement of electrons in the atomically thin material.The experiments captured a process known as Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions, in which electrons move between energy bands without occupying the forbidden energy states separating them.The findings could help scientists understand how electrons behave under intense electric fields and develop new ways to control electronic materials using light.Tracking electrons in real timeIn solids, electrons occupy specific ranges of energy called bands. These bands can be separated by energy gaps where electrons cannot normally exist.However, quantum mechanics allows electrons to move between bands through a process known as tunneling. The likelihood of such a transition depends on how quickly an electron approaches the energy gap.To observe the process, the researchers combined extremely short laser pulses with a photoemission momentum microscope.Unlike conventional microscopes, which produce enlarged images of physical objects, the instrument measures the energies and motion of electrons to map their distribution inside a material.The laser pulses generated strong, rapidly changing electric fields that accelerated electrons through graphene’s electronic energy structure.“If you want to know who has won a race, you have watch all participants,” said Vincent Eggers, the study’s first author.“Likewise, we must observe as many electrons as possible at one time to catch those that undergo a quantum mechanical transition while moving.”The measurements showed that electrons could cross the energy gap with a tunneling probability reaching 100% under the experimental conditions.The result demonstrates that transitions between separated energy states can become highly probable when electrons are driven rapidly enough.Light-driven quantum controlThe team used specially prepared graphene samples produced at Forschungszentrum Jülich.Graphene consists of a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal structure. Its electronic properties make it useful for investigating how electrons respond to external electric fields.For the experiments, the researchers used exceptionally pure samples, including rotated graphene structures that made the quantum dynamics easier to observe.“These precision experiments require material that is nearly perfect at the atomic level. This ensures that impurities do not obscure the delicate quantum dynamics of the electrons,” said Stefan Tautz of Forschungszentrum Jülich.The technique also allowed the researchers to examine how interactions between electrons and the crystal lattice disrupt their initially coordinated motion.Understanding these effects could help identify the physical limits of controlling electrons with rapidly oscillating light fields.Such control is being investigated as a possible route toward electronics that operate faster than devices relying on conventional voltage switching.The researchers said their approach could also be applied to other quantum materials, allowing scientists to investigate electronic behavior that has previously been difficult to observe directly.“Our experiment opens a panoramic window into the quantum world. Now, we can follow in real time how electrons move through the energy landscape of a material. And this is just the beginning,” said Giacomo Inzani of the University of Regensburg.The study appears in Nature.

title: Shape-shifting space tiles to assemble spacecraft in 2028 orbital test
content: Spacecraft could one day change their shape after reaching orbit, allowing operators to add capabilities without launching an entirely new vehicle. Rendezvous Robotics has raised $20 million to develop that technology, with its first orbital demonstration planned for 2028.The startup intends to launch seven independent spacecraft tiles that will join together in space. They will then separate and assemble into a different configuration, testing whether autonomous spacecraft can build and reshape larger structures without external robotic assistance.MaC Venture Capital and Toyota Ventures led the oversubscribed seed round. Rendezvous will use the funding to advance its spacecraft designs and prepare for flight demonstrations.Seven tiles will join in orbitRocket fairings dictate the dimensions of conventional spacecraft before they leave Earth. Engineers must fit every component within that envelope, limiting the size of equipment such as antennas and power systems.Rendezvous wants to move some of that construction work into orbit. Its spacecraft launch as individual tiles that maneuver independently before connecting with one another. The resulting structure can exceed the dimensions of any single module.Reconfiguration presents a further engineering challenge. The seven tiles must coordinate their movements and establish connections before separating and forming a new arrangement. The planned mission will test whether they can complete those operations autonomously in low Earth orbit.CEO Joe Landon believes the approach could eventually support spacecraft with megawatt-scale power generation. He also sees potential for much larger communications and sensing apertures. Those capabilities could support missions that face significant constraints under conventional spacecraft designs.MIT experiment goes commercialThe technology originated with TESSERAE, a modular self-assembly concept developed by Ariel Ekblaw at MIT. Ekblaw later advanced the research through the Aurelia Institute, which she founded, before co-founding Rendezvous Robotics.Earlier TESSERAE generations flew aboard Blue Origin’s New Shepard rocket and during two missions to the International Space Station (ISS). These experiments helped researchers investigate how the underlying concept behaves in microgravity.Ekblaw said the research aimed to rethink spacecraft construction itself. “What began as an experiment in self-assembly is now becoming a new way to build spacecraft in orbit,” she said.Rendezvous is developing larger tiles that operate independently. Ground demonstrations are testing their ability to move and align before connecting. The next phase must establish whether those mechanisms can perform reliably under spaceflight conditions.Two tests are approachingA parabolic flight campaign scheduled for November 2026 will examine electromagnetic actuation and tile mobility in microgravity. The company has reserved a rideshare launch for its orbital demonstration, which is scheduled no earlier than April 2028.Another milestone will take place aboard the ISS in December 2026. Researchers plan to assemble 32 fifth-generation TESSERAE tiles into a three-dimensional structure inside a controlled microgravity environment.That experiment will conclude the earlier TESSERAE research program as Rendezvous advances its free-flying spacecraft architecture. The two demonstrations address different challenges, with the ISS test examining assembly in a controlled setting and the 2028 mission targeting autonomous reconfiguration in open space.The new financing also includes significant participation from the University of Michigan Endowment. Astera, co-founded by Jed McCaleb, joined the round as a new investor. Existing backers Aurelia Foundry, ATX Venture Partners and Mana Ventures also participated.Rendezvous must now turn laboratory research into a system that works beyond controlled experiments. Its 2028 mission will test whether independent spacecraft can reliably connect and reorganize in orbit, a capability that could change how engineers design future space infrastructure.

title: 24,000-ton nuclear submarine launches 5,160-mile-range Bulava missile
content: Russia has test-fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from a submerged nuclear-powered submarine in the Sea of Okhotsk. The missile headed toward a designated test range in Russia’s Arkhangelsk region, according to the Russian Defense Ministry.The launch took place on October 28 as part of a scheduled combat training exercise. The submarine, Generalissimo Suvorov, belongs to Russia’s Pacific Fleet and carries weapons designed for the country’s sea-based nuclear deterrent.The test involved launching a strategic missile from beneath the surface, with the submarine operating in the Russian Far East. Its target lay thousands of miles away in northwestern Russia.Testing the Bulava missileThe Russian Defense Ministry said the crew launched the Bulava missile toward the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region. The ministry did not disclose the missile’s flight time or provide detailed results from the test.Launching a ballistic missile from underwater requires careful coordination between the submarine and its weapon systems. The crew must follow the launch sequence while the vessel remains submerged, allowing it to fire without surfacing first.That capability is central to the role of ballistic missile submarines. Their ability to operate at sea gives them greater flexibility than fixed land-based launch sites.The Bulava serves as the primary weapon aboard Russia’s Borei-class strategic submarines. These missiles give the Russian Navy a sea-based option for delivering nuclear weapons as part of the country’s broader deterrent.Inside the Borei-A submarineThe Generalissimo Suvorov, also known as K-553, belongs to the Project 955A Borei-A class. Russia developed these nuclear-powered submarines to carry strategic missiles while improving on earlier submarine designs.The Generalissimo Suvorov measures around 558 feet long and displaces approximately 14,720 metric tons on the surface. Its submerged displacement rises to about 24,000 metric tons. Powered by a nuclear reactor, the Borei-A class submarine can reach speeds of around 15 knots on the surface and up to 29 knots underwater. It also carries 16 Bulava intercontinental ballistic missiles.The vessel incorporates updated equipment and technical systems. Its design also aims to reduce detectable physical signatures and improve protection during operations.Rubin Central Design Bureau for Marine Engineering, based in St. Petersburg, designed the submarine. Construction began at the Sevmash shipyard on December 26, 2014, and the Russian Navy commissioned the vessel in 2022.The submarine initially served with Russia’s Northern Fleet. It transferred to the Pacific Fleet in October 2023 and arrived at its permanent base in Kamchatka.That move placed the vessel within Russia’s Pacific submarine force, which operates across the country’s eastern maritime approaches. The Sea of Okhotsk provides an important operating area for Russian naval forces based in the region.Russia’s sea-based nuclear forceBorei and Borei-A class submarines carry 16 Bulava intercontinental ballistic missiles, according to the Russian report. Nuclear propulsion allows them to remain at sea for extended periods without the refueling needs of conventional submarines.The combination of underwater launch capability and long-range missiles makes these vessels an important part of Russia’s strategic arsenal. Submarines can operate away from fixed launch facilities, complicating efforts to track their movements.The latest test confirms that the Generalissimo Suvorov continues to participate in Russia’s combat training program. However, the ministry released few details about the missile’s performance or the exercise’s specific objectives.The launch also provides no indication of changes to the Bulava’s capabilities. Its significance lies in demonstrating the submarine’s continued role in training with one of Russia’s principal sea-based nuclear weapons.

title: 6,000-ton frigate that can launch missiles offered to US Navy
content: A London-based defense manufacturer has offered its powerful Arrowhead 140 frigates to the U.S. Navy. Developed by Babcock, these vessels could form a proposed fleet of the U.S. Navy.The Arrowhead 140 is a general-purpose frigate and its design is derived from Denmark’s Iver Huitfeldt-class warships. It was selected as the foundation of Britain’s five-ship Type 31 programme, which is being built at Babcock’s Rosyth shipyard in Scotland. The design has also been selected for export programmes in Poland and Indonesia, giving it a growing international footprint.Frigate integrates diesel propulsion, offers speeds exceeding 28 knots In its baseline configuration, the Arrowhead 140 is approximately 452-feet (138 metres long), has a beam of around 20 metres and displaces approximately 5,700-6,000 tons. It uses a conventional combined diesel-and-diesel propulsion system and is capable of speeds exceeding 28 knots.Babcock does not operate a shipyard in the United States, making an American industrial partner central to its proposal. Huntington Ingalls Industries is expected to be a potential partner because of its experience building warships for the U.S. Navy and its established industrial infrastructure.The two companies already have working relationships in the submarine sector, including activities associated with components supporting American and British nuclear-powered submarine programmes. These existing connections could provide a foundation for broader cooperation in surface shipbuilding.For the U.S., the Arrowhead 140 represents a potential route to broadening its frigate options and reducing dependence on lengthy new-design development. If the ship can be adapted economically and produced at scale, it could help the Navy expand its surface fleet while preserving larger combatants for more demanding missions.Recently, Babcock welcomed suppliers, industry partners and Indonesian and UK Government stakeholders to London for a UK-Indonesia Supplier Day, highlighting opportunities for British businesses to support the delivery of Indonesia’s ambitious Maritime Partnership Programme (MPP). The event reinforces our commitment to building a strong, collaborative supply chain that delivers economic growth, innovation and long-term maritime capability in both nations.“Strong partnerships are essential to delivering growth, innovation and capability. This Supplier Day demonstrates the momentum behind the Maritime Partnership Programme and our commitment to ensuring UK industry plays a meaningful role in its success,” said Harry Holt, Group CEO, Babcock. “The programme is about more than ships. It is about building long-term industrial partnerships, developing skills, supporting technology transfer and creating economic opportunities across both nations. By bringing together suppliers, industry leaders and government stakeholders, we are helping create the foundations for lasting collaboration and sustainable growth.”American frigate requirement has gained urgencyThe American frigate requirement has gained urgency following the cancellation of the Constellation-class programme. Originally intended to provide a modern, multi-mission frigate based on the European FREMM design, the programme encountered significant delays and escalating costs as the ship was extensively modified to meet U.S. Navy requirements.The experience highlighted a central problem in warship procurement; selecting an existing design does not necessarily guarantee faster or cheaper construction if the customer substantially changes its architecture.The U.S. Navy could use a frigate of Arrowhead 140 type for maritime security, escort operations, independent deployments and other missions that do not always require its more expensive destroyers. Such a division of responsibilities could allow Arleigh Burke-class destroyers to concentrate on demanding tasks such as area air defence, missile defence and long-range strike operations.

title: Fire at US nuclear site triggers emergency, airspace restrictions
content: A fire at the US Department of Energy’s Savannah River Site in South Carolina prompted officials to declare a Site Area Emergency on Wednesday evening, October 28, with local media reporting a radiological release and restrictions on nearby air traffic.The emergency was declared at 5:39 p.m. local time at the federal nuclear facility near Aiken, South Carolina, according to updates posted on the site’s official X account.Officials confirmed that the fire broke out at Savannah River National Laboratory, which operates within the nuclear complex. The blaze has since been extinguished.Local broadcaster WRDW/WAGT reported that an emergency dispatch described an “unfiltered ground-level radiological release” associated with the incident.However, Savannah River Site officials said no contamination had been reported outside the affected facility, and there was no indication of consequences beyond the site’s boundaries.According to WRDW/WAGT, the fire was confined to a single room at the laboratory. Sources told the broadcaster that the incident began shortly after 5 p.m.The cause of the fire and whether anyone was injured have not been disclosed.Emergency response activatedSavannah River Site officials said the incident triggered emergency response activities at the Department of Energy facility. “An event is in progress that has triggered emergency response activities at the Department of Energy’s Savannah River Site,” officials said in an initial notification.According to local media reports, employees in Area A, where the laboratory is located, were instructed to shelter in place for approximately 30 minutes.A fire was reported at the Savannah River National Laboratory but has since been extinguished. No contamination has been reported outside the affected facility.— Savannah River Site (@SRSNews) October 28, 2026Some employees were subsequently allowed to leave, although access to the affected area remained restricted. Officials also closed barricades at site entrances to incoming traffic. Employees not involved in emergency response or shutdown operations were instructed to shelter as a precaution.Rail, river, and air traffic near the facility were restricted, according to a statement from site officials. The Federal Aviation Administration imposed a temporary flight restriction covering a 15-nautical-mile radius around the facility, extending up to 10,000 feet above sea level, according to local media reports.The restriction was reportedly scheduled to remain in place until midnight Thursday. However, Highway 125 remained open, with officials confirming that the road had not been closed.Savannah River Site officials said they were directing the emergency response and had notified appropriate state and local government agencies.Nuclear complex’s Cold War historyThe Savannah River Site covers approximately 310 square miles across Aiken, Barnwell, and Allendale counties in South Carolina.Established in the early 1950s during the Cold War, the facility originally produced materials for nuclear weapons, including plutonium-239 and tritium.Today, the complex handles radioactive waste, spent nuclear fuel, and excess plutonium. It also continues tritium operations supporting the country’s nuclear deterrent. Savannah River National Laboratory conducts research involving nuclear materials, environmental management, energy technologies, and national security.Officials said additional information would be released through the site’s public information staff as it becomes available.

title: Battery manufacturing breakthrough cuts formation time by 60%
content: Researchers at Cornell University have developed a method that cuts a critical stage of lithium-ion battery manufacturing by up to 60%, potentially saving large factories as much as $100 million in production costs.Developed in collaboration with New York-based battery company Charge CCCV (C4V), the approach uses real-time measurements to monitor chemical changes inside batteries during their initial charging and discharging cycles.The process, known as battery formation, creates protective layers inside a battery that influence its performance and lifespan. It is among the most expensive and time-consuming stages of lithium-ion cell production.According to the researchers, formation accounts for roughly one-third of battery production costs and occupies about a quarter of a manufacturing facility’s floor space.By accelerating this stage, manufacturers could reduce production bottlenecks, free up factory space and lower overall electricity consumption by an estimated 10% to 15%.Monitoring batteries in real timeBattery formation typically involves repeated charging and discharging cycles under carefully controlled conditions. These cycles help establish protective interfaces between the electrodes and electrolyte.However, manufacturers have limited visibility into how these layers develop during the process. Determining whether a particular formation protocol will maintain long-term battery performance can require months or years of testing.“Evaluating formation processes is typically very trial and error,” said Vibha Kalra, a professor of chemical engineering at Cornell and the study’s principal investigator.“It can take months to years to effectively evaluate long-term performance because you’re letting the battery run for thousands of cycles.”To address this limitation, the researchers combined two diagnostic techniques that observe batteries while they operate.Operando Raman spectroscopy tracks chemical changes occurring at electrode surfaces, while electrochemical impedance spectroscopy measures changes in electrical resistance.Together, the techniques allowed researchers to monitor the development of protective layers and identify when important chemical and electrical properties stabilized.The team found that slower charging helped create more uniform, inorganic-rich protective layers, which are important for maintaining stable battery performance.However, the discharge stage could be accelerated without compromising the formation process.Crucially, key resistance measurements stabilized after just 1.5 cycles, providing an early indication of how the protective interfaces were developing.Factory tests show savingsUsing these findings, the researchers developed two accelerated formation protocols and tested them at C4V’s battery manufacturing facility in Binghamton, New York.Both protocols maintained performance comparable to the company’s conventional process while reducing formation time by approximately 60%.The results suggest that manufacturers could shorten a costly production stage without sacrificing the battery performance measured during testing.“This work demonstrates why strong partnerships between research institutions and cell manufacturers are so important for moving the battery industry forward,” said Shalabh Gupta, system engineering manager at C4V.Formation also accounts for approximately one-quarter of a battery factory’s electricity consumption.Gupta estimated that reducing formation time by half or more could lower overall factory electricity use by 10% to 15%.For large-scale operations producing more than 10 gigawatt-hours of batteries annually, the approach could deliver up to $100 million in reduced formation costs.However, those savings remain projections rather than independently verified commercial results.The research was supported through the National Science Foundation’s Energy Storage Engine in Upstate New York, which brings together universities and industry partners to advance battery technology.The findings could help manufacturers increase battery production capacity without proportionally expanding factory space or energy consumption.The findings were published in the journal Energy Storage Materials.

title: US Army rocket switches targets midflight to hit moving threats
content: Lockheed Martin has demonstrated a new way to redirect a rocket after launch, potentially giving U.S. Army units greater control over precision strikes. The test showed that an existing Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System (GMLRS) rocket could change targets during flight and destroy a moving target.The demonstration took place at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. Lockheed Martin worked with the U.S. Army to integrate a communications link and guidance system into the rocket’s existing architecture. The approach could help the Army adapt its precision fires capabilities without requiring a fundamental redesign of the weapon.Redirecting rockets in flightThe test began with a GMLRS rocket launched from a High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS). After launch, the team used Lockheed Martin’s Strigo datalink and Remote Interceptor Guidance-360 (RIG-360) system to send updated targeting information to the rocket.The rocket then adjusted its target assignment and successfully struck a moving target. The result demonstrated how communication between a weapon and external targeting systems could influence an engagement after the rocket leaves its launcher.Conventional rocket artillery missions rely heavily on targeting information established before firing. Updating that information during flight introduces another layer of flexibility, particularly when a target changes position or battlefield conditions shift.Lockheed Martin funded the integration work internally. The demonstration focused on connecting existing technologies rather than developing an entirely new rocket. That distinction could make the approach relevant to weapons already in the Army’s inventory.Connected kill chainThe test also points to a broader shift in how the Army could coordinate precision strikes. Networked targeting allows information from sensors and other battlefield assets to reach weapon systems, potentially helping commanders respond to changing threats.A moving target presents a different challenge from a stationary aim point. Its position can change between launch and impact, making updated information valuable during an engagement. An in-flight targeting update could give commanders another option when an original firing plan no longer matches battlefield conditions.The capability does not eliminate the need for accurate targeting data or reliable communications. Its practical value will depend on how effectively the systems exchange information under operational conditions. Nevertheless, the successful demonstration provides evidence that existing rocket artillery can support more dynamic targeting methods.Lockheed Martin Advanced Programs Vice President Randy Crites said the integration brings together established company technologies to give troops greater flexibility. He also emphasized the importance of integrating proven systems to help commanders respond to complex battlefield situations.Future missiles could benefitThe same integration package could extend beyond the standard GMLRS. Lockheed Martin identified Extended Range GMLRS and the Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) as potential applications for the technology.Extended Range GMLRS is designed to reach targets beyond the standard rocket’s range. PrSM is a next-generation surface-to-surface missile developed for the Army’s HIMARS and M270 launcher platforms. Applying similar networking capabilities to these weapons could expand the options available for precision engagements.However, the demonstration does not establish that every compatible weapon can already receive midflight target updates. Each application would require appropriate integration and testing before operational use.The central engineering challenge is connecting weapons to a wider targeting network without replacing their underlying designs. If further testing validates the approach, the Army could gain more flexibility from its existing launchers and munitions while preparing future precision fires systems for increasingly mobile battlefield threats.

title: Sodium batteries target 3 GWh of storage with 15,000 charge cycles
content: China’s largest battery maker, CATL, is likely to expand Its Sodium energy storage system network in Europe over the next five years as it entered into an agreement with a German counterpart.A memorandum of understanding (MOU) was signed Monday between CATL and German energy storage solutions provider, Intilion, to install 3 GWh of sodium-ion energy storage systems in Europe by 2031. Under the latest agreement, these battery systems for grid-scale, commercial, and industrial applications would expand into the German, Swiss, and Austrian markets.Robust alternative in harsh wintersSince 2022, the companies have deployed more than 30 energy storage projects in Germany, including lithium-ion batteries. Going forward, CATL aims to strengthen its existing project partnership with Intilion while scaling up adoption of new battery technologies this year.Tener Sodium, the world’s first field-validated sodium-ion energy storage solution, which is expected to enter the European market this year, was launched by the Chinese Energy company over four years ago in June.Sodium-ion batteries are viewed as a potential alternative because they maintain stronger performance in cold conditions. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, sodium-ion systems use sodium, a more abundant raw material than lithium. This could help diversify battery supply chains and reduce exposure to fluctuations in lithium prices. Their ability to operate in freezing conditions also makes them a potential fit for renewable energy storage, where reliable power delivery is essential.“Built for Europe’s harsh winter climates, CATL TENER delivers over 15,000 charge cycles across a 25-year operational lifespan while maintaining high power discharge even at -20°C (-4 degrees Fahrenheit). This level of reliability helps stabilize local grids and strengthen regional power security,” said CATL in a social media post. Swappable packsThese sodium-ion battery solutions have been built with dimensions compatible with lithium-ion batteries, the company said, offering flexibility to choose between these battery technologies, safeguarding the users against the global lithium price volatility.In June this year, CATL unveiled a new battery pack architecture that allows sodium-ion and lithium-ion batteries to be used inside the same enclosure, a move aimed at accelerating sodium-ion deployment in electric vehicles, battery-swapping networks, and energy storage systems.The announcement of the partnership comes as Europe’s energy storage market expands rapidly. According to South Korean market research firm SNE Research, European lithium-ion energy storage battery shipments reached 72.7 GWh in the first half of 2026, marking a year-on-year rise of 74 percent.Earlier in July 2026, the Chinese company signed an agreement with European energy integrator Alfen N.V. to deploy sodium-ion energy storage systems in Western Europe, including the Netherlands. The planned deployment capacity was 5 gigawatt-hours and would begin in 2027.The company also signed a 2 GWh cooperation agreement with Eastern European renewable energy company Solarpro in the same month.The latest announcements suggest China’s sodium-ion battery sector is moving beyond laboratory-scale development and into large-scale commercial deployment. With standardized pack designs, longer lifetimes, and expanding material production, manufacturers are positioning sodium-ion batteries as a complementary technology to lithium-ion systems rather than a direct replacement.

title: 1.5 GPa spider silk inspires new push for sustainable textile fibers
content: Spider silk can withstand a pulling force equivalent to 150 newtons per square millimeter of its cross-sectional area before breaking.They are investigating ways to produce spider silk artificially because spiders produce much less silk per animal.The key challenge is turning liquid silk protein in spiders’ specialized glands into an actual fiber.Strength like steelSpider silk is a biomaterial produced by these arachnids, and it is mostly in the form of threadlike fiber with high elasticity and strength comparable to steel.The interesting thing about this silk is that it comes in many forms, each with its own purpose. While thin threads are the most familiar form, which the spiders use to make webs, there are a few other forms as well that this animal uses – sometimes to catch a prey or to protect eggs, or to use it as a safety rope.Among its many properties, spider silk’s tensile strength is quite intriguing, reaching up to 1.5 billion pascals (GPa). That means it can withstand a pulling force equivalent to 150 newtons per square millimeter of its cross-sectional area before breaking. This is comparable to high-grade steel.Due to their tensile strength, toughness, light weight, and biodegradability, they have a potential for their usage, especially in the textile industry. Researchers are investigating ways to produce it artificially because spiders produce much less silk per animal, and they can’t be raised in large numbers like silkworms because they are cannibalistic.Scaling up is challengingUniversity of North Carolina (UNC) ‘s Sarah Stellwagen, who studies silk from arthropods (insects and arachnids) at the material and genetic levels, said in an interview that the challenge is turning liquid silk protein in spiders’ specialized glands into an actual fiber.“Researchers have made plenty of protein soup, as a spider does, but unlike spiders, they haven’t been able to spin that protein into solid threads at a scale that is relevant for the public,” said Stellwagen, who is an assistant professor in the Department of Biological Sciences at UNC Charlotte.The spider does this by passing the fluid from its gland through a narrow duct, changing its chemical environment and assembling it into a tightly packed structure called a beta-sheet. The fiber then emerges through its spinnerets in the solid form.However, there has been some progress as well. Researchers at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (SLU) have shown that protein can be produced in larger quantities and more efficiently, which can also reduce production costs. Researchers Anna Rising and Benjamin Schmuck, who earlier this year received a grant of EUR 200,000 from H&M Foundation, are now working to produce fibers and yarn from protein for textile tests.The group is also exploring the fiber’s use for medical purposes.“The award (grant and support program) gives us the opportunity to take the next step: do more trials, improve the manufacturing process, and produce enough material to test yarn and textiles,” says Anna Rising, professor at the Department of Animal Biosciences.Earlier research from King’s College London and San Diego State University (SDSU) in California has decoded the “molecular stickers” that make spider silk stronger than steel and tougher than Kevlar.

title: US firm unveils synthetic modular kits for customizable AI, drone hubs
content: What if you could build an office, security checkpoint, or robotics facility using Lego-like blocks? The structure could be assembled near where it is needed, expanded as requirements grow, and even dismantled and moved to another location.Two U.S. companies are working to turn that idea into reality. Florida-based Tesseract Ventures Tuesday announced an initiative to develop modular technology-enabled infrastructure in partnership with Kentucky-based Lok-N-Blok that can be rapidly deployed and customized for different applications.The infrastructure, called Tesseract Synthetic Brick Technology Kits, will use Lok-N-Blok’s modular building components, which resemble Lego-like blocks.​Rather than adding technology to conventional buildings or shipping containers, the kits are designed with the technology built into the structure from the beginning, the company said in a statement.Tailored to needs​According to the company, the systems can be digitally designed, packaged for transport, assembled near the deployment site, expanded as requirements change, and dismantled and redeployed elsewhere.​To meet the customer’s needs, Tesseract will tailor the finished solutions, read the statement. Depending on the application, the kits could include sensors, cameras, communications equipment, drone storage and launch systems, robotic fabrication equipment, and other integrated technologies.​”We see an opportunity to rethink the relationship between infrastructure and technology,” said John Boucard, Founder and CEO of Tesseract Ventures. “Instead of putting our technology inside a box that was designed for something else, Tesseract Synthetic Brick Technology Kits allow us to design the structure around the mission.”​Company officials said the kits can start as small installations using standardized building blocks and technology modules before expanding into larger operational environments.​”Lok-N-Blok was created around the idea that construction could become more modular, efficient, and adaptable,” said John Lewis, CEO of Lok-N-Blok.“Tesseract brings a powerful technology layer to that idea. Together, we have an opportunity to explore how modular construction can become the foundation for intelligent, rapidly deployable operational environments,” he added.Reusable components to fit different roles​Beyond rapid deployment, the companies are positioning reusability as another key advantage. Standardized technology components can be reused to create different configurations without redesigning an entire system for every deployment.​The partnership could also enable Tesseract to develop reusable technology packages, such as Access & Security, Smart Space, Drone Operations, Communications, Sensor, and Forge Fabrication kits, that can be incorporated into different structural configurations.​Initially, the companies expect the technology kits to serve four key markets: defense, construction, critical infrastructure, and agriculture, the statement read.​In defense, the systems could support drone operations, forward command centers, communications nodes, sensor hubs, and mobile fabrication capabilities. Construction applications include project command centers, secure workspaces, guard stations, and autonomous drone inspection stations.​For critical infrastructure, the kits could be used as remote operations centers, emergency-response facilities, utility inspection hubs, and communications nodes. In agriculture, the systems are envisioned as field operations centers, drone stations, equipment hubs, and distributed farm intelligence facilities.​

title: Spy drone integrated with grenades can conduct long-range strikes
content: A German company has made upgradation to its long range drone. Called Reliant, the drone’s upgraded version offers increased payload capacity, broader mission flexibility. Developed by Quantum Systems, the latest generation of Reliant featured a hybrid-electric power unit and increases the system’s payload capacity to up to 9 kg, enabling a much broader range of missions.Depending on operational requirements, Reliant can now carry electro-optical sensors, laser-target designators, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), SIGINT and electronic warfare payloads, as well as SATCOM, relay and other mission-specific capabilities. Drone offers impressive range, and long-range endurance“Reliant’s upgrades are the result of continuous feedback from military users and partners, and our answer to enhance long-range capabilities for NATO, Europe and our allies,” said Martin Karkour, Chief Revenue Officer at Quantum Systems. “We can now offer a truly unique capability, with a minimal logistical footprint, payload superpower and impressive range and endurance – completely built on a resilient supply chain. We are very proud of that.”Beyond the platform itself, Reliant is fully integrated into the MOSAIC UXS software platform, making it interoperable with other unmanned systems in multi-domain operations. Together with operator workstations, training, sustainment and lifecycle support, Quantum Systems delivers a complete long-range unmanned capability rather than a standalone aircraft, according to a press release. Reliant also completes Quantum Systems’ Family of Aerial Systems, complementing the short-range Twister and the mid-range Vector AI platforms. Quantum Systems UAS solutions are already in service with a range of NATO and allied armed forces, notably with the German Armed Forces and the Armed Forces of Ukraine, as per the release.Reliant drone will now compete for major global contractsReliant is built around a secure European supply chain and supported by Quantum Systems’ growing industrial base, providing customers with a system without any Chinese components or ITAR restrictions. Designed around a fully European supply chain and minimal logistical footprint, Reliant will now compete for major global contracts.The MOSAIC UXS software ecosystem’s integration is intended to improve interoperability between RELIANT and other unmanned platforms, supporting coordinated operations across multiple domains. Quantum Systems also offers operator workstations, training, sustainment and lifecycle support as part of a broader capability package.The approach reflects a wider shift in defence technology, where the effectiveness of unmanned aircraft increasingly depends not only on their flight performance but also on their ability to exchange information and operate alongside other systems.This expanded payload flexibility could make RELIANT suitable for a broader range of defence and security applications, including persistent surveillance, reconnaissance, communications support and electronic intelligence gathering.Despite its increased capabilities, RELIANT retains an emphasis on compact logistics and ease of deployment. The aircraft can be assembled by a two-person team and operated by a single operator, according to the manufacturer.The upgrade comes amid growing interest in unmanned systems that can deliver flexible surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities without requiring extensive infrastructure. Its increased payload capacity, hybrid-electric propulsion and integration with MOSAIC UXS represent a broader effort to combine platform performance with networked, software-enabled operations.

title: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon AI finds 88.2% of security flaws
content: Google has introduced Gemini 4 Carbon, a new artificial intelligence model designed to identify software vulnerabilities, generate security patches, and handle complex engineering tasks that can take days to complete.The model achieved an 88.2% score on SEC-bench Pro, a cybersecurity benchmark that tests an AI system’s ability to identify vulnerabilities in real-world software. It also scored 71% on CWE-bench for fixing security flaws and 54.8% on ExploitGym for validating whether vulnerabilities can be exploited.Google says the results place Carbon ahead of competing models across all three cybersecurity benchmarks.The announcement comes just two weeks after the launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Google’s previous frontier model. Carbon builds on that release with improvements in coding, reasoning, cybersecurity, and autonomous task execution.Unlike conventional AI assistants that respond to individual prompts, Carbon is designed to carry out extended workflows involving multiple steps, tools, and decisions.Google said its internal teams have observed the model working for days on complex engineering problems, including identifying the causes of software bugs and developing patches across large codebases.However, these extended operations were reported by Google and have not been independently verified.Stronger security and codingCarbon’s cybersecurity capabilities cover three major stages of software security: finding vulnerabilities, determining whether they pose a genuine risk, and developing fixes.On SEC-bench Pro, the model achieved 88.2%, while its 54.8% ExploitGym score reflects its ability to validate security vulnerabilities through controlled exploitation tests.Introducing Gemini 4 Carbon, our latest frontier model.Carbon delivers improved performance across domains — ranking #1 on v5.0 of the @ArtificialAnlys Intelligence Index and sets a new state-of-the-art in cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities.It’s rolling out starting… pic.twitter.com/oQrHzxvMSo— Google (@Google) October 28, 2026Its 71% CWE-bench result measures performance in generating working patches that address underlying software weaknesses.Google also reported that Carbon more than doubled Argon’s success rate in generating secure code during internal testing.The Chrome team found that Carbon performed more than 10 times better than a competing frontier model in producing high-quality security patches, according to Google. The company did not identify the competing model.Beyond cybersecurity, Carbon ranked first on version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, scoring 59.It also improved its WebDev Arena score by 89 Elo points, reaching 1,768 and placing fourth on the leaderboard.Google said the improvements extend to scientific tasks, multimodal understanding, and full-stack web development.Safety improvements and rolloutGoogle has also introduced additional safeguards intended to reduce unreliable behavior during extended AI workflows.In internal testing, Carbon reduced unsupported claims by approximately half compared with Argon. High-severity misalignment alerts fell by nearly 80% in live coding environments involving Google’s teams.The company also reported a 0% attack success rate on Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark, compared with 0.7% for Argon.These results reflect performance under specific testing conditions and do not establish that the model is immune to manipulation.Google is initially restricting Carbon to a selected group of cybersecurity defenders, with additional trusted partners gaining access through its Fairwind Program.The company is also participating in the US government’s voluntary pre-release model testing process.Broader availability for developers, businesses, and consumers is planned, although Google has not announced a specific release date.Carbon will carry the same introductory pricing as Argon: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Cached input tokens will receive a 95% discount.The phased rollout reflects the dual-use nature of advanced cybersecurity AI, which can help defenders identify weaknesses but may also provide capabilities that could be misused.

title: Simple squeeze changes magnetism in exotic materials, US team finds
content: Scientists in the U.S. have found a new way to alter the magnetic behavior of tiny crystals after discovering that squeezing them between two metal plates can change their properties.The experiments were carried out at the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) in Tennessee. To test the method, the team examined two materials from an emerging class of magnets known as altermagnets.Altermagnets are a third fundamental class of magnetic materials that combine traits of both ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. They reportedly have zero net magnetization like antiferromagnets, and exhibit strong momentum-dependent spin polarization and band splitting like ferromagnets.Lab tests showed that mechanical pressure could change the materials’ magnetic domains and electron flow. This, according to the team, could allow better control of magnetism in future electronic devices. Pressure alters magnetismFor the experiments, the research team used tiny crystals of manganese telluride (MnTe) and iron sulfide (FeS). They then placed the crystals between two titanium plates and applied mechanical pressure. They then examined the materials using neutron diffraction at ORNL’s Spallation Neutron Source (SNS), which produces some of the world’s most intense pulsed neutron beams. The facility uses an accelerator to fire short proton pulses at a liquid mercury target. This releases neutrons that scientists use to study materials and their properties. It revealed how pressure affected the magnetic structure of the crystals.According to ORNL, even a small mechanical squeeze was enough to change the populations of these domains. The researchers also saw changes in an electrical response known as the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) which is associated with the magnetic properties of the materials.The anomalous Hall effect (AHE) occurs when an electric current flows through a magnetic material and creates a voltage across it. Unlike the ordinary Hall effect, it is driven by the material’s internal magnetic properties rather than an external magnetic field.Applications in electronicsThe results suggest that pressure can provide a simple way to control magnetism and electron flow in altermagnets. The researchers reported them in two separate studies. Feng Ye, PhD, an ORNL neutron scientist and co-author of both studies, stressed the role of neutron scattering in understanding these magnetic changes. “What’s exciting is that one creative experimental idea, a small mechanical squeeze between two plates, can reveal entirely new magnetic behavior and push the field forward,” Ye pointed out in a press release.Ye added that the findings could be particularly important for an emerging field known as spintronics, also known as spin electronics. The field uses the spin of electronics, rather than just their electric charge, to store and process information. The technology could lead to faster, and more energy-efficient electronic devices, such as advanced memory and computing systems. “By controlling the magnetic domains, we can directly influence the transport behavior, and that opens the door to exploring these materials for spintronic technologies,” Pengcheng Dai, PhD, a researcher at Rice University and former neutron scientist at ORNL, said. The findings have been published in the journals Physical Review X and Advanced Materials.

title: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro revives its iconic glowing logo
content: Apple has brought touchscreen controls to the MacBook Pro for the first time, pairing the long-awaited feature with a tandem OLED display and its new M5 Pro and M5 Max processors. The redesigned 14-inch and 16-inch laptops also weigh less than their predecessors and promise up to 24 hours of battery life.The redesigned MacBook Pro also brings back Apple’s glowing logo on the lid, reviving a signature design feature last seen on the MacBook Pro in 2016. The return comes a decade after Apple dropped the illuminated emblem during its shift to thinner laptop designs.The announcement marks Apple CEO John Ternus’ third major product launch this year, following the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo debut, then the OLED-equipped iPad mini. The MacBook Pro’s new display and touch interface represent a significant change for Apple’s professional laptop lineup.Preorders opened October 28, with deliveries and retail availability starting November 6. Prices begin at $2,899 for the 14-inch model with M5 Pro.Brighter OLED displayApple’s new PROLED XDR display uses tandem OLED technology to improve brightness, contrast, and image consistency. It reaches 2,000 nits of peak brightness and delivers a claimed 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. A variable refresh rate of up to 120Hz also keeps motion smooth during editing and other demanding tasks.We’re glowing with excitement over the new MacBook Pro. You’ve gotta touch it to believe it. pic.twitter.com/BLiGkGaefL— John Ternus (@johnternus) October 28, 2026The panel supports P3 and Adobe RGB color spaces, making it suitable for photographers, designers, and video editors. Apple claims more than 80% coverage of the Rec. 2020 color gamut for HDR video work. An antireflective coating helps users work in bright environments, while an optional nano-texture finish reduces glare further.Apple also uses dedicated processing algorithms to regulate individual pixels and maintain consistent brightness. Factory calibration helps keep color accuracy aligned with professional standards. The company has added reference modes for specialized work, including nondiagnostic medical image review.Touch comes to MacThe touchscreen introduces another way to navigate macOS without replacing the keyboard or trackpad. Users can pinch to zoom, move presentation slides, and rearrange windows directly on the display. An integrated touch sensor reduces latency by placing the sensing technology within the panel.Creative professionals have more specialized options, too. Designers can draw directly across the screen, while musicians can play software instruments using onscreen controls. Developers can also test touch interactions in their iOS and iPadOS applications.Apple redesigned the hinge to provide greater stability during touchscreen use. Existing applications can recognize touch input through automatic translation into clicks. Developers can also use updated gesture APIs to build interfaces specifically for the new display.M5 chips power workloadsThe M5 Pro targets professionals handling software development, scientific computing and intensive video editing. M5 Max caters to heavier workloads, including 3D animation, visual effects and large language models running locally.Both processors feature GPU cores with dedicated neural accelerators and a third-generation ray-tracing engine. Apple says these improvements accelerate graphics rendering and demanding computational tasks. Configurations offer up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of storage.The redesigned laptops also shed weight without sacrificing sustained performance, according to Apple. The 14-inch model weighs 3 pounds, while the 16-inch version weighs 4 pounds. Both include Thunderbolt 5, HDMI, an SDXC card slot, and Wi-Fi 7.Pricing and availabilityThe 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro starts at $2,899 in the US. The 16-inch M5 Pro version starts at $3,399. M5 Max configurations begin at $4,499 for the 14-inch model and $4,799 for the 16-inch version.Apple has also upgraded the six-speaker sound system, promising 50% deeper bass. The laptops support up to three external displays with M5 Pro and four with M5 Max, giving professionals more room for complex workflows.

title: Oxford researchers identify new semiconductor for more efficient solar cells
content: Researchers at the University of Oxford have discovered that bismuth sulfide material can overcome a major limitation in solar energy. The problem was that materials that absorb sunlight strongly usually lose electrical charge too quickly to generate efficient power. The identified semiconductor material has an unusual internal energy setup that acts like a temporary waiting room. Specifically, it holds onto captured energy longer and reducing charge loss by about 75% at room temperature. “One of the longstanding challenges in developing efficient solar-energy materials is that the properties which make a semiconductor very good at absorbing sunlight also tend to make the resulting electrical charges disappear quickly. Our work shows that this trade-off is not inevitable,” said Professor Laura Herz, corresponding author from the Department of Physics, University of Oxford.The key technology Solar panels generate power by capturing freed electrons before these charges recombine with positively charged holes and dissipate energy as heat.Materials designed to absorb maximum sunlight naturally create a crowded environment where these charges collide almost instantly. This rapid recombination creates an efficiency barrier for standard light-harvesting semiconductors.Bismuth sulfide-based semiconductors could help change this. The Oxford team used ultrafast terahertz spectroscopy, which basically fires laser pulses lasting mere fractions of a second. This technique helped to probe thin films of the material.What they found surprised them. Bismuth sulfide features a rare quantum arrangement known as a pseudo-direct semiconductor.Light energy enters through a primary, high-energy pathway where sunlight is strongly absorbed. Immediately below this entrance lies a lower-energy state that captures the excited charges. Acting as a temporary holding tank, this secondary state stores the charges safely before dissipating them.This secondary route dissipates charges poorly, allowing electrons to rest safely in storage until harvest time. At room temperature, this microscopic waiting room slashes charge loss by a 75% compared to conventional materials.“By uncovering how an unusual electronic structure can combine strong light absorption with much slower recombination, we have identified a new principle for designing semiconductors that could help us harvest solar energy more efficiently,” Herz added. Non-toxic bismuth sulfideThe material is not yet a market-ready rooftop panel. The Oxford team noted that the study proves a fundamental physical mechanism rather than a commercial product.However, knowing that this electronic shortcut exists is what matters the most. Researchers can now scan materials databases and design custom semiconductors with the same trapdoor property. “What makes this discovery particularly exciting is that we are not simply improving an existing semiconductor property but identifying a different way in which semiconductors can behave,” said Professor Herz. “Understanding this mechanism gives us a roadmap for discovering and potentially engineering other materials with similarly advantageous properties.”It could unlock not only solar panels but also longer-lived charges for solar-to-chemical fuel conversion.Bismuth sulfide provides environmental and manufacturing advantages as an Earth-abundant and non-toxic alternative to materials containing lead or cadmium. Researchers can produce these thin films efficiently using accessible methods such as low-cost solution processing, thermal evaporation, and chemical bath deposition.The study was published in the journal Nature on October 28.

title: 370,000 tons of CO₂ to be captured using innovative purification tech
content: A French company is set to deliver innovative CO₂ purification technology for UK’s first carbon capture plant at a waste-to-energy facility. Veolia has been awarded a significant contract by Kanadevia Inova AG to design and supply two CO₂ purification and dehydration units to be installed at Encyclis’ energy-from-waste facility near Ellesmere Port, Cheshire. Veolia’s cutting-edge purification and dehydration technology will support the capture and storage of 370,000 tons of CO₂ annually, which is equivalent to removing 200,000 petrol cars from the road.Facility will become a negative emitter“This pioneering project establishes Veolia at the forefront of industrial decarbonization and environmental security,” said Anne Le Guennec, CEO of Veolia’s water technology activities. “We are delivering on our promise to drive ecological transformation by enabling industries to transition toward net zero, in line with our GreenUp strategic program. With active carbon capture projects across Europe and the US, Veolia is the partner of choice for organizations seeking to decarbonize at scale, and we look forward to accelerating additional carbon capture, utilization and storage projects worldwide.”The Protos project, the UK’s first full-scale carbon capture facility integrated with an energy-from-waste plant, will process up to 500,000 tons of non-recyclable waste annually, generating up to 49.9 MW of baseload electricity for the National Grid while capturing approximately 370,000 tons of CO₂ each year. Once operational in mid-2029, the facility will become a negative emitter, with captured CO₂ transported via the HyNet North West pipeline network for permanent geological storage in depleted gas reservoirs beneath Liverpool Bay, according to a press release.Full-scale carbon capture marketThis contract marks Veolia’s entry into the full-scale carbon capture market and reinforces its commitment to accelerating industrial decarbonization and environmental security through innovative technology.Veolia’s compact, modular purification and dehydration units were specifically designed to fit within the constrained space of the Protos ERF building envelope. The technology will ensure the captured CO₂ meets the stringent purity standards required for safe transport and long-term storage, a critical factor in the project’s success and a testament to Veolia’s ability to deliver tailored decarbonization solutions for complex industrial challenges, as per the release.Carbon dioxide captured from industrial processes often requires further treatment before it can be transported through pipeline infrastructure or stored underground. Purification removes unwanted impurities, while dehydration reduces moisture content. Both processes are essential to ensure that the CO₂ meets the required specifications for transportation and storage.Veolia’s compact, modular systems have been specifically designed to accommodate the space constraints of the existing energy-from-waste facility. Their integration into the plant will help address the technical challenges associated with installing carbon capture infrastructure within an operational industrial site.The contract highlights the importance of specialized gas treatment and purification systems in making large-scale carbon capture projects technically viable.For the waste management sector, carbon capture could provide an additional pathway for reducing emissions from residual waste treatment, complementing waste prevention, reuse and recycling. It should not, however, replace efforts to reduce waste generation or improve material recovery.The Protos project offers an opportunity to assess how these approaches can be integrated into a broader environmental strategy.

content:

title: Saab unveils naval radar with 155-mile air threat detection range
content: Swedish defense company Saab has introduced Sea Giraffe Agile Multi Beam D (AMB D), a naval radar designed to detect and track aircraft, drones, missiles, and surface vessels. The system offers a reported range of up to 250 kilometers (155 miles) against air targets and 50 kilometers (31 miles) against surface targets.The latest evolution of Saab’s Sea Giraffe AMB radar family combines active electronically scanned array (AESA) hardware with updated software and processing capabilities. According to the company, the system is designed to improve air surveillance while allowing naval forces to adapt its capabilities as threats and operational requirements evolve.Electronic scanning for naval surveillanceSea Giraffe AMB D provides three-dimensional surveillance of air and surface targets, helping naval crews establish a more complete picture of their surroundings. It can detect, track, and classify a range of objects, including aircraft, uncrewed aerial vehicles, missiles, and crewed or uncrewed vessels.The radar uses AESA technology, which employs an array of antenna elements to steer radar beams electronically rather than relying solely on mechanical movement. This allows the system to redirect its beams rapidly and perform multiple surveillance tasks.The multi-beam approach is particularly relevant to naval operations, where a radar must monitor different parts of the surrounding environment while providing timely information about potential threats.Saab has not disclosed all the technical specifications of the AMB D, including its detailed detection performance against individual target types. The advertised ranges should also be understood as maximum figures, as actual detection distances depend on factors such as target size, altitude, and radar signature.Designed to resist electronic interferenceModern naval sensors must contend with electronic warfare, including jamming attempts to disrupt radar signals. Saab says Sea Giraffe AMB D incorporates electronic counter-countermeasures (ECCM) to help maintain surveillance performance in environments where adversaries try to disrupt detection and tracking.The radar also features a modular architecture that integrates with other naval systems. This can help ships incorporate its data into broader sensor and combat management networks, although specific integration options will depend on the vessel and its configuration.Its software-defined architecture is another central feature. Saab says the design enables continuous upgrades as operational needs change, potentially allowing new processing capabilities to be introduced without replacing the entire radar system.Building on an established radar familySea Giraffe AMB D builds on more than two decades of operational experience with Sea Giraffe AMB radars, according to Saab. The company says the new system combines the family’s established radar technology with modern processing and software architecture to enhance air surveillance performance.Saab has also emphasized the radar’s relatively small footprint, an important consideration aboard warships, where antenna size, weight, and available installation space can constrain equipment choices.The company has not provided pricing, delivery schedules, or specific customer orders in its announcement. The introduction therefore establishes a new radar offering, rather than confirming its deployment aboard a particular class of warship.With its combination of air and surface surveillance, electronic-warfare countermeasures, and upgradeable software, Sea Giraffe AMB D is intended to give naval forces a sensor that can adapt to changing threats without requiring a complete hardware overhaul.

title: The Future of Electromagnetic Shields Could Be Lighter, Stronger, and Greener
content:
The review explores preparation methods, toughening mechanisms, and 1D, 2D, and 3D structural designs of MXene/nanocellulose composites, highlighting their excellent mechanical strength and electromagnetic shielding performance. Credit: Nano Research, Tsinghua University Press
Researchers are exploring a new generation of electromagnetic shielding materials that combine exceptional conductivity with improved strength and flexibility.
Electromagnetic shielding materials must block unwanted signals without adding excessive weight or sacrificing durability. Conventional options, including metals, conductive polymers, and carbon-based materials, can be heavy, inflexible, or expensive. Researchers are now exploring composites that combine exceptional electrical conductivity with the strength and flexibility needed for practical applications.
One promising approach pairs two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) with nanocellulose, a lightweight material derived from natural biomass. MXenes offer excellent conductivity and chemical stability, but films made from them alone tend to be brittle. Adding nanocellulose can improve mechanical strength while preserving the electrical properties needed to shield electronics from electromagnetic interference.
How Material Structure Changes Electromagnetic Shielding
A research team led by Prof. Ming-Guo Ma of Beijing Forestry University in China has published a comprehensive review of MXene/nanocellulose composites, examining how their structure, fabrication methods, and strengthening mechanisms influence performance.
The researchers identified important differences between one-dimensional fibers, two-dimensional layered films, and three-dimensional networks. Dense films primarily block electromagnetic waves through reflection, while porous aerogels favor absorption by allowing waves to penetrate interconnected structures and interact with conductive surfaces. Hydrogels can provide a more balanced combination of reflection and absorption. Layered designs, including sandwich, Janus, and structures inspired by nature, offer additional ways to control shielding behavior.
Building Stronger, More Flexible Materials
Improving durability requires more than simply combining MXene sheets with cellulose fibers. The review examines several strengthening approaches, including physical interactions such as hydrogen bonding, fiber entanglement, and metal-ion crosslinking. Chemical techniques introduce stronger covalent bonds using agents such as polydopamine or PMDI.
Combining reversible physical bonds with permanent chemical networks can produce materials with greater strength, toughness, and stability. The researchers also compared manufacturing techniques, ranging from solution mixing and vacuum filtration to 3D printing, freeze-drying, electrospinning, and layer-by-layer assembly. Each method presents different trade-offs between mechanical properties, shielding effectiveness, and manufacturing complexity.
What Must Improve Before Widespread Use?
Despite encouraging laboratory results, several obstacles remain. MXene production needs more environmentally friendly synthesis methods, and composite materials must maintain their performance under prolonged exposure to humidity and high temperatures. Scaling manufacturing processes while retaining consistent mechanical and electrical properties also presents challenges.
Future research may expand shielding capabilities across a broader frequency range, from gigahertz to terahertz, while incorporating magnetic or temperature-responsive components. Such advances could support smart shielding materials that adjust their electromagnetic behavior in response to changing conditions.
“This review provides a holistic perspective that connects fabrication methods, toughening mechanisms, and structural architectures,” said Prof. Ming-Guo Ma, the corresponding author. “It will greatly advance the rational design and practical application of high-performance MXene/nanocellulose electromagnetic shielding composites.”

title: Scientists Discover 3 Strange Quantum Materials That Could Finally Reveal Dark Matter
content:
Dark matter is an invisible form of matter believed to account for about 85% of all matter in the universe. Although it does not emit, absorb, or reflect light, its gravitational influence helps hold galaxies together and shapes the large-scale structure of the cosmos. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
Scientists have identified three unusual quantum materials that could transform the search for dark matter.
Quantum simulations suggest that a material called titanium diselenide could make future detectors up to 1,000 times more sensitive to certain forms of light dark matter than current benchmark materials. The finding could help researchers search for particles whose interactions with ordinary matter are too faint for conventional detectors to register.
In a study published in
Physical Review Letters
, an international research team identified three promising materials: titanium diselenide (TiSe₂), strontium ruthenate (Sr₂RuO₄), and hole-doped diamond. Each has unusual electronic properties that could make it particularly effective at detecting the tiny energy transfers expected from lightweight dark matter particles.
Why Dark Matter Is So Difficult to Detect
Dark matter is thought to account for approximately 85% of all matter in the universe. Its gravitational effects help explain how galaxies move and how large cosmic structures form, yet no experiment has directly detected a dark matter particle. Because dark matter does not emit, absorb, or reflect light, scientists must search for other evidence of its interactions with ordinary matter.
One approach involves looking for small amounts of energy deposited when a dark matter particle encounters a detector. The challenge becomes greater for lighter particles, which may transfer so little energy that existing detector materials cannot reliably register the interaction.
Quantum Materials Could Reveal Previously Undetectable Signals
The three proposed materials contain collective electronic excitations known as plasmons. These involve coordinated movements of electrons and can respond to exceptionally small energy deposits. Their properties could allow detectors to register interactions that would otherwise produce signals too weak to measure.
Using advanced quantum mechanical simulations based on fundamental physical principles, the researchers calculated how each material would respond to hypothetical dark matter interactions. Their results indicate that these materials could outperform existing benchmark candidates across a broad range of particle masses, potentially reaching regions that current detection approaches cannot effectively explore.
The calculations identified titanium diselenide as particularly promising, with projected sensitivity improvements of two to three orders of magnitude. These gains remain theoretical and have not yet been demonstrated in working dark matter detectors.
Earth’s Rotation Could Help Identify Dark Matter Signals
Two of the materials also showed a potentially valuable property: directional sensitivity. Their predicted responses depend on the direction from which a dark matter particle enters relative to the crystal’s internal structure.
As Earth rotates, the orientation of a detector changes relative to the expected incoming dark matter flux. This could produce a repeating daily variation in the signal, helping researchers distinguish potential dark matter interactions from background events that do not follow the same directional pattern.
Toward a New Generation of Dark Matter Detectors
The proposed materials have practical advantages beyond their predicted sensitivity. All three can be produced using established synthesis techniques, while titanium diselenide appears particularly suitable for larger-scale manufacturing. Incorporating these materials into existing detector technologies could provide a route toward future experiments, although their performance must first be tested.
The research was conducted by Prof. Yonit Hochberg and Rotem Ovadia of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Dr. Dino Novko of the Institute of Physics in Croatia, and Prof. Antonio Politano of the University of L’Aquila.
“Dark matter remains one of the greatest mysteries in physics, and discovering its nature requires us to rethink not only the particles we are searching for, but also the materials we use to search for them,” said the researchers. “By identifying quantum materials that naturally amplify the tiny signals expected from light dark matter, we’ve uncovered a promising new path toward experiments that are significantly more sensitive than those available today.”
The calculations also suggest that the search need not be limited to these three candidates. Other quantum materials with suitable low-energy electronic excitations may offer additional opportunities to detect elusive dark matter particles.
Reference: “Unconventional Materials for Light Dark Matter Detection” by Yonit Hochberg, Dino Novko, Rotem Ovadia and Antonio Politano, 2 September 2026,
