title: A Mysterious Particle Could Explain Why Anything Exists at All
content:
Crab Nebula in the Taurus constellation. Credit: NASA, ESA, J DePasquale (STScI)
A long-lived heavy neutrino could have reshaped the early universe’s expansion and tipped the balance toward matter, according to a theory that predicts traces in primordial gravitational waves.
If matter and antimatter had annihilated each other completely after the Big Bang, the universe would have been left with energy and no matter. Explaining why matter survived, when current theories suggest the two should have wiped each other out, remains one of the biggest puzzles in modern physics.
Physicists at the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur have proposed an explanation involving a particle largely overlooked for decades. Known as a “decoupled” heavy neutrino, it is a heavier relative of the neutrino, one of the lightest particles in the universe. Most theories explaining the matter-antimatter imbalance have ignored this heavy relative because its interactions with other particles were considered too weak to have an impact.
“The fact that we are here at all proves that an asymmetry between matter and antimatter occurred,” said study author Dr. Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton.
Paper author Dr Rishav Roshan from the University of Southampton. Credit: University of Southampton
The new research, published in
Physical Review Letters
, connects that imbalance to the early universe’s expansion. Co-author Dr. Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said the findings change our understanding of how quickly the cosmos expanded after the Big Bang.
Roshan explained, “This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.
“However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period.”
A matter-dominated period describes the universe’s energy budget, with matter contributing more energy than radiation. That is different from an imbalance between matter and antimatter. In the team’s proposed account, the connection between the two depends on how this period changed the conditions for other particles.
“The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles—like electrons and other leptons—interacted with their anti-particles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson,” Roshan said.
“This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up.”
Possible traces in primordial gravitational waves
Show said, “It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.
“The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.
“These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang.”
Reference: “Delayed Charged Lepton Yukawa Equilibration in Minimal Seesaw” by Rishav Roshan and Sudipta Show, 8 September 2026,
Physical Review Letters

title: New Research Reveals How Chronic Inflammation Silently Damages the Heart
content:
New research connects social conditions, mental health, and genetic susceptibility to inflammation, identifying potential pathways for preventing heart damage before symptoms develop. Credit: Shutterstock
Silent changes in the heart may signal cardiovascular danger long before symptoms emerge.
The effects of chronic inflammation may be reshaping people’s hearts long before they experience any warning signs. In a study of nearly 480,000 UK adults, researchers found that higher inflammation levels were associated with thicker heart walls, smaller heart chambers, and a reduced ability of the heart to fill with blood. These changes can develop silently for years and may eventually contribute to heart failure.
People with the highest inflammation levels (the top 20%) also faced a 43% greater risk of heart attack and stroke than those with the lowest levels (the bottom 20%). The research suggests that chronic inflammation may help explain how socioeconomic disadvantage, psychological distress, and lifestyle factors become linked to cardiovascular disease.
Hidden Inflammation and the Changing Heart
Led by scientists at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS) and Imperial College London, the study combined heart imaging, genetic information, and blood measurements from the UK Biobank. Researchers assessed inflammation using glycoprotein acetyls (GlycA), a blood marker associated with ongoing inflammatory activity.
Inflammation normally helps the body respond to injury and infection. When it remains active at low levels over long periods, however, it can contribute to diseases including diabetes and cancer. The new findings strengthen evidence linking persistent inflammation to changes in the heart’s structure, even in people without previously diagnosed heart disease.
Professor Declan O’Regan, British Heart Foundation Chair of Cardiovascular AI at Imperial College London and Head of the Computational Cardiac Imaging Group at the LMS, warned that “millions of people could be living with hidden inflammation, which is slowly changing their heart and causing long-term damage.”
How Social Conditions and Genetics Influence Risk
Inflammation levels were closely associated with economic disadvantage, poor mental health, smoking, and excess body fat. These relationships suggest that the conditions in which people live may influence cardiovascular health partly through prolonged immune system activity, although the observational findings cannot establish direct cause and effect.
“The surprising thing was how much social factors and mental health are linked to inflammation and damage to the heart,” O’Regan said. “There was also a strong genetic factor, with some people being naturally more resilient or susceptible to the inflammatory damage that comes from different lifestyles.”
Genetic susceptibility does not mean that heart disease is unavoidable, and the researchers emphasized that inflammation can be addressed through preventive measures. “But while tackling health inequalities remains an issue, there are things that we can do about inflammation, including reducing risk factors like smoking and obesity,” O’Regan added.
Could Inflammation Become a Target for Heart Disease Prevention?
The researchers identified inflammatory proteins from the interleukin-1 and TNF families as possible contributors to structural heart damage. Some of these proteins are already being targeted by drugs in clinical trials, suggesting that treatments designed to reduce specific inflammatory processes could eventually help protect the heart before symptoms develop.
Professor Bryan Williams, Chief Scientific and Medical Officer at the British Heart Foundation, said: “Inflammation is part of the body’s healing process, but there is also a darker side to it. This large-scale study found people with higher levels of inflammation experienced silent changes to the structure of their hearts and had a higher risk of major cardiac events, including heart attacks and strokes.”
“The research provides valuable insights into how our genes and lifestyle factors, such as smoking, poor mental health and socioeconomic status, can converge to trigger inflammation. It also identifies several inflammatory proteins that appear to play a key role in the heart changes linked to chronic inflammation, and it is to be hoped that anti-inflammatory medicines could become an important tool in preventing cardiovascular disease.”
Identifying Heart Damage Before Symptoms Appear
The findings also point toward a potential strategy for earlier detection. Combining inflammation blood tests with genetic risk scores could help identify people who are particularly susceptible to cardiovascular damage and may benefit from preventive treatment. Further studies will be needed to establish whether targeting the identified inflammatory pathways can prevent heart damage and reduce cardiovascular events.
“These findings reinforce the importance of tackling the causes of inflammation and poor cardiovascular health, while also supporting people to make lifestyle changes that can help protect their hearts,” Williams said.
Reference: “Gene–environment interactions shape cytokine-mediated inflammation and cardiovascular risk” by Mattia Corianò, Shamin Tahasildar, Ling Huang, Khaled Rjoob, Majid Vafaeezadeh, Soodeh Kalaie, Jin Zheng, Lara Curran, Parisa Gifani, Marc-Emmanuel Dumas and Declan P O’Regan, 18 September 2026,
European Journal of Preventive Cardiology

title: A Natural Molecule Already in Your Body Could Hold the Key to Clearing Brain Fog After Cancer Treatment
content:
Brain fog can make everyday activities unexpectedly difficult, affecting memory, concentration, mental clarity, and the ability to process information. Although it is often temporary, these cognitive difficulties can persist for months or even years, particularly after cancer treatment, and scientists are still working to understand the underlying causes. Credit: Shutterstock
A supplement containing a molecule naturally found in the body showed promise for easing lingering brain fog and fatigue after breast cancer treatment.
Troubles following a conversation, remembering details, or organizing everyday tasks can linger long after breast cancer treatment ends. A small study now suggests that a supplement containing oxaloacetate, a molecule the body already uses to produce energy, could help ease this mental fog and the fatigue that often accompanies it.
Researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center found that survivors who completed eight weeks of supplementation reported clearer thinking, less fatigue, and better physical functioning. Cognitive tests also detected improvements in processing speed and executive function, the skills that help people plan, focus, and manage tasks.
The results, published in
JCO Oncology Advances
, support further research into the supplement’s potential benefits.
Why Breast Cancer Brain Fog Can Persist
An estimated 15% to 25% of breast cancer survivors experience lasting cognitive difficulties after the disease and its treatment. Often called “chemo brain” or “brain fog,” these symptoms have historically been associated with chemotherapy. Researchers now recognize a broader set of possible contributors, including cancer itself, endocrine therapy, inflammation, hormonal changes, and other biological and behavioral factors.
“Cancer-related cognitive impairment can persist long after treatment ends and can have a significant impact on a person’s daily life, yet we still have very few effective treatments for it,” said Dr. Patricia Ganz, the study’s first author and a distinguished professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA and the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.
Oxaloacetate interests researchers because it supports both cellular energy production and the regulation of glutamate, a chemical involved in brain signaling. Inflammation associated with cancer and its treatments may disrupt these processes, potentially contributing to cognitive problems and mental fatigue. The team wanted to find out whether supplementing oxaloacetate could help address those symptoms.
What Eight Weeks Of Oxaloacetate Revealed
The phase II trial included women with early-stage breast cancer who were one to five years past diagnosis and reported substantial cognitive difficulties. Their average age was about 50. Most had received chemotherapy, and nearly 90% were taking endocrine therapy during the study.
Participants took 500 milligrams (about 0.018 ounces) of oxaloacetate twice daily for eight weeks. Researchers used questionnaires and standardized neuropsychological tests to assess attention, memory, processing speed, and executive function before and during treatment. They also tracked fatigue, sleep, anxiety, depression, physical and mental health, and side effects.
Sixteen women completed the treatment, and all 16 reported significant improvement in cognitive symptoms. Their average score on the primary measure of perceived cognitive impairment rose from 29.1 to 55.5, moving the group from a range considered impaired into one considered normal. Improvements were apparent after four weeks and generally grew by week eight.
Less Fatigue, With Important Questions Remaining
Beyond the reported gains in memory and concentration, participants experienced significant reductions in fatigue, including mental fatigue, and improvements in physical functioning. Neuropsychological tests showed better processing speed and executive function, although the researchers described these results as preliminary given the trial’s size.
Oxaloacetate was generally well tolerated. The most common side effects involved the digestive system, including indigestion, bloating, constipation, diarrhea, and nausea. Two participants stopped treatment because of gastrointestinal symptoms, and no serious adverse events were reported.
“These early findings give us a strong reason to continue studying oxaloacetate as a potential approach for managing cognitive problems after breast cancer treatment,” Ganz said.
The team is preparing a randomized, placebo-controlled phase II trial in survivors with cancer-related cognitive impairment, expected to open in late 2026. Preclinical studies in mice are also underway to explore how oxaloacetate works and whether similar outcomes (improved fatigue and physical function) occur in a placebo-controlled mouse study.
Reference: “Results From a Phase II Single-Arm Trial Evaluating the Safety and Efficacy of Anhydrous Enol-Oxaloacetate on Improving Cognitive Complaints in Breast Cancer Survivors” by Patricia A. Ganz, Kathleen Van Dyk, Catherine M. Crespi, Laura Petersen, Mina S. Sedrak and Julienne E. Bower, 1 October 2026,
JCO Oncology Advances
DOI: 10.1200/OA-26-00063
The study was funded in part by the Breast Cancer Research Foundation and the National Cancer Institute.

title: Scientists Separate Psilocybin’s Brain-Rewiring Power From Its Hallucinations
content:
Psilocybin, the naturally occurring psychedelic compound found in certain “magic mushrooms,” is gaining attention for its potential to treat depression and other mental health conditions. Credit: Stock
Mouse experiments suggest psilocybin’s ability to rebuild brain connections may be separable from its psychedelic effects, opening new possibilities for non-hallucinogenic psychiatric medications.
Chronic stress can strip away connections between brain cells, disrupting the circuits they form. Researchers at the
University of California, Santa Cruz
, found that psilocybin, the psychoactive compound in “magic mushrooms,” reshapes this wiring differently in healthy mice and those affected by stress.
The study, published on October 15 in
Nature Neuroscience
, also identified a group of brain cells that supported new connections without triggering a rodent behavior used as a proxy for hallucinogenic activity.
“I consider this work a major advance, particularly in our understanding of how psilocybin reshapes neural circuits and its potential implications for treating mental disorders,” said senior author Yi Zuo, professor of molecular, cell, and developmental biology at UC Santa Cruz.
Psilocybin’s effects depend on prior stress
Using two-photon microscopy, a high-resolution imaging technique, the team tracked individual dendritic spines on living mouse brain cells over several weeks. These tiny protrusions act as receiving docks, collecting signals from neighboring neurons at junctions called synapses. Within 24 hours of administering psilocybin, the researchers observed a rapid increase in new spine formation.
In mice subjected to unpredictable mild stress, a model that mimics aspects of human depressive states, psilocybin produced a significantly larger surge in new spines than in healthy controls. It also halted the excessive loss of existing connections. In healthy mice, the growth spurt was temporary. As some connections that predated treatment were removed over three weeks, connectivity gradually returned toward baseline, preserving structural stability while the wiring changed.
An artistic illustration of the dual effects of psilocybin, the psychedelic compound derived from “magic mushrooms,” on a mouse’s brain. Psilocybin promotes the formation and maturation of dendritic spines, tiny protrusions from the dendritic branches that serve as neuronal connection sites, here portrayed as little mushrooms. At the same time, psilocybin induced the mouse’s head to twitch rapidly, a proxy of hallucinations in humans. Credit: Illustration by Emily Kogan, UC Santa Cruz
“These findings challenge the prevailing view that psilocybin simply increases neural connectivity and suggest that its effects depend on the brain’s underlying condition,” Zuo added. “This provides a new perspective on how psychedelics might help restore neural circuits disrupted by stress, with potentially important implications for understanding their therapeutic effects in depression and other psychiatric disorders.”
In untreated mice, newly formed spines typically had an immature “stubby” shape and were unstable and short-lived. Psilocybin accelerated their development, with a significantly higher proportion quickly growing into large “mushroom” shapes. These mature, stable structures have abundant neurotransmitter receptors, which receive chemical messages from other neurons and help sustain strong signals involved in memory and mood.
“Psychedelics are fascinating compounds because they have the potential to profoundly transform who we are by reshaping the neural circuits in our brains,” said lead author Jacob Baker, a Ph.D. student in Zuo’s lab. “These newly formed connections can integrate into existing neural circuitry and persist over time, leaving a lasting structural trace of psilocybin’s effects on the brain.”
Psychedelic therapies reach the FDA’s agenda
Psychedelic research has changed course several times over the past century. Natural psychedelics entered Western scientific study in the mid-20th century, and researchers identified active compounds such as psilocybin and LSD that profoundly altered consciousness and mood. Early clinical investigations suggested potential uses in psychiatric care, but research largely stalled after passage of the federal Controlled Substances Act in 1970.
Renewed interest now focuses on psychedelics as “psychoplastogens,” compounds capable of rapidly stimulating changes in neural structure and function after a single dose. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) previously granted Breakthrough Therapy designations for substances including psilocybin and MDMA.
Last month, the FDA hosted a
public hearing
“Considerations for Potential Future Therapeutic Use of Psychedelic Drugs.”
Experts addressed standardized frameworks for provider credentialing, protocols for Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS), and clinical-trial designs as regulators consider how psychedelic-assisted therapies might fit into healthcare.
Brain rewiring without a marker of hallucinations
One question could shape the development of those treatments, according to Baker: whether lasting changes in brain connectivity require the psychedelic experience itself.
To investigate the cellular pathways involved, the team focused on serotonin 2A receptors, also called 5-HT2ARs. These proteins sit on cell membranes and help mediate psilocybin’s effects. They are particularly abundant on Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, principal output cells in the cerebral cortex. Using specialized mouse lines, the researchers manipulated the receptors specifically in those neurons.
When serotonin 2A receptors were restored exclusively in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin triggered new synapse formation and structural stabilization. Yet the mice did not show the head-twitch response, a rodent movement widely used to assess hallucinogenic activity. The reverse experiment produced the opposite pattern. Selectively deleting the receptors from those neurons prevented structural synapse growth, while leaving the head-twitch response fully intact.
In these experiments, serotonin 2A signaling in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons was both necessary and sufficient for psilocybin’s structural effects, but was not required for the head-twitch behavior. Whether this separation could support effective treatments for depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), or other psychiatric conditions in people remains to be tested.
“By showing that therapeutic circuit remodeling and hallucinogenic effects operate through distinct cellular pathways, our study provides a promising blueprint for designing non-hallucinogenic drug analogs,” Zuo said. “Such therapeutics could deliver the fast and lasting antidepressant benefits of psychedelics while eliminating hallucinogenic side effects—making neuroplasticity treatments safer, more scalable, and accessible to a broader patient population.”
Reference: “5-HT2A receptors in layer 5 pyramidal neurons mediate the neuroplastic but not the hallucinogenic effects of psilocybin” by Jacob J. Baker, Emily Kogan, Shaorong Ma, Ju Lu and Yi Zuo, 15 October 2026,
Nature Neuroscience
DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02490-y
This research was supported by grants from the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute on Aging.
Disclosure: Psilocybin was provided by the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Drug Supply Program.

title: Scientists Discover a New Dinosaur Species Hiding in Plain Sight for 25 Years
content:
A reconstruction of the iguanodontian dinosaur Paludohadros proudlovii walking through mud along the edge of a shallow body of water. In the distance, the large predatory dinosaur Baryonyx can be seen. Credit: Guilherme Gehr
A dinosaur fossil unearthed in England more than two decades ago has now been identified as an entirely new genus and species.
A dinosaur discovered in an English clay quarry 25 years ago has finally been recognized as an entirely new genus and species. Named
Paludohadros proudlovii
, the plant-eating dinosaur lived about 125 million years ago, when muddy wetlands covered much of southern England. Its identification is also prompting scientists to reconsider other fossils that have spent decades in museum collections.
The four-legged herbivore measured approximately 5 meters (16 feet) long and weighed an estimated 1.5 to 2 metric tons (3,300 to 4,400 pounds), making it comparable in size to a rhinoceros. However, its bones were not fully developed, suggesting that the individual was still young when it died. A mature
Paludohadros
might have grown to twice its size.
A Prehistoric Predator May Have Hunted This Dinosaur
Paludohadros
shared its Early Cretaceous environment with
Baryonyx walkeri
, a large, two-legged carnivore discovered at the same Surrey quarry in 1983. Although
Baryonyx
is particularly well known for eating fish, evidence of a young iguanodontian in its last meal suggests that other dinosaurs were also part of its diet.
Professor Susannah Maidment, a senior author of the research from the Natural History Museum, London, and the University of Birmingham, explains: “Paludohadros was found just 100 meters (about 330 feet) away from Baryonyx, whose fossils we also look after at the Natural History Museum. While Baryonyx is best known for eating fish, this dinosaur’s last meal also included a baby iguanodontian.”
“We can’t tell for certain which species this came from, so it’s possible that Baryonyx could have been scavenging on the remains of young Paludohadros or even hunting them when it had the opportunity.”
In situ skull bones Credit: Tim Burgess (Wienerberger Ltd)
Why Scientists Are Discovering New Dinosaurs in Old Fossils
Paludohadros
belonged to the iguanodontians, a widespread group of plant-eating dinosaurs distinguished in part by their characteristic thumb spikes. For many years, iguanodontian fossils from southern England were generally assigned to one of two genera:
Iguanodon
or its smaller relative,
Mantellisaurus
A detailed scientific reassessment of
Mantellisaurus
, published by Natural History Museum researchers in 2023, clarified anatomical differences that had previously been overlooked. These distinctions have helped paleontologists recognize several separate iguanodontian dinosaurs, including
Brighstoneus
Comptonatus
, the sail-backed
Istiorachis
, and now
Paludohadros
The latest identification has also led researchers back to older museum specimens. Several fossils collected as early as the 1950s have now been recognized as belonging to
Paludohadros
, suggesting that additional examples of the dinosaur were preserved long before scientists understood that it represented a separate genus.
A Dinosaur Named in Memory of a Quarry Manager
The original
Paludohadros
fossil was unearthed in 2001 at wienerberger’s Ewhurst brick and roof tile works (Ewhurst Works) in Surrey and subsequently donated to the Natural History Museum. Its genus name reflects the wetland environment it inhabited, drawing on the Latin word
, meaning “swamp.”
The species name,
proudlovii
, honors Will Proudlove, a former employee who worked his way up to become the quarry’s manager. Proudlove had a strong interest in the fossils exposed by quarrying operations but died at age 35, shortly before the dinosaur was discovered. He was survived by his wife, Rachael, and their young children, Ellie and Matt.
Rachael Proudlove says, “Will always had an interest in dinosaur fossils and was fascinated about what, if anything, would be uncovered each time a layer of clay was removed from the quarry. Sadly, this dinosaur was only discovered the year after he died, but its story has become a part of our lives since then.”
“We were invited to go and look at it being excavated back in 2001, so it’s amazing to hear all this time later that it’s not just a new species of dinosaur, but a new genus too. We’re absolutely overjoyed and honored that Will’s name and legacy will live on in this dinosaur.”
More Unknown Dinosaurs May Be Hiding in Museum Collections
The research was led by Ricardo Sacamoto, a PhD student at the Natural History Museum, London, and the University of São Paulo. He plans to continue examining the museum’s extensive collection of iguanodontian fossils, looking for anatomical differences that could identify additional unrecognized species.
Paludohadros
is the first species I’ve ever named and I’m honored to have been able to work on it. I still remember the incredible moment when I realized that this was a new species that no one had ever identified before,” Sacamoto says.
“I’m now going to go through the Natural History Museum’s iguanodontian collections to identify what’s there as part of my PhD. This could lead to the discovery of more new dinosaur species that haven’t yet been recognized.”
Reference: “A new iguanodontian dinosaur from the Weald Clay Formation (Lower Cretaceous) of Smokejacks Brickworks, southern England” by Ricardo J. Sacamoto, Jeremy A. F. Lockwood, Max C. Langer, Brett Clark, Paul M. Barrett, Alice Turner and Susannah C. R. Maidment, 26 October 2026,
Journal of Systematic Palaeontology

title: Something Strange Is Happening to Barn Owls: They’re Changing Color
content:
Barn owls are nocturnal birds of prey known for their distinctive heart-shaped faces, pale feathers, and nearly silent flight. Credit: Shutterstock
DNA from more than 3,000 barn owls reveals natural selection at work, but the advantage behind their changing feathers may involve coping with stress rather than color itself.
Swiss barn owls have become more reddish-brown and more heavily spotted over the past 30 years. By tracking the DNA variants linked to their plumage, researchers have found evidence of natural selection acting over about ten generations, offering a detailed view of evolution unfolding in the wild.
The study, published in
Nature Communications
, was led by Dr. Tristan Cumer, a research fellow in the Department of Ecology and Evolution at the University of Lausanne (Unil)’s Faculty of Biology and Medicine. Working in Professor Jérôme Goudet’s team, Cumer and his colleagues examined how genetic variants associated with color and spotting became more or less common over time. The challenge was to distinguish changes that could occur randomly from those shaped by natural selection.
“We compared the changes observed in the population with simulations in which evolution was entirely random. A genetic variant associated with reddish-brown plumage became far more common than chance alone could explain. Only simulations that included natural selection reproduced the changes we observed,” explains Cumer, the paper’s first author.
Redder feathers may be a byproduct
The analysis depended on both extensive genetic sequencing and records collected through decades of fieldwork.
“Drawing on the exceptional volume of data collected by Alexandre Roulin and his group, who have monitored these birds of prey in the field for decades, we were able to sequence the complete genomes of more than 3,000 owls and identify the DNA variants associated with color and spotting. This is one of the most in-depth genetic analyses ever conducted on a wild population,” says Goudet, the study’s last author, who is also affiliated with the SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics.
Barn owls. Credit: Quentin Fort
The researchers identified genetic regions that play a major role in the birds’ appearance. These include MC1R, a gene already known to affect pigmentation, and a region on a sex chromosome whose contribution to both color and spotting they clarified. Identifying these links, however, does not establish which trait natural selection is favoring.
“We also do not know whether plumage color is itself the trait directly favored by natural selection,” says Goudet. “MC1R plays a role in pigmentation, but it is part of the melanocortin system, which has also been linked to other traits, including stress responses and aggression. Selection may therefore be acting on one of these traits, with the change in the owls’ appearance simply arising as a consequence.”
Food and stress could shape plumage
Barn owl plumage ranges from pure white to deep reddish-brown, with shades of golden brown in between. Some birds have only a few faint dark spots on their chests, while others carry many more prominent markings. Research at Unil has linked this variation to aspects of the birds’ lives beyond their appearance.
Plumage color is associated with fertility, hunting strategies, and diet. White barn owls, for example,
use moonlight to their advantage when attacking prey
, as described in an earlier Unil report in French. Spotting is associated with immunity and the ability to cope with stress. Birds with large black spots appear better able to withstand certain stressful conditions, including food shortages and parasites.
These connections offer possible explanations for the recent changes, although the ecological factors driving them remain unidentified. Roulin, a professor in Unil’s Department of Ecology and Evolution and a co-author of the study, suggests that shifts in food supplies or environmental stress could be involved.
“A change in prey availability may have favored reddish-brown barn owls, which eat more voles, whereas white owls tend to feed more on wood mice. The increase in spotting could be linked to greater environmental stress. Despite the striking differences in color between individuals, it remains extremely difficult to determine which ecological factors explain these variations.”
Evolution tracked across ten owl generations
The study’s evidence for natural selection is clearer than the explanation for what is driving it.
“Conducted in collaboration with the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach, this study is one of the rare cases in which the genetic basis of recent evolution has been traced with such precision in the wild. This kind of demonstration is much harder in animals living in their natural environment than in a laboratory,” adds Goudet.
For almost a decade, Goudet and his team have been working to decode the barn owl genome and establish the species as a model for studying evolution in the wild. Their work includes sequencing and assembling its
reference genome
, a DNA sequence that serves as a guide for genetic research, and reconstructing its
evolutionary history across Europe and the Mediterranean
. They have also investigated
genetic recombination
, which reshuffles DNA from one generation to the next, and studied
how mutations arise
and are passed on within populations.
“Research on this scale is possible because field teams, genomics specialists, and members of the Faculty of Biology and Medicine’s core facilities work together,” says Professor Goudet.
The changes documented in the owls show that detectable genetic evolution need not take millions of years. Cumer sees potential implications for how wild species respond to changing conditions, while the pressures acting on these owls remain unresolved.
“The study carries an encouraging message: it shows that species living in the wild can evolve over a short period. This capacity for rapid adaptation could help them cope with environmental change, including climate change,” says Cumer.
The team now plans to use computer analysis of photographs to measure color and spotting more precisely. Researchers also intend to reconstruct the plumage color of birds that died very young using their genetic data, allowing them to investigate whether particular plumage features are associated with better chances of survival.
Reference: “Genomic bases of short-term evolution in wild barn owls revealed by long-term monitoring and population-scale sequencing” by Tristan Cumer, Alexandros Topaloudis, Eleonore Lavanchy, Anne-Lyse Ducrest, Sonia Sarmiento Cabello, Anna Hewett, Paolo Becciu, Céline Simon, Julien Marquis, Aline Charpagne, Bettina Almasi, Alexandre Roulin and Jérôme Goudet, 12 October 2026,

title: Why Are Octopuses So Smart? The Answer May Lie in How Their DNA Folds
content:
Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish are among the most intelligent invertebrates, possessing remarkably sophisticated nervous systems. Octopuses can solve puzzles, navigate mazes, and manipulate objects, while cuttlefish demonstrate impressive learning and memory abilities. Credit: Shutterstock
The extraordinary intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may be linked to more than just their genes.
Octopuses can solve problems, squid can rapidly change their appearance, and cuttlefish display remarkably sophisticated behaviors. These abilities rely on unusually complex nervous systems, but how such biological complexity evolved remains an open question. A new study suggests that part of the answer may lie in the three-dimensional structure of DNA rather than in genes alone.
Scientists at the
University of Vienna
discovered evidence that extensive genome rearrangements hundreds of millions of years ago changed how different regions of DNA interact in cephalopods. Published in
Nature Communications
, the study suggests that these ancient changes may have helped establish new patterns of gene regulation, potentially contributing to the evolution of their elaborate nervous systems.
How Ancient Genome Changes Reshaped Gene Regulation
DNA is not arranged as a straight strand inside the cell nucleus. Instead, it folds into a complex three-dimensional structure that brings distant genetic regions close together. This positioning influences which regulatory elements can interact with genes and control their activity.
Californian two-spot octopus (Octopus bimaculoides). Embryo at the final stage before hatching. The species is named after the two prominent blue eyespots that can help deter predators. Credit: Natalie Grace Schulz
“The genome isn’t just a sequence of genes. It’s folded into a complex three-dimensional structure,” said lead author Dr. Thea Rogers. “Understanding how that structure evolves is becoming increasingly important for understanding how new forms of biological complexity arise.”
Why Some Parts of the Genome Change More Than Others
The study also found that different levels of genome organization have evolved at strikingly different rates. Large structural regions called chromatin domains remained relatively stable over evolutionary time, even as other features of the genome changed substantially.
Smaller structures known as chromatin loops showed much greater variation across species, tissues, and developmental stages. These loops bring distant sections of DNA into physical proximity, allowing regulatory elements to influence genes that may be far away along the DNA sequence. Many occurred near genes associated with distinctive cephalopod characteristics, including those linked to the nervous system.
The researchers propose that regulatory entanglement may allow genomes to develop new patterns of gene expression while preserving essential biological functions. Stable chromatin domains could help maintain existing regulatory organization, while more flexible loops provide opportunities for evolutionary changes.
The findings suggest that the physical arrangement of DNA may actively influence evolutionary processes rather than simply reflect changes that have already occurred.
Reference: “Genome reorganisation and expansion shape 3D genome architecture and define a distinct regulatory landscape in coleoid cephalopods” by Thea F. Rogers, Jessica Stock, Natalie Grace Schulz, Gözde Yalçin, Simone Rencken, Anton Weissenbacher, Tereza Clarence, Darrin T. Schultz, Clifton W. Ragsdale, Caroline B. Albertin and Oleg Simakov, 9 October 2026,
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77625-7

title: Nearly 20 Years Later, Physicists Finally Detect a Long-Predicted Effect in Graphene
content:
Researchers have shown that tiny wrinkles in graphene can change the material’s electrical properties. By harnessing this characteristic, scientists may one day control electricity in atomically thin materials — such as graphene — by changing their shape instead of adding new chemicals or materials, potentially powering more responsive sensors and ultrathin electronic devices. Credit: Mario Norton / Rice University
A nearly 20-year-old scientific prediction has gained experimental support, revealing how graphene’s atomic structure could unlock new possibilities for advanced sensors and electronic devices.
A wrinkle in graphene just a few atoms wide can dramatically alter how electricity behaves in the material. Scientists have now measured this effect in exceptionally sharp folds, providing experimental evidence for a phenomenon predicted nearly 20 years ago.
The discovery, published in
Advanced Materials
, suggests that researchers could eventually control electrical properties by changing a material’s shape rather than its chemical composition. Graphene, a remarkably strong and conductive material consisting of a single layer of carbon atoms, is already being explored for batteries, computer chips, and other advanced electronics.
How Tiny Wrinkles Change Graphene’s Electrical Properties
The effect is known as flexoelectricity, which occurs when uneven bending causes electrical charges to separate within a material. In graphene, extreme curvature can shift electrons toward one side of its atomically thin structure, creating an electric dipole with oppositely charged regions.
The researchers examined naturally occurring wrinkles whose sharpest bends were compressed into spaces only a few atoms wide, less than a billionth of a meter (about 0.00000004 inches). They found that the sharpness of a wrinkle mattered far more than its overall height. Their estimates indicated that these highly curved regions produced electrical polarization between 100,000 and 10 million times stronger than that associated with much larger, gentler bends.
“The sharpness of the wrinkle turned out to be much more important than its overall size,” said lead author Sathvik Ajay Iyengar, who earned his doctorate at Rice University and is now at the University of California, Berkeley. “That tells us we can potentially tune electrical behavior by carefully controlling curvature at the nanoscale.”
A Scientific Prediction Nearly 20 Years in the Making
The theoretical foundation for the discovery dates back nearly two decades. Vincent Meunier, now head of Engineering Science and Mechanics at Penn State, and Sergei V. Kalinin, now at the University of Tennessee, predicted in a
Physical Review B
paper that sharply bending graphene could rearrange its electrons and produce an electrical response. At the time, sufficiently clean samples were difficult to fabricate, preventing researchers from directly testing the prediction.
The breakthrough began when Iyengar reexamined experimental data collected with collaborator Manoj Tripathi, now at South Dakota Mines. Their measurements showed unusual electrical signals concentrated around graphene’s sharpest wrinkles. Iyengar brought the findings to Meunier, who had co-advised his doctoral research.
“When Sathvik showed me the measurements he and Manoj had collected, we realized that the unusual signals could provide an experimental connection to an idea we had predicted many years earlier,” Meunier said. “I calculated the effect we had predicted for the specific geometry and compared it to the experiment, and it turns out the fit was almost perfect.”
Measuring Electricity at Atomically Sharp Bends
To investigate the mechanism, the team combined specialized microscopy, laser measurements, and computer modeling. Microscope probes mapped the wrinkles’ shapes, local electrical energy, and current, while Raman spectroscopy revealed where graphene’s atoms were stretched or compressed. Simulations performed using Penn State’s Roar supercomputer helped predict how extreme bending would influence electrons.
Comparing sharply curved wrinkles with nearby flat graphene allowed the researchers to separate the effects of curvature from other influences. The wrinkle tips altered local electrical energy and consistently showed electrical current when approximately one volt was applied. These observations closely matched the team’s calculations and simulations.
The wrinkles effectively acted as microscopic obstacles to electrical transport. Their extreme curvature changed the local electronic environment, providing evidence that flexoelectricity can produce a substantial response even in a material only one atom thick. The measured current required an externally applied voltage, so the results do not demonstrate electricity generation without an external power source.
Toward Electronics Controlled by Shape
The findings point toward a possible method for adjusting the electrical properties of ultrathin materials through precisely controlled bending. Future devices might exploit this behavior to create more sensitive sensors or electronic components whose responses depend on nanoscale geometry.
“Nature already creates these tiny wrinkles for us,” Iyengar said. “Understanding how they influence electrical behavior gives scientists another tool for designing future technologies using the structure of a material itself.”
Reference: “Sub-Nanometer Curvature Unlocks Quantum Orbital Flexoelectricity in Graphene” by Sathvik Ajay Iyengar, James G. McHugh, Jonathan P. Salvage, Robert Vajtai, Venkataramana Gadhamshetty, Alan B. Dalton, Manoj Tripathi, Pulickel M. Ajayan and Vincent Meunier, 25 July 2026,
Advanced Materials
DOI: 10.1002/adma.202518224

title: No Batteries, No Plugs: Scientists Create a Tiny Sensor That Powers Itself
content:
Technology
Soldering a graphene-based sensor. Credit: Russell Cothren
Scientists have developed a tiny temperature sensor that harvests energy from magnetic fields near electrical wiring.
Electrical wiring produces weak electromagnetic fields that typically go unnoticed, but researchers have found a way to turn some of that energy into a power source for tiny electronic devices. Scientists at the
University of Arkansas (U of A)
University of Michigan
have developed a graphene-based energy harvester capable of powering an ultra-low-power temperature sensor without a conventional battery.
The prototype operates using energy collected from its immediate surroundings, consuming power measured in nanowatts, or billionths of a watt. It represents another advance toward the team’s goal of developing autonomous sensors that could function unattended for decades.
Turning Electrical Wiring Into a Power Source
The technology captures energy from magnetic fields generated by electrical wiring carrying alternating current. In the United States, electricity typically operates at 60 hertz, meaning the current changes direction 60 times each second. The researchers designed their sensor to harvest energy from these low-frequency fields.
A graphene inductor collects the energy and sends an alternating electrical signal to a custom circuit, which converts it into direct current. That electricity charges capacitors that store energy for the sensor to use. Unlike a battery, a capacitor stores energy in an electric field rather than through chemical reactions.
“The inductor adds charge to these capacitors at a slow rate,” explained University of Arkansas physics professor Paul Thibado, “but it’s faster than the rate the sensor uses up the charges from the capacitors.”
Because the sensor consumes energy more slowly than the system replenishes it, the capacitors can maintain an electrical reserve. Thibado estimates that this stored energy could keep the device operating for at least 24 hours during a power outage, potentially extending to a week.
Building Sensors That Can Power Themselves
The new device is the second graphene-powered temperature sensor developed by the research team. Their earlier work demonstrated that graphene-based solar cells could supply enough electricity to operate temperature sensors, establishing another possible source of energy for autonomous electronics.
Graphene, a material consisting of a single layer of carbon atoms, has electrical properties that make it useful in energy-harvesting technologies. Thibado has investigated these properties for more than a decade and invented the graphene energy harvesters used in the team’s research.
The researchers ultimately want to combine several methods of collecting environmental energy, including sunlight, heat, sound, motion, and ambient electromagnetic fields. A sensor equipped with multiple harvesting systems could continue operating when one energy source becomes unavailable, reducing its dependence on any single power supply.
Applications Beyond Temperature Monitoring
Although temperature measurement provides a practical demonstration, the technology could eventually support sensors used in agriculture, environmental monitoring, medical tracking, wearable electronics, and supply chain management. These applications often require devices to operate in locations where replacing batteries is expensive, inconvenient, or impractical.
Thibado describes the long-term vision as “set it and forget it,” with sensors designed to operate for extended periods without routine battery replacement. Eliminating disposable batteries could also reduce maintenance demands and electronic waste, although decades of reliable operation have not yet been demonstrated.
The research was published in the
Journal of Vacuum Science and Technology B
, with MD Rezaul Kabir, a doctoral candidate in materials science and engineering at the University of Arkansas, serving as first author. The project also involves researchers at the University of Michigan, including electrical engineering and computer science professor David Blaauw, whose work focuses on low-power wireless sensors and embedded systems.
Commercial Development and Future Possibilities
NTS Innovations, a nanotechnology company, holds the exclusive license to commercialize the graphene energy-harvesting technology. The company has supported patent development, business planning, and efforts to identify potential customers and commercial partners.
More than 60 parties have expressed interest in testing the technology and exploring ways to integrate it into products. Ongoing discussions are helping establish practical requirements, including the minimum electrical power needed for different applications.
The researchers envision networks of self-powered sensors that can collect information for years with little human intervention. Combining graphene-based energy harvesting with electronics that consume extremely small amounts of electricity could help make that goal achievable, particularly as connected devices become more common in homes, industries, and environmental monitoring systems.
Reference: “Graphene powerline energy harvester powers a batteryless sensor” by Md R. Kabir, Ashaduzzaman, T. B. Amin, J. M. Mangum, S. M. Rahman, H. Do, G. Carichner, D. Blaauw and P. M. Thibado, 20 October 2026,
Journal of Vacuum Science & Technology B
DOI: 10.1116/6.0005814

title: Experts Spent Decades Searching for the Secret to Happiness. Here’s What They Found
content:
Scientists suggest that happiness is neither constant nor entirely determined by circumstances. Their findings reveal how everyday choices may shape long-term well-being. Credit: Shutterstock
After decades of studying happiness, some of the world’s leading researchers have changed how they live.
Some of the world’s leading happiness researchers have changed how they live because of what they have discovered. After decades of studying well-being, several have made a conscious effort to spend more time with family and friends, reflecting one of the strongest findings in happiness science.
Their insights come from a discussion involving 13 international experts with a combined 600 years of research experience. The conversation, which explored both scientific evidence and personal experience, led to a new paper published in the
Journal of Happiness Studies
Five Key Lessons From Happiness Research
The key takeaways:
Strong relationships are central to happiness.
Social connections consistently emerge as powerful predictors of well-being. Several researchers have applied this finding by deliberately making more time for the people closest to them.
More money does not guarantee greater happiness.
Financial security helps support a good life, but additional income generally has a smaller effect on happiness once essential needs are met.
Meaningful activities support well-being.
Work and other pursuits can contribute to happiness when they provide purpose and reflect a person’s values.
Daily habits can help cultivate happiness.
Researchers described using strategies supported by scientific evidence, including practicing gratitude, savoring positive experiences, volunteering, strengthening relationships, and becoming more socially involved.
Being happy does not mean always feeling good.
Lasting well-being involves living according to personal values, building supportive connections, and adapting to difficulties rather than avoiding negative emotions altogether.
Why Relationships Matter So Much
“Happiness emerges from a symphony of factors, but if I had to pinpoint one secret to happiness, relationships with other people might be it,” says Lara Aknin, a professor of social psychology at Simon Fraser University.
Aknin coauthored the paper with Harvard University’s Säde Stenlund and Kelsey O’Connor, a senior researcher at Luxembourg’s National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies. She emphasizes that social connections are among the most consistently supported findings in happiness research.
“Having relationships is one of the most reliable predictors of happiness that has emerged from a robust body of evidence spanning the social sciences,” says Aknin.
“We know that having just one person you can count on is extremely consequential. Having more relationships and more communities that you feel a part of compounds that sense of well-being.”
How Much Control Do We Have Over Happiness?
Although genetics and life circumstances influence happiness, researchers emphasize that well-being is not necessarily fixed. People who generally consider themselves happy still experience setbacks, stress, and negative emotions. Their overall well-being can depend partly on how they respond to challenges and the activities they choose to pursue.
Some influential models of happiness have estimated that life circumstances, including where someone lives, employment, age, and relationship status, account for roughly 10% of happiness, while voluntary activities may contribute as much as 40%. These figures are model-based estimates rather than fixed proportions that apply to everyone, but they highlight the potential role of personal behavior.
“That leaves a lot of opportunity for people who may be more innately pessimistic to start practising research-backed strategies like meditation or gratitude that might help them see the world in a more positive way,” she says.
Happiness Research Is Still Evolving
The scientific study of well-being has expanded considerably since the 1970s, when the modern field began taking shape. What was once a relatively small area of research now encompasses numerous approaches to understanding happiness, life satisfaction, social relationships, and psychological health.
Aknin, who also coedits the annual
World Happiness Report
, says this expansion has brought challenges. As researchers pursue increasingly specialized questions, some early leaders worry that the field has become fragmented. Despite these differences, the scientists who participated in the discussion shared a commitment to rigorous research that can be translated into practical ways to improve people’s lives.
Why Happiness May Benefit More Than Just the Individual
The researchers also considered how personal well-being affects people’s willingness and ability to support others. Studies have linked happiness with positive outcomes beyond individual life satisfaction, including greater motivation to help other people.
“With many large and threatening realities taking place in the world right now, I sometimes worry that the pursuit of happiness can seem trite. But one reason I remain committed to the scientific study of happiness is that happiness in and of itself predicts a number of valuable outcomes, including the motivation to help other people,” she explains.
“When people feel they are doing well, they have the ability, the capability, and the motivation to engage in world affairs—to take care of the people they love and take care of their communities.”
Aknin describes generosity as a process that can benefit both those who give and those who receive. Supporting others can strengthen relationships and communities, creating opportunities for care and connection to spread.
“Generosity is not zero-sum.”

title: SunFlex deploys flexible perovskite solar modules on shared bikes and at a smart bus stop in China
content:
SunFlex deploys flexible perovskite solar modules on shared bikes and at a smart bus stop in China
SunFlex New Energy
has deployed flexible perovskite solar modules in two new applications in China: shared bicycles and a smart bus stop.
SunFlex’s flexible perovskite solar applications deployed at smart bus stops. Image Credit: SunFlex New Energy
In a partnership with the bike-sharing company Hello, SunFlex launched what it describes as the world’s first batch of shared bicycles covered with flexible perovskite film. The bicycles are fitted with a lightweight film and an onboard smart positioning system, and have been deployed at the Yangcheng Lake Peninsula tourist resort in Suzhou, where road testing has begun. The company says the film keeps generating electricity in overcast and rainy conditions and is impact-resistant, with stable power supply. No power output or battery details were given.
SunFlex has also installed a basketball-themed smart bus stop in Zhuji, Zhejiang province, tied to the city basketball brand “Zhe BA”. It uses SunFlex’s smart power supply system, and the company says the light weight of the flexible perovskite modules allows direct installation on ordinary structures with low load-bearing capacity. It estimates that the system generates about 1,000 kWh per year, avoids about 0.68 metric tons of carbon emissions per year and saves RMB 700-800 (about US$105-120) a year in electricity costs.
SunFlex points to sites where power connections are hard, such as remote suburbs, scenic areas, new roads and islands. A solar-powered stop there needs no road excavation or long cable runs, and the company says this can save up to RMB 20,000 (about US$3,000) per stop in grid connection and labor costs. It expects to launch a purely solar-powered version of its smart power supply for public facilities in 2027.

content:
“六张网”中的电网是经济社会发展的“硬支撑”。从高山到戈壁，从沙漠到深海，各地大型电网加快建设，更绿的电能、更智能的调节正加速升级。
在海拔3600多米的四川阿坝米亚罗山，国家西南立体枢纽大电网重点工程——阿坝至成都东特高压工程进入投运前的冲刺，年底建成后，川西北的水、风、光等清洁能源能直送川渝负荷中心，每年可向川渝地区输送清洁电能超150亿千瓦时，助力成渝双城经济圈发展。
在内蒙古的沙漠边缘，蒙西—京津冀±800千伏特高压直流输电工程进入全线铁塔组立关键节点，这条跨区域的电力“大动脉”输送的主要是库布其1200万千瓦沙戈荒基地的绿电。明年投产后，大漠绿电将点对点直送河北，赋能京津冀绿色低碳发展。
新疆的戈壁风区里，哈密1500兆瓦光热储一体化项目的土建工程日前已完成约95%。项目依托丰富的太阳能资源，创新采用“光伏+光热+储热”一体化协同模式，在夜间或阴天也能持续向电网输出稳定、可调节的绿色电力。
在广东，汇集了4个海上风电场电能的三山岛海上风电柔直输电工程完成建设，进入海上换流站的联调联试。这个被称为“海上电力心脏”的换流站把收集的风电，通过上百公里的海底电缆输送至陆地，并入电网。投产后，每年可向粤港澳大湾区输送清洁电能约60亿千瓦时，满足粤港澳大湾区200万户家庭全年的用电需求。
数字智慧电网建设取得新进展。近日，浙江虚拟电厂完成新一轮与大电网的互动，常态化参与发电端和用电端的市场调节，依托人工智能大模型智能调控，实时预判用电需求变化，快速给出解决方案，以实现富余电力合理调配运用。目前，我国已建成虚拟电厂超530个。预计2030年，全国虚拟电厂最大调节能力将突破5000万千瓦。

title: Boskalis awarded UXO IDC campaign at Gennaker Offshore Wind Farm
content:
Boskalis has secured a second unexploded ordnance (UXO) identification
and clearance (IDC) campaign for the Gennaker
offshore wind farm,
located in the German Baltic Sea.
The award follows the completion of a survey and UXO IDC campaign along
the project's inter-array cable routes .
Boskalis Hirdes EOD Services will use its vessel Kamara to investigate
an estimated 850 additional targets and remove identified UXO where required.
The campaign will prepare seabed corridors that allow the foundation installation
vessel to safely deploy and manoeuvre anchors during foundation installation
at the wind farm.
The company is also responsible for the project's inter-array cable package.
Boskalis Subsea Cables and consortium partner TKF Subsea Solutions were
awarded a contract to supply and install around 130 kilometres of 66 kV
inter-array cables.
Cable Installation is currently scheduled to begin in late 2027 using the
cable-laying vessel BOKA Ocean.
With an installed capacity of up to 976.5 MW, the Gennaker offshore wind
farm is expected to become the largest offshore wind farm in the German
Baltic Sea.

title: Red Eléctrica begins underground cable installation
content:
Red Eléctrica has begun laying underground cable for the electricity interconnection
project linking the Iberian Peninsula and France.
The project is expected to increase electricity exchange capacity between
the two countries from 2,800 MW to 5,000 MW, enhancing energy security
and improving the efficiency and resilience of their power systems.
The high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables, which measure 13 cm in diameter,
will run for approximately 13 km between the Gatika converter station and
the coast of Lemoiz. Preparatory work for the cable installation has already
been completed, including a land to sea drilling operation.
According to Red Eléctrica, the company has worked closely with local authorities
and the fishing sector throughout the project's development to minimise
impacts on coastal communities and marine activities.
The interconnection has also been designed to reduce environmental impacts.
To support this objective, Red Eléctrica partnered with AZTI, a technology
centre specialising in the marine environment.
As part of the initiative, Red Eléctrica and AZTI have launched Ecos del
Océano (Echoes of the Ocean), a monitoring program that will track marine
mammals and commercially important fish species along the cable route.

title: Encryption Under Siege? OpenAI, Anthropic Disprove Key Cryptography Theorem
content: Cryptographers who develop encryption technologies may not be sleeping very well these days. OpenAI and Anthropic both said Monday that their internal AI models had disproven the Exponential Time Hypothesis , a longstanding computer science theorem that predicts the minimum difficulty of solving a certain category of problems. Cryptographers had long assumed the hypothesis was true, and built other findings on the basis of that assumption. Disproving the Exponential Time Hypothesis won’t endanger any current encryption methods, said Matthew Green , professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University and founder of encryption startup Zeutro . But the finding is a big theoretical step, showing that some problems are easier to solve than cryptographers had thought. That means cryptographers could also be wrong about other assumptions underlying core encryption methods such as elliptic curve encryption , a method underlying the majority of internet traffic, which would create a scramble to find new ways to keep information on the internet secure. “Our intuition about what‘s hard is very human, and what human beings think is hard doesn’t matter anymore,” Green said. OpenAI and Anthropic have contacted outside experts to review their results on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. The experts include academics working on complexity theory, a field of research that measures the complexity of certain math or science problems, and thus how difficult they are to solve. Ryan Williams , a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who is one of the outside experts reviewing OpenAI’s research, said the company told him it “didn’t necessarily find anything” that would impact existing encryption systems. But OpenAI’s Exponential Time Hypothesis result is “the kind of finding that would make one wonder about those things,” he said. The fact that a spokesperson for OpenAI did not have a comment to us about whether it’s tried to use its models to solve practical cryptography problems won’t make such researchers wonder any less! Yael Kalai , a professor of electrical engineering and computer science at MIT , said it was possible the finding could prompt the National Institute of Standards and Technology , a U.S. agency governing innovation and tech, to increase its recommended security strength for encryption. That would increase the costs of memory and computation needed for any organization that uses encryption processes, Kalai said. If OpenAI or Anthropic do end up finding flaws in existing encryption algorithms, we would imagine they would probably inform the National Security Agency first, long before disclosing it publicly. In other news… Harvey Acquires AI Sales Startup Aida Legal AI startup Harvey has acquired Aida , which develops AI assistants for sales reps to help them catch deals that may be falling through the cracks, the company told The Information exclusively. The deal, whose terms weren’t disclosed, marks Harvey’s fifth acquisition this year, following its most recent acquisitions of AI security startup Guardrails AI in September and Benchmark , which develops AI for investment firms, in July. With Aida’s tech, Harvey hopes to help its customers better organize their proprietary data, so its legal tools can make use of that data, which may be siloed in different organizations right now. Aida’s leaders have experience in this field, otherwise known as AI for enterprise search; its CEO, Piyush Prahladka , for example, was a cofounder at AI search startup Glean . It’s a sign of how AI application startups are hoping to differentiate themselves from model developers that are also releasing vertical-specific products by leveraging hard-to-access data from their customers.— Stephanie Palazzolo Moonshot’s Influencer Backlash Moonshot AI’s release of a new model last week was supposed to be a much-needed breakout moment for a Chinese firm aiming to go public soon. Instead, it was quickly overshadowed by allegations that the company asked influencers to promote the model without disclosing that it was paying them. Moonshot unveiled Kimi K3.1 Pro last Friday as an upgrade to its popular predecessor, Kimi K3 . Hours later, an X user with the account name of Elshayib , a software developer in Jordan who often comments on AI products, said he had boycotted Moonshot’s paid campaign for the new model because the company told him and other influencers not to label their posts as a paid sponsorship. Elshayib argued that doing so would violate X’s terms of service. Elshayib had the receipts: he posted screenshots that he said showed Moonshot’s instructions for influencers participating in the campaign. The instructions in his screenshots suggested that influencers had to use certain talking points , such as “Kimi K3.1 is literally Opus 5.5 open-source, but 5x cheaper” or “China just made Opus 5.5 free to use for everyone,” referring to Anthropic’s flagship Opus 5.5 closed-source model. Some of the recommended talking points put K3.1 Pro in the context of the U.S.-China tech rivalry. One of them said: “The U.S. cut China off from advanced chips, Kimi trained new [state of the art] model without the compute American labs take for granted.” Moonshot hasn’t addressed the allegations publicly, and a Moonshot spokesperson declined to comment. The PR crisis is the last thing the company, valued at $50 billion in a recent private funding round, needs as it moves toward a public listing in Hong Kong. The exact timeframe for its IPO is unclear, and the market sentiment for publicly traded Chinese AI firms, such as MiniMax and Z.ai , has soured in recent months. The controversy comes as closed-source developers such as Anthropic and OpenAI appear to have maintained their lead against open-source rivals when it comes to capabilities, despite recent rumblings that the gap was closing.— Juro Osawa Government Checks In on Anthropic’s Evaluators The White House has checked in with Anthropic about the company’s work with embedded evaluators, Anthropic head of public policy Sarah Heck said at The Information’s Women in Tech and Finance summit on Wednesday. Current evaluators include employees from AI research nonprofit METR and consulting company Accenture , who work inside the company with “employee-like” access to assess safety risks and practices. “We‘re frankly only a couple weeks into it, and I think we’re all learning,” Heck said at the conference. “I‘ve had many conversations with folks in the administration that want to know how it’s going. They want to know what they're seeing.” Here’s what else is going on… Overheard Areas of weakness are emerging within the broader AI market as the cost of capital is set to continue rising, Kim Posnett , Goldman Sachs ’ global co-head of investment banking, said at The Information’s WTF Summit on Tuesday. Posnett noted that while she’s “hugely bullish” on AI overall, investors are growing more discerning. Anthropic ’s highly anticipated megalisting has been looming over the broader initial public offering market, holding back other companies gearing up for debuts, Lynn Martin , president of the New York Stock Exchange Group , said at The Information’s WTF Summit on Wednesday. Earnings Report Oracle shares rose more than 10% Wednesday after the company sketched out a timeline for when it would begin to slow its capital spending for data centers and start generating cash again. Microsoft revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion in the September quarter, 1 percentage point faster than the growth it reported in the second quarter. Accelerating sales in its Azure cloud unit, driven in part by server rental revenue from OpenAI, offset the slight revenue decreases in its Xbox and devices units. Google’s cloud sales surged in the latest quarter but overall revenue at parent Alphabet grew a slower-than-expected 25% to $127.6 billion, disappointing investors. ServiceNow shares dropped 19% after its third-quarter earnings. ServiceNow says adoption of its AI products is continuing to grow, but investors seem to remain wary of the potential threat AI could pose to its business. Here’s what else is going on… Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Chipmaker Marvell Technologies has been in talks to buy data center optics maker Lumentum , The Information and others reported. A deal for Lumentum would rank as one of the largest semiconductor deals, as Lumentum has a market capitalization of more than $80 billion. The status of the deal couldn’t be learned, but Bloomberg reported that a transaction could be announced as soon as next week. Cognition , the AI coding startup behind Devin , is weighing a new funding round before year's end after receiving offers valuing it at $70 billion to $80 billion — up sharply from the $48 billion valuation it announced just weeks earlier, Business Insider reported. FuriosaAI , a South Korean company that designs AI chips for data-center inference, raised $620 million (KRW 820 billion) in a Series D funding round at a $2.9 billion valuation led by South Korea's National Growth Fund. Upwind Security , which provides security around cloud infrastructure and AI agents, raised $400 million in a Series C funding round at a $3.8 billion valuation led by Bessemer Venture Partners. BioGeometry , a Beijing-based AI-native biopharmaceutical company, raised more than $100 million across its Series A financing rounds, led by China Life Capital . Lumaril , which develops AI software for optimizing industrial production, raised $66 million in Series A funding led by Elad Gil . Broccoli AI , which sells AI agents that answer calls and book jobs for plumbing, HVAC and electrical contractors, disclosed $52 million in combined funding: a previously unannounced $22 million Series A and a new $30 million Series B, both led by Khosla Ventures. Easol , an AI platform for businesses like festivals and wellness retreats, raised $30 million in a Series A extension funding round with investors including Y Combinator . Circuit Mind , which uses agentic AI to design circuit boards, raised $25 million in new funding: an $18.5 million Series A led by Norwest and a previously unannounced seed round led by Third Prime. Plato , which builds simulated workplaces where AI models can practice real jobs, raised $16 million in a Series A funding round led by Nava Ventures. Sava , which builds agentic software infrastructure for the US trust and estate industry, raised $10 million in funding led by Gradient Ventures. Amazon has significantly expanded its Shop Direct program to list more than 250 million products from rivals, up from around 100 million in March, as rival AI agents make it easier to buy across retailers. title: Why Publishers Are Adding Invisible Ads for AI Agents
content: For as long as there have been ads on the internet, marketing has targeted human eyeballs. But as AI agents crowd onto the web, advertisers and publishers are beginning to deliver ads only AI can see, sparking consternation among some of the agents’ developers, who fear marketers could try to sway agents to take actions without their users’ knowledge. The first publisher to experiment with these types of invisible ads was venerable Time magazine, which continues to generate a significant portion of its revenue from ads on Time.com. Those ads—for Ally Bank and Project Management Institute, a trade group for project managers—first showed up online in August and were developed in a partnership with Mobian, a New York–based ad tech startup. The ads were designed to give agents information about the institute’s expertise in project management and Ally Bank’s online banking services and ATM network. Following the ads’ debut, Time has had over 30 meetings with brands about doing similar ads for AI agents, and several new advertisers are launching them now, said Time Chief Operating Officer Mark Howard. Since Time launched its ads for agents, 10 more publishers have started running such ads, said Mobian CEO Jonah Goodhart, who previously sold Moat, a data analytics startup, to Oracle for nearly $1 billion in 2017. Those other publishers are mostly niche sites. One is Daily.dev, a news website for developers, which has signed a one-year revenue-sharing deal with Mobian. Its ads for agents launched around September . Goodhart hopes more than two dozen publishers will be running such ads by December. These ads for AI agents exist on a separate, text-only website version designed to be easily read by the agents. A site using these ads, like Time.com , identifies an agent as soon as it arrives and serves it the stripped-down version of the site rather than the one human visitors see. Paul Bannister, chief strategy officer at Raptive, a New York digital ads company, said he is planning to begin pitching ads for AI agents to brands in the next couple of weeks. And over at PMG, roughly a fifth of the Texas-based digital marketing agency’s 60 or so clients plan to run Mobian’s agent ads over the next month, according to a person close to PMG. If those clients go ahead and launch such ads, the agency expects to know by early next year just how successful they are at getting agents to pay attention to those brands. The past year has brought a frenzy of interest around agentic AI—software that can autonomously carry out tasks on behalf of people. Much of the technology’s development has focused on coding and office tasks, but attention has lately turned to agents people can use for everyday tasks like shopping. In September, Meta Platforms launched its Muse agent, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently said shopping is the most popular use of the app. A few weeks after Muse launched, OpenAI debuted a competing tool, Dots. Another competitor is Instinct, from a San Francisco–based startup by the same name that was founded last year and is valued at $10 billion. The enthusiasm around agentic shopping has drawn a mixed reaction from web retailers. Amazon, for instance, has blocked agents from its site. Other companies, including Walmart and Expedia, have struck partnership deals with Meta to allow it access to their sites. Agentic shopping is very much in its infancy. While 80% of consumers in the U.S., Japan, Mexico, Brazil and the U.K. use AI as part of their shopping experience, only 7% feel comfortable letting it place orders without their approval, according to a study published in late October by Riskified, a New York firm that sells software to prevent online fraud. Still, publishers and advertisers are eager to figure out how to push their brands to agents. Many of them have been energized by how AI has overturned the digital ads world, with chatbots replacing internet searches and direct visits to websites, the two main traditional avenues for selling ads online. At the same time, publishers are trying to figure out exactly how to commercialize those ads and how much a brand is willing to pay for ads visible only to agents compared to traditional ads meant for humans. Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have all held informal discussions with publishers about ads aimed at agents, according to two people familiar with these discussions. In those conversations, the companies have expressed their worry that marketers could include hidden instructions with an ad—perhaps telling an agent to ignore a competitor’s product—and they want the content clearly labeled as an advertisement, these people said. (Anthropic, OpenAI and Google wouldn’t comment for this story.) Some advertising executives worry they could be criticized for using agent-targeting ads and have drawn a comparison between such ads and cloaking, a tactic in which a website shows search engines different content than it shows people visiting the site in order to manipulate search results. Google has long treated cloaking as a form of spam. The comparison irks Goodheart, the Mobian CEO, who insists that humans and AI see the same advertising content. Nimrod Kramer, CEO of Daily.dev, thinks brands will self-police themselves and won’t use the agent-targeting ads to deceive consumers and their agents. He believes such deception might lead the companies developing the agents to blacklist those brands, effectively banning them “from one of the most important sources of traffic over the next 10 to 20 years.” Within two weeks of Time’s launch of its agent ads, Perplexity said it began blocking those ads from influencing its AI agents and search results, calling the practice deceptive. After Time began its experiment, the Interactive Advertising Bureau, the chief trade group for online publishers and ad agencies, polled publishers and advertisers about their thoughts on the ads. More than half of the respondents said they felt it was “too early to tell,” while more than a quarter said they viewed the ads as deceptive or manipulative. “The Time experiment struck a nerve,” said John Dawson, vice president of strategy at Jellyfish, a London-based digital marketing company. “We’re at an inflection point where advertisers need to think about messaging to machines in some pretty explicit ways.” To figure out how much traffic comes from agents, four publishers have signed up to use a new tool from Resemble AI, a startup best known for deepfake detection software used by The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times. None of those publishers has started using the tool yet, which will be released on Thursday, said Resemble CEO Zohaib Ahmed. The tool identifies whether a website visitor is a person or an agent based on behavior such as mouse movements and clicks. In internal testing, it caught 98.8% of agents designed to look human, Ahmed said. If the websites see a large amount of AI traffic, it could spur them to add their own ads meant for agents, he said. Right now, publishers that want to include ads for agents aren’t sure exactly when the best moment is to show them to agents. Some ads are shown to an agent when it is carrying out initial shopping research, while others are shown just as it is completing a purchase. While agent ads remain experimental, publishers are feeling pressured to figure out what will work best whenever they look at the numbers of bots visiting their site: It’s a veritable onslaught. When Daily.dev’s Kramer first heard about Time’s experiment with such ads, he checked to see how many bots were crawling his site. “I was shocked,” he said. “It was millions and millions.”
