title: How Instacart Ended Up in DoorDash’s Cart
content: That was fast! DoorDash said this morning that it agreed to buy grocery delivery app Instacart for roughly $17 billion, mostly in cash financed by borrowing, just a few days after we reported that Instacart was in talks to sell itself . After our report, DoorDash and Instacart rushed to seal the deal at a roughly 30% premium to where Instacart shares traded before we broke the news of their talks. They wanted to get it signed before both reported quarterly earnings, which were originally scheduled for next week, say people familiar with the matter. Both companies reported earnings today instead. A deal could take a year or longer to close. So how did this deal come together? Over the years, DoorDash’s leaders have thought about buying Instacart to buttress their grocery sales, according to people familiar with the discussions. Uber, a competitor to DoorDash in restaurant deliveries through Uber Eats, had also talked to Instacart about an acquisition before 2026, and it has had a commercial partnership with Instacart for years. Since going public, Instacart’s annual revenue growth has slowed considerably—to 11% in 2025. (In the third quarter, sales increased 17%, according to the earnings report the company released today.) It faces considerable competition from Amazon and Walmart, which both offer grocery deliveries: Walmart accounted for nearly 32% of all online grocery sales in 2025, while Amazon had almost 23%, according to a report from eMarketer, a market research firm. And last year it lost longtime CEO Fidji Simo to OpenAI and Chief Product Officer Daniel Danker to Walmart. So this year, Instacart’s leaders believed it was the right time to sell, according to people familiar with the matter. Instacart leaders also didn’t want to miss a window to merge with a competitor during the Trump administration, which it viewed as being friendlier to such deals, said the people familiar with the deal. Around late August, Instacart leaders shopped the company to Uber, according to people familiar with the matter. Uber executives felt obliged to take a look and started talking. Instacart told Uber that it thought a deal could make it past antitrust regulators by arguing that Walmart and Amazon were larger, formidable competitors, according to a person familiar with the pitch. Instacart brought on Goldman Sachs, which took Instacart public in 2023, to advise them on a deal. (The grocery delivery firm has long been close to the investment bank, and Goldman partner Nick Giovanni served as Instacart’s chief financial officer from 2021 to 2024.) After talking with Uber, Instacart began conversations with DoorDash , people with knowledge of the discussions. Working with boutique bank Centerview Partners, DoorDash sprang to action, the people said. In 2021, DoorDash had considered buying Instacart in a deal that would’ve valued Instacart at more than $40 billion. Nothing happened partly because they thought the acquisition would face antitrust opposition from the Biden administration. While Instacart’s revenue growth has slowed since then, it has started to generate plenty of cash. Uber wasn’t as keen on a deal. It wasn’t necessarily convinced that regulators would sign off, and it had recently announced another big acquisition, a $15 billion deal for Europe-based Delivery Hero, people close to Uber said. Uber ultimately pulled away from the Instacart talks in September. Instacart then moved ahead with DoorDash. A sale to DoorDash could help Instacart compete against Amazon and Walmart by getting in front of relatively well-to-do customers who regularly use the restaurant-delivery app. DoorDash already offers grocery delivery from retailers such as Safeway, in addition to its core restaurant-delivery business. (Some grocers like Kroger already work with both companies, however.) Research firm Bernstein estimated Tuesday that a combination of DoorDash and Instacart would account for 23% of all online grocery sales in the U.S. Wedbush Securities analysts said in a note to investors this week that they expect regulators will be OK with DoorDash buying Instacart. Still, some grocers that work with both companies might not love the deal, so even if U.S. authorities approve it, state attorneys general might review the merger of competitors themselves. It isn’t clear what will happen to Instacart’s partnership with Uber, in which customers can order Uber Eats from the Instacart app. But DoorDash said it’s keeping Instacart as a separate brand after the deal closes. Apoorva Mehta, the founder of Instacart and its former CEO before Simo joined, said in a statement that he and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu “have explored bringing Instacart and DoorDash together on and off over the years. We kept coming back to it because the industrial logic has always been clear.” Now that “the biggest companies in the world” are moving deeper into grocery delivery, Mehta says “retailers and restaurants need the technology and service to compete,” and Instacart and DoorDash can be their “partner in that fight.” Today on TITV New From Our Reporters Exclusive OpenAI’s Astra Model Becomes Top Distillation Target for China’s AI Labs By Jing Yang, Juro Osawa and Qianer Liu ‘Nobody’s Ready’: AI-Found Bugs Spark a Corporate Security Spending Spree By Aaron Holmes Recommended Newsletter AI Agenda by Stephanie Palazzolo separates hype from reality and explains how AI is transforming industries. title: Everyone’s Using AI But Divisions Are Growing:  WTF Highlights
content: Artificial intelligence has thoroughly infiltrated business and politics, but it’s also starting to divide companies and investors. That was the takeaway from leaders at The Information’s WTF Summit, a gathering of senior women in the technology and finance industries this week. Investors are increasingly picking AI winners and losers, and favoring companies that can train models and control the chips and data centers that undergird them, said Goldman Sachs’ global co-head of investment banking Kim Posnett . “What you’re seeing is not a change in AI sentiment,” she said, but “you’re seeing a repositioning and differentiation across the AI trade.” Meanwhile, the largest tech companies are starting to square off over essential policies that govern the progress of the technology, such as chip export control. Amanda Peterson Corio, Google’s global head of data center energy, warned that fast-moving cloud upstarts are prompting the need for new industry-wide standards and regulation around data centers’ use of resources. Leaders from these companies as well as NYSE Group, Goldman Sachs spoke at the conference, alongside CBS News Editor In Chief Bari Weiss and Bumble’s co-founder Whitney Wolfe Herd . Anthropic Policy Chief Hopeful ‘Compromise’ on Chip Export Controls Will Pass Anthropic Head of Public Affairs Sarah Heck said the chip export controls the AI lab has been lobbying to include in the U.S. government’s annual defense bill are the best chance to pass such controls before year end, though she emphasized that the legislation passing is “not assured.” The maker of Claude Code has advocated for stronger chip export controls, warning that without them, governments like China could use American technology to “cement authoritarianism .” Heck said Anthropic has been working with Republicans, Democrats and the White House to “get language that people feel they can live with” in the National Defense Authorization Act. Congress is still debating whether to include three bills that would curb the sale of chips and chipmaking equipment to China. Anthropic Head of Public Affairs Sarah Heck. Photo by Erin Beach. These bills have also divided the tech industry. In September, Anthropic quit a major tech trade group after the organization, which includes Nvidia and OpenAI as members, urged lawmakers not to include the chip export control bills in the NDAA. The group argued that some of the measures could slow the progress of American AI companies and turn some customers toward China because of the country’s relative lack of regulation. “This is an area where there has been a bit of compromise,” Heck added of the bill. “But if something gets passed, it will be the NDAA.” Heck was dismissive of the argument that China would be able to catch up or pass America’s AI lead without using American chips. “If you believe China is somewhere between six and 12 months behind us, they’re not going to be able to build chips fast enough to close that gap,” she said. Heck acknowledged that Anthropic and other U.S. AI companies may need to work with China on AI safety in the future, but said that could be possible even with chip exporting restrictions. “I think we can do both. I think we can walk and chew gum at the same time,” she said. — Jemima McEvoy AI is Accelerating Trading, NYSE President Says New York Stock Exchange President Lynn Martin. Photo by Erin Beach. AI is the latest technology to change the nature of trading itself, New York Stock Exchange President Lynn Martin said. It’s a far cry from when Martin started her career in financial services, when a trader’s physical stature influenced their effectiveness on the trading floor, she recalled. “A guy who was six foot eight could yell a lot louder over a woman who is five four. That actually mattered,” Martin said. That advantage shrank with the rise of electronic trading, which also made markets more liquid and more efficient. She said AI is accelerating that process. NYSE processes 1.2 trillion to 1.3 trillion incoming order messages every single day, according to Martin. She predicts AI will significantly increase the volume of inbound messages the exchange has to process. While technology can help manage that volume, Martin argued the increase will make the role of human intervention more important. “If the model is trading with [other] models, that’s not a good scenario, or if there’s a bug in the model’s code” and the model itself doesn’t have the judgment or discretion to react appropriately, “that’s not good for markets,” Martin said. “Having that human interacting with the AI is, in my mind, the optimal market.” Martin also noted Anthropic’s highly anticipated megalisting has been looming over the broader initial public offering market, holding back other companies gearing up for debuts.— Anita Ramaswamy Google Data Center Power Head: ‘I Live in 2031’ Amanda Peterson Corio. Photo by Erin Beach. The timeline for AI server chip production is much shorter than the time it takes to build out enough power to run AI data centers, said Amanda Peterson Corio, Google’s Global Head of Data Center Energy. That means Corio is thinking today about data centers that get built and switched on in 2031 or later. It takes five to ten years to build out new power on the grid, but Google churns out new versions of tensor processing units—the company’s AI chips—about once a year. “That inherently doesn’t work with a seven-year build out of power,” Corio said. To solve that mismatch and prevent a potential chip glut, Corio foresees a rise in power sources like gas generators or clean energy sources built directly on or near data center sites and bigger upfront capital commitments to fund the buildout of new grid and transmission infrastructure. Corio said she just returned from a trip to India to explore pumped hydropower solutions. Local community concerns are also a major factor in whether a data center is built and powered on time. Corio pushed back against broader concerns that data centers use too much water, don’t create enough jobs or pay enough in taxes. She also said that some newer entrants into the space are rushing to build data centers and don’t have the same “history or sophistication” as Google, making industry-wide regulation critically important. “We’re very supportive of that for the industry,” she said. — Phoebe Liu Goldman Sachs Investment Banking Co-Head Sees ‘Repositioning’ Amid AI Boom Goldman Sachs’ Kim Posnett. Photo by Erin Beach. Areas of weakness are emerging within the broader AI market as the cost of capital is set to continue rising, said Kim Posnett, Goldman Sachs’ global co-head of investment banking. Posnett said that while she’s “hugely bullish” on AI overall, investors are growing more discerning. Posnett noted that AI projects won’t drive expected returns should rates stay elevated for a long period. “While AI itself is not a bubble, I think you can have bubbles within that,” she said. Investors are starting to favor vertically integrated companies that produce frontier models, business applications and AI chips, Posnett added. Goldman is playing leading roles in major deals announced this week for some of the biggest AI companies, including SpaceX’s GPU financing , Meta’s stock offering and Anthropic’s planned initial public offering. Asked about circular financing across the AI ecosystem, Posnett said she’s thinking “more about demand” but acknowledged the risk in tech giants like Nvidia funding their own suppliers and customers. “It makes sense that they want to build closer partnerships with each other,” she said. “And I think it creates greater risk. I think both are true.”— Laura Bratton Flock Co-Founder: ‘Not Our Call’ if Police Share Footage With ICE Flock Safety co-founder and chief people officer Paige Todd said the “most challenging” part of running the startup has been navigating an early decision to not restrict law enforcement’s legal use of its technology. “I have a lot of personal beliefs on a lot of legislation out there, as does everyone. We decided it was not our call to actually decide how laws would be implemented with our technology,” said Todd. “If it is legal in a market to work with [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement], then that is their decision.” Founded nine years ago, venture-backed Flock makes license plate recognition technology designed to help local officials enforce traffic laws and find criminals. As President Donald Trump sent more federal agents across the country to crack down on illegal immigration, some residents warned the cameras were aiding forced deportations. The company does not have a contract with ICE, said Todd, though “local law enforcement may choose to share their footage with Immigration.” “It’s not our call, because at the end of the day, we actually don’t own the footage ourselves,” she said. Todd added that, despite protests against Flock cameras, the company internally has “actually been pretty calm.” The company offered voluntary buyouts to its U.S.-based employees in September because “people were sitting at the dinner table with their family or going out with their friends on a weekend, and people were like, ‘I cannot believe you work there,’” Todd said. “And after a while, no matter how much they believe in what we’re doing, it just hurt.” — Julia Hornstein Arm, Nscale Executives: There is No Chip Glut Arm’s Ami Badani and Nscale’s Nidhi Chappell. Photo by Erin Beach. Some data center developers, market analysts and investors have become increasingly worried about a future glut of specialized AI server chips that don’t have a functional data center to plug into, due to delays in obtaining power, political pushback and technical issues. Ami Badani, chief marketing officer of semiconductor firm Arm, said she is not aware of any Arm-based chips currently sitting idle in warehouses due to a lack of power. Nidhi Chappell, president of AI infrastructure at data center and cloud company Nscale, said Nscale was also monitoring its supply chain to prevent such power and chip mismatches. In recent months, fears that a shortage of data centers connected to power could lead to chip deliveries going unused has prompted Nvidia to obsessively track power supply . Badani also said Arm was seeing more customer interest than ever in designing custom chips, called ASICs. Arm has helped design chips for Nvidia, Apple and all of the largest cloud computing providers. Designing your own chip can have higher up-front cost, but it can afford companies more control, according to Badani. Shifts in how consumers are using AI are also driving changes to chip demand, Chappell and Badani said. One trend is tighter integration between the different hardware components within a datacenter, which can include different types of chips specialized to different purposes, in order to make the best use of all components. Chips are also getting more specialized for specific types of work, such as training or running AI, Chappell said.  — Tiffany Li 23andMe’s Wojcicki: AI Can Find Medical Insights Anne Wojcicki. Photo by Erin Beach. Anne Wojcicki, who heads the 23andMe Research Institute, said she believes AI will help find new medical insights and concrete actions people can take to improve their health by mining the nonprofit’s huge DNA database. “It is the power of scale,” she said. Wojcicki recounted her personal journey co-founding 23andMe, which became a pioneer in the direct-to-consumer DNA testing market but never came up with a sustainable business model. The company ended up filing for bankruptcy in 2025. Wojcicki spent more than $300 million of her own money to buy the company back last year and turned it into a nonprofit research institute. At the summit, Wojcicki cited a recent scientific collaboration that demonstrated the potential for making new discoveries from the 23andMe database, which includes DNA from more than 3.3 million people who have agreed to participate in research. She said that researchers from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston and the 23andMe Research Institute identified a rare genetic mutation that puts people at exceptionally high risk of getting lung cancer. People who have never smoked but have the gene mutation are 60 times more likely to get lung cancer as people without the faulty gene. Wojcicki’s sister, Susan, the former CEO of YouTube, died in 2024 from lung cancer. “I care a lot about this cause,” Wojcicki said. Wojcicki said she met the Dana-Farber researchers at a scientific conference. They told her they were studying the gene mutation but only had 20 people and how difficult it was to find more patients. “Oh, I have 500 of these people with that genetic variant,” she told them. She said 23andMe can now contact the people and suggest they do screening to make sure they do not have cancer. “I can save these lives,” Wojcicki said. The 23andMe Research Institute is working on a new feature called the Health Summary that can use AI to find connections between people’s DNA and all the other health data they share to make health recommendations. “The more information we get,” she said, “we can give you insights.” — Amy Dockser Marcus

title: OpenAI’s Astra Model Becomes Top Distillation Target for China’s AI Labs
content: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, the most powerful model the company has released, has met with strong demand since its release in early September. One growing customer base: Chinese AI labs that look to extract Astra’s capabilities. DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, two of China’s leading AI developers, relied heavily on outputs from Astra when training their own latest models, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter. The practice, known in the industry as distillation, continues to be one of the biggest contributors to the progress made by Chinese open-weight models despite repeated criticism of such efforts by OpenAI and rival Anthropic . Moonshot AI distilled Astra during the development of its new model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, which was released last week, according to three people with direct knowledge of the matter. Similarly, DeepSeek’s V4.1-Flash 1017, an Oct. 17 upgrade to its V4.1-Flash model that demonstrated substantial improvements from the original version released in September, also benefitted from distilling Astra, according to two other people with direct knowledge of that. Until recently, Anthropic’s Claude models were the biggest target of Chinese distillation efforts. Moonshot didn’t comment. DeepSeek didn’t respond to a request for comment. Anthropic and OpenAI have both repeatedly accused Chinese labs including Moonshot and DeepSeek of distilling their models. Chinese labs haven’t publicly responded to the allegations. Distillation is a common technique in developing AI; Anthropic and OpenAI have said they distill their own models when creating smaller, faster and cheaper versions of them. But the practice becomes controversial when outside companies target proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Both companies have policies barring others from distilling their models and don’t release their models in China. Distillation targeting them requires tricking their models into spewing out the steps taken to complete a user’s query, secrets that the developers don’t willingly share. Distillation isn’t the only reason Chinese models are competitive, though. U.S. export controls on advanced chips and other resource constraints have forced Chinese labs such as DeepSeek to explore innovative techniques to train and run models with fewer chips. But researchers at Chinese labs say the technique has played a critical role in enabling China’s AI sector to closely trail U.S. frontier models at a fraction of what OpenAI and Anthropic spend on compute. How OpenAI and Anthropic Are Fighting Distillation The rising popularity of Astra as a distillation target is due in significant part to Anthropic’s intensifying efforts to crack down on what the company has called an “industrial-scale, covert campaign” to extract the capabilities of its Claude models, the people with direct knowledge of Chinese labs’ efforts said. Earlier this month, Anthropic said it had made “substantial progress” in reducing the effectiveness of distillation attacks, with new methods helping reduce the amount of data harvested by distillers by around 90% to 99%. The company, for example, made it harder for distillers to use proxy networks to try extracting Claude’s protected reasoning—the hidden thinking process before the model generates an answer. Users who make repeated attempts to extract reasoning face stricter usage limits and account bans, it said. Use of such proxy networks, which violates Anthropic’s policies, is a common set-up underpinning distillation. Anthropic said this week in the prospectus for its planned initial public offering that customers that violated its terms contributed between roughly 5% and 7% of its revenue for the first nine months of this year. One of the operators of such proxy networks in China estimated that their customers have contributed roughly $10 million a month to Anthropic’s revenue, The Information reported . Anthropic’s revenue this year through September totaled more than $33 billion, according to the prospectus and The Information’s reporting . An OpenAI spokesperson said the company is closely tracking distillation attempts by Chinese AI labs and actively working to detect and disrupt them, including by banning or restricting fraudulent accounts, tightening signup and infrastructure controls, and expanding monitoring. It remains unclear to what extent the practice has contributed to OpenAI’s revenue growth. OpenAI’s third-quarter financials haven’t come out, but its annualized revenue neared $50 billion last month , up 70% from the end of June. An OpenAI spokesperson declined to provide an estimate for how distillation affects revenue but said the company takes the issue “extremely seriously” and is continuing to work on it. “As we deploy new defenses, attackers adapt their tactics, requiring continued improvements,” the spokesperson said. OpenAI has stepped up its measures against distillation. In late September, it said it had identified and mitigated a “coordinated model-distillation campaign” in July involving individuals associated with Moonshot. OpenAI said the operators of the campaign tried to extract protected reasoning by interacting with models in ways that could make their reasoning visible. OpenAI’s models remain accessible for distillation, but gathering usable training data from them, which requires more than 10 times as many prompts as normal use, requires distillers to use many accounts to avoid triggering detection, according to two of the people with knowledge of Moonshot and Deepseek’s distillation efforts. Prior to Anthropic’s heightened crackdown in the past two months, Claude was the go-to model for Chinese labs looking for shortcuts as they seek to stay ahead in the fierce AI race. DeepSeek CEO Liang Wenfeng initially didn’t want to resort to distillation when developing the company’s new generation V4 model, according to the two people with direct knowledge of DeepSeek’s model development. But he had to succumb to competitive pressure after seeing the success of domestic rivals such as Z.ai , whose GLM models, also developed with distillation, were gaining traction, the people said.

title: Google Cloud Closes In on Azure, but Microsoft Wins the Day With Investors
content: There was a lot to digest from Wednesday’s earnings reports from Microsoft and Google, long the No. 2 and 3 players in cloud computing, respectively. But let’s start with the most interesting takeaway: Google’s cloud unit revenues are now within spitting distance of Microsoft’s Azure cloud revenues, thanks in part to Google’s sales of its AI chips, known as tensor processing units. For those of us who remember the days not long ago when Google was an also-ran in cloud, that’s a pretty stunning development. But we’re getting ahead of ourselves. The stellar third-quarter growth in Google’s cloud computing business was overshadowed by other financial results that disappointed Wall Street analysts, particularly weak growth in Google’s search advertising revenues. Google’s stock dropped nearly 10% in after-hours trading. Microsoft’s growth, meanwhile, played better with investors, sending its stock up about 3% in after-hours trading (Microsoft shares are up 12% for the year, compared to 2% for Google). First, let’s look at Google’s numbers. Alphabet, the search giant’s parent company, reported a 25% jump in revenue to $127.58 billion, which fell slightly short of Wall Street forecasts. Due to its enormous spending on AI, the company showed negative free cash flow of over $9 billion compared to positive free cash flow of over $24 billion in the same period a year ago. The figures that seemed to alarm some investors the most were Google’s search revenues, which grew 12% to $63.35 billion—the softest growth in the business since the second quarter of 2025. Those results seemed discordant with the fact that people are using Google search more than ever. Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said Google’s year-over-year search query growth rate is the highest it has been in five years, which he attributed to the company’s AI investments. But for the moment, Google isn’t showing as many ads in AI Mode, its AI-powered search results, as it typically does. “It’s worth noting the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode,” Google Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said on a call with analysts, in explaining the disconnect. Still, there were those Google Cloud results to admire. Revenue from that business more than doubled in the quarter to over $30 billion, while the unit’s operating income tripled to $11.12 billion. That revenue figure was just shy of Microsoft’s $33 billion in Azure revenues for the period, which grew 48%. If Google Cloud keeps up its superior growth rate, it won’t be long before the business is bigger than Azure. Of course, the comparison isn’t totally apples-to-apples. Google Cloud revenues include a burgeoning server hardware business , through which the unit sells TPU systems to customers that put the chips in their own data centers. Google didn’t disclose exactly what its TPU sales were in the quarter, though it did say they were a “meaningful contributor to revenue growth.” Google executives primed analysts to expect TPU sales to have an even bigger impact on Google Cloud next year. “We’re seeing extraordinary demand,” Thomas Kurian, Google Cloud’s CEO, told them. Less is More at Microsoft Last month, when Microsoft announced it was overhauling how it reports its business segments’ quarterly results, CEO Satya Nadella promised “increased transparency.” Today though, one figure they had disclosed in the prior quarters—the number of paying users of its flagship Copilot AI software—was conspicuously absent. Previously, the company had said it had 30 million paying users of Copilot as of the end of June, up from 15 million at the end of 2025. Those customers each pay a $30 per month fee to use Copilot in its Office and Teams software, on top of fees they pay separately for those applications. That solid growth planted Microsoft’s flag as the second-biggest seller of AI software after OpenAI , and helped assuage some investors’ concerns about whether Microsoft’s core enterprise software business was getting returns from its ballooning AI spending. The company’s decision to stop disclosing the figure raises the question of whether Copilot subscriptions are growing as robustly as they had in the past. The good news for Microsoft is that its AI-infused software business still seems to be strong . Revenue in its 365 Commercial Cloud unit—which includes Copilot as well as sales of its broader suite of Office software—rose 17% to $27.7 billion, a slight acceleration from the June quarter. Overall revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion in the September quarter, 1 percentage point faster than the growth it reported in the prior quarter. There are other reasons Microsoft might want to get investors to pay less attention to the growth of per-seat subscriptions of Copilot. The company overhauled its Copilot software late last month to combine various features under one application; part of the reason for the change was to steer Copilot users towards newer features like agents that compete with Meta’s Muse and vibe-coding tools, which are billed on a pay-as-you-go basis. In other words, Microsoft is now trying to get more Copilot revenue growth to come from people using the software more, rather than just from selling additional seats. Nadella hammered this point during Wednesday’s call with analysts, stating that the number of customers paying for usage-based features in Copilot grew 75% in the September quarter, and CFO Amy Hood said average revenue per user grew thanks to increased use of the pay-as-you-go AI tools. Whether Microsoft can keep its AI software revenue growth going will be more telling, especially as it starts to offer steeper per-seat discounts on the software in a broader pricing war with the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. —Aaron Holmes In Other News Apple launched its first touchscreen computer, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, which will start at $2,899. That’s a steep premium to its latest MacBook Pro without a touchscreen, which starts at $1,999. Oracle provided a roadmap for when its capital expenditures will begin to slow, describing fiscal 2028 and 2029 as a “period of peak capex.” The company’s free cash flow will turn positive in fiscal 2028 and exceed $30 billion in fiscal 2029, it said. Oracle’s shares rose 10%. Google launched Gemini 4 Carbon, the company’s second major model release in a month. Marvell is in advanced talks to buy data center optics maker Lumentum. title: CBS’ Bari Weiss Tells Critics to ‘Judge Us by the Journalism’
content: CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss said critics of her leadership of the network should “judge us by the journalism” in a wide-ranging interview with Jessica Lessin of The Information Wednesday. Speaking at The Information’s WTF Summit , a gathering of senior women in the technology and finance industries, Weiss acknowledged the “unusual” and “exceptionally loud year” she’s had. Weiss has grabbed headlines for months over her efforts to reshape CBS News, including venerable programs like “60 Minutes.” “Change is hard,” she said. What has gotten much less attention about her efforts at CBS, she said, is that the majority of producers, journalists and correspondents at CBS “have shifted to a much more entrepreneurial mentality and culture.” Among the examples she cited were live events hosted by veteran correspondent Norah O’Donnell, the launch of Tony Dokoupil’s new podcast “Great Question” and coverage of the war in Ukraine by CBS correspondent Aidan Stretch. Weiss mentioned she’s also trying to get Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted founder of now-defunct blood-testing firm Theranos, to appear on CBS, floating the possibility of Holmes appearing live on the network’s free streaming app. Holmes was the subject of a lauded documentary by comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder released this month. Weiss vaulted into the spotlight last year when Skydance, the owner of CBS formerly known as Paramount Skydance, bought her publication The Free Press for more than $100 million and promoted Weiss to the top role at the broadcast network’s news division. A journalist and columnist known for attacking left-leaning bias in the media, Weiss has had to juggle the challenges of leading a legacy news organization suffering from ratings declines, an aging audience and broader shifts in media consumption away from television. At the same time, her critics have alleged that Weiss has injected her own political views into the network’s news coverage. Most recently, her editorial leadership came under scrutiny when Status’ Oliver Darcy reported that a CBS editor pushed back on including the number of Palestinians killed by Israel in a report on the anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attacks on Israel. CBS reported the Gaza death toll in a morning story about the Hamas attack, but not in its evening news report. Weiss, who noted that CBS has about 1,200 people in the newsroom, said she wasn’t involved in editing the stories. She likened the issue of including the Gaza death toll to how a news organization might cover the anniversary of the September 2001 al Qaeda terrorist attack on New York. She said it was “a question of taste” to focus on the victims of the Hamas attacks rather than the Palestinian victims of Israel’s bombings that followed. “You can make a legitimate argument on either side of that. It seemed like in the morning we went with one perspective. In the evening, we went with another,” Weiss said. “I don’t think there’s anything scandalous or controversial about that.” Weiss defended the network’s approach to covering national and world events, arguing that it is guided by a desire to ensure “the information that people are getting is accurate and fair, and again, reflects reality.” She pointed to Lesley Stahl’s investigative report on Israeli settler violence in the West Bank this month and the way correspondent Matt Gutman has covered the Israeli election. “The myth that anyone has a view from nowhere and is a perfectly blank slate, has been exploded by social media,” she said. “The question is whether or not you can strive to get outside of your own perspective to understand what your blind spots are and to make sure that the product, the information that people are getting, is accurate and fair.” Weiss indicated that CBS could test subscriptions after focusing on making content viewers would want to pay for. CBS doesn’t have such paywalls now, though its content is available on the subscription based Paramount+ streaming app. “I’m a total believer” in subscription-based pricing, Weiss said. “And so, obviously, that’s the future.” ‘Civilizational Role’ There’s been wide speculation that Skydance CEO David Ellison could seek to consolidate CBS and CNN following the completion of Skydance’s buyout this month of Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns CNN. That cable news network has around 3,000 employees worldwide, while CBS has far fewer staffers. Weiss didn’t address whether layoffs at the combined company’s news operations are on the table. She acknowledged misgivings over the topic among staffers, saying “everyone feels anxiety whether or not their company has just merged with another giant company as ours had.” Still, she spoke favorably about CNN’s potential. “The possibilities here are really, really incredible,” she said. “CNN is an unbelievable organization.” Asked whether she would want to run CNN, Weiss said: “I want to focus on doing CBS News, trust me. This is a big enough challenge.” CNN CEO Mark Thompson was previously the chief executive of The New York Times when Weiss was an opinion columnist and made a fiery exit, claiming that the newspaper’s staff was hostile to other political points of view. Weiss said she and Thompson recently laughed about the episode during a plane ride. Asked about declining ratings and her overhaul of CBS’ flagship show, “60 Minutes”—the network’s management has fired several prominent staffers, including longtime correspondent Scott Pelley, roiling the team—Weiss defended the changes she’s made to the show, which she said is doing “tremendously well.” “I am focused on transforming the business,” she said. In response to a question about the decline in ratings at “60 Minutes,” she said: “I could never build anything if I were focused on the precise number of people that happen to tune in to the second feature on 60 Minutes on a given Sunday.” Weiss dismissed the idea that Trump has been particularly sympathetic to CBS and Ellison, noting the U.S. president has called her a “gay dictator.” (Weiss is married to the journalist and The Free Press co-founder Nellie Bowles.) Weiss noted that the Trump administration has been a loud critic on social media of CBS’ work, including journalist Gianna Toboni’s reporting on the U.S. government’s deportations of immigrants to countries that aren’t their country of origin. Weiss said her “only way to function” as the leader of CBS is to “put the blinders on, tune out the noise and focus,” when discussing what it is like to be in the media spotlight. Otherwise her “entire life” would be devoted to being “a reply guy on the internet,” she said. She said of her new role, “I’m not doing anything I’m doing for popularity’s sake.” “Journalism and journalists have a civilizational role to play,” she said. “And that’s my focus.”

title: At Peak Energy, the Focus is on Avoiding the Missteps of a Big Battery Industry Failure
content: General Motors–backed startup Peak Energy boasts that it’s on a pathway to undercut China’s dominance of the massive batteries that power AI data centers and the grid. Its approach involves deploying an entirely different chemistry from the lithium-based ones China controls. But success, Peak executives say, requires always keeping a dreaded word in mind: Northvolt. In one of modern history’s worst business failures, Swedish battery maker Northvolt went bankrupt last year after squandering some $13 billion in equity and debt its founders had raised with the goal of building a European battery behemoth. The collapse made Northvolt a cautionary tale in the battery industry. The company seemed to have the wind at its back: It had $55 billion in orders and the support of Volkswagen and BMW, in addition to the EU. Yet it never managed to reach commercial production. Northvolt’s failure is a particularly top-of-mind lesson for Peak Energy co-founder and CEO Landon Mossburg, former president of Northvolt’s North America arm and a former Tesla executive. Mossburg co-founded Peak in 2023 to build sodium-ion stationary storage batteries that would leapfrog the lithium-based ones currently dominating backup power for AI data centers, the grid and other industrial deployments. Last week, Peak announced that it had raised a $108 million Series B round, led by GM, to fund the build-out of the first stage of a 4-gigawatt-hour sodium-ion battery assembly plant in Sacramento, Calif., enough to power roughly 2.8 million homes for an hour. GM previously said its investment in Peak was approximately $30 million. The Sacramento plant plans to fulfill $1.1 billion in orders starting in the first quarter of next year. Eventually, Mossburg wants Peak, in a partnership with GM, to make multiple components of the battery, including the cathodes and cells as well as the raw powders that go into making them. Tesla has successfully begun manufacturing cathodes, along with battery cells, showing that it’s possible to carry out what Peak has in mind. But in a conversation this week, Mossburg seemed a lot less focused on that and far more mindful of Northvolt’s fatal missteps. Chief among those, in his view, was its attempt to do too much at once, which resulted in mastering little . “The contrast is very stark for me,” Mossburg told me, “because I went from Tesla to Northvolt. And one clearly worked, and the other one clearly didn’t.” Peak is hardly alone in its fixation. Since its collapse, Northvolt has become an industry byword for everything that could possibly go wrong in producing batteries. In 2017, two former Tesla executives, Peter Carlsson and Paolo Cerruti, launched Northvolt. They rapidly raised $13 billion for what they sold as a European battery champion that would compete on equal ground with industry giants, including Chinese behemoth Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd. Carlsson and Cerruti began splashing around the cash, launching divisions to refine lithium, make cathodes, build complete cells and recycle them—all functions usually carried out by stand-alone companies. They also set out to build plants not only at home in Sweden but also in Germany, Poland, Norway and Canada. They acquired Cuberg, a California startup that was developing next-generation aviation batteries. By 2024, however, Northvolt was still unable to reliably make battery cells at its flagship Swedish plant, as I reported at the time . Northvolt’s “first cathode plant didn’t work pretty much at all,” Mossburg said. In summer 2025, Lyten—a relatively tiny San Jose, Calif., startup— scooped up most of Northvolt’s assets for pennies on the dollar. Mossburg said he is intent on avoiding these blunders. His business thesis is that sodium—1,000 times more prevalent in the Earth’s crust than lithium—will be cheaper than lithium once manufacturers scale up processing it. And if that processing occurs outside China, sodium would also reduce lithium’s geopolitical risks for the U.S. That’s if everything goes well. To avoid what happened to Northvolt, he said, Peak will do things one at a time. First, it will assemble batteries in Sacramento. Later, it will manufacture the sodium-ion cells it is currently developing alongside GM. Mossburg also intends to make cathodes. “We have told everybody who’s asked us to help catalyze the sodium-ion supply chain, which we’re very interested in doing, [that the] way to do it is sequentially and do it very, very fast sequentially. Don’t do it in parallel,” Mossburg said. Where things can go wrong for battery makers like Peak is when they try to do everything at the same time, he said. Invariably, hiccups arise in the development or supply of one component or more. “You have a whole supply chain that needs to run together, and it’s the first time all of these factories are going to come online,” he said. “They all have to come online at the exact same time, just like a concert. If anything’s delayed, the whole thing is delayed. And you’re going to have some stuff delayed, especially as you get into active material production. “Building three businesses at once like Northvolt did is pretty tough,” Mossburg said. “And you don’t have to, because you can do it just as fast. You just do it sequentially.”

title: The Download: AI agent tracking and climate feedback loops
content:
The Download: AI agent tracking and climate feedback loops
Plus: Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
—Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance.
AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, from hacking websites to accessing private government files. In many cases, they’ve eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.
As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability.
In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. Because right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools.
Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
Climate change itself increasingly fuels climate change. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up global temperatures, creating dangerous feedback loops that aren’t fully represented in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.
Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming. Now, a growing number of observations and studies are indicating how powerful these cascading effects could be. By extension, they’re also showing how much faster the planet may warm this century.
Read more about the dangerous feedback loops accelerating global warming.
—James Temple
This article is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
Are we there yet? Solid-state batteries
Lithium-ion batteries power everything from personal electronics to grid-scale energy storage, but their liquid electrolytes have drawbacks, not least a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer.
The technology promises faster charging, longer life, greater energy density and improved safety, and a new generation of companies aims to bring it to market. If their bets pan out, the tech could ease the shift away from fossil fuels.
Find out how close solid-state batteries are to delivering on their promise.
—Alexander C. Kaufman
This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue.

title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
content:
This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to
on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent
accessed
private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.
AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why
EU regulators
US agencies
are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.
Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today.
As agents roll out across critical sectors, from
government
medicine
, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences.  And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires
observability
: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent
research
shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.
Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.
With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we
the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.
The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken.
Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from.
Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it.
OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have
yet to be finalized
. The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the
privacy implications
of agent ID that links to real people.
Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used.
No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.
AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist.
Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here:
NIST’s agent standards initiative
in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.
No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too.
Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance.
Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.
Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.
A study in
Environmental Research Letters
in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires,
hotter lakes and reservoirs
, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the
2.6°C of warming
above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to
monthslong heat waves
and expose
hundreds of millions
of people to flooding.
None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.
A separate
analysis published in
One Earth
in March
, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.
Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.
At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the
Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project
, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.
But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.
So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in
a recent feature story
). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has
backed lab research
on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.
Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into
suppressing the lightning strikes
that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.
Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.
The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.

Von Karlsruhe über Zürich nach Bremen: Am 1. Oktober 2026 hat Prof. Dr. sc. ETH Julian Ferchow die Professur für Produktentwicklung und Produktlebenszyklus-Management am Fachbereich Produktionstechnik – Maschinenbau und Verfahrenstechnik der Universität Bremen übernommen. Gleichzeitig ist er auch in die Geschäftsführung des BIBA – Bremer Institut für Produktion und Logistik an der Universität Bremen eingetreten und leitet nun den BIBA-Bereich Informations- und kommunikationstechnische Anwendungen in der Produktion (IKAP). Er folgt auf Prof. Dr.-Ing. habil. Klaus-Dieter Thoben.
In der Forschung interessiert sich Ferchow für die Zukunft der Produktentwicklung und Produktion. Die Systeme, Prozesse, Organisationen und Netzwerke von Morgen arbeiten und entscheiden datenbasiert und lernend mit Unterstützung durch künstliche Intelligenz (KI). So nutzen zum Beispiel KI-Tools Daten aus dem gesamten Produktlebenszyklus, um innovative Konstruktionsvarianten vorzuschlagen, die wirtschaftlich, ressourcen- und energieeffizient sowie auf Wiederverwendung ausgelegt sind. Ingenieurinnen und Ingenieure steuern diese Prozesse und bewerten die Varianten.
Ferchows wissenschaftliche Arbeit zielt zum einen darauf ab, die Digitalisierung der Konstruktion und Fertigung ganzheitlich über alle Phasen des Produktlebenszyklus umzusetzen. Zum anderen forscht er zum industriellen Einsatz von KI-Tools für die Konstruktion, zu Advanced-Manufacturing-Technologien und zur Robotik. Im Mittelpunkt steht dabei stets der Mensch in seiner sich wandelnden Rolle und im Kontext neuer KI-Tools – sowohl in der Entwicklung als auch in der Anwendung.
Ein entscheidender Erfolgsfaktor: Technologietransfer
Damit widmet sich Ferchow grundlegenden industriellen Herausforderungen: Es gilt, zunehmend komplexere Produkte in immer kürzerer Zeit zu entwickeln und dabei stetig weniger Ressourcen einzusetzen. Die Etablierung einer wettbewerbsfähigen Kreislaufwirtschaft sei dabei einer der wichtigsten Faktoren, sagt er. Ob zum Beispiel Klimawandel, demografischer Wandel oder der strukturelle Wandel in den globalen Lieferketten – in Produktion und Logistik bedarf es ganzheitlicher Betrachtungen der Prozesse. Die Wirtschaft braucht immer schneller Lösungen. Das Tempo beim Technologietransfer wird zunehmend zum entscheidenden Erfolgsfaktor.
Das BIBA steht für Dialog und Transfer. So auch Ferchow: „Für die Forschung ist es zentral, einen engen Praxisbezug zu haben und einen intensiven Austausch zu pflegen. Wichtig für den Technologietransfer ist es auch, dass Unternehmen wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse und technologische Innovationen bestenfalls schon in der Forschungsphase in realitätsnahen Umgebungen praktisch erleben und erproben können, ohne bereits in großem Maßstab investieren zu müssen. Zum Beispiel mithilfe von Demonstratoren.“
„Für die Industrie lassen sich neue Technologien durch Forschungsprojekte frühzeitig nutzbar machen“, sagt Ferchow. „So können Unternehmen ihre Wettbewerbsfähigkeit stärken und sich einen Vorsprung am Markt verschaffen. Ich verstehe mich da als Sparringspartner auf Augenhöhe, als ein Bindeglied zwischen der theoretischen Forschung und der industriellen Anwendung.“
Am BIBA mit seinen interdisziplinären Kompetenzen zum Beispiel auf den Feldern Informatik, Produktionstechnik und integrierter Produktentwicklung finde er hierfür ein ideales Umfeld vor, auf das weiter aufgebaut werden könne. Zudem sei das Institut sehr gut in internationalen Projekten aufgestellt und rage durch ein starkes Projektmanagement heraus, sagt Ferchow. Ein Fokus seiner wissenschaftlichen Arbeit in den vergangenen Jahren lag im Bereich generatives Design. Dem wolle er sich künftig auch am BIBA intensiv widmen.
„Besonderes Potenzial“
In der Lehre setzt Ferchow stark auf die praxisnahe Projektarbeit in Teams in realen Umgebungen. Die enge Verknüpfung des BIBA mit der Universität sowie seine disziplinen- und institutionen-übergreifende Arbeit in vielfältigen Netzwerken bieten ihm dabei zahlreiche Optionen. „Durch die künstliche Intelligenz wandeln sich die Bedarfe der Unternehmen und die Berufsbilder im Ingenieurwesen sehr stark“, sagt Ferchow. Er wolle die Kompetenzen der Folgegenerationen in der Produktentwicklung zukunftsfähig forcieren und freue sich über die vielen Möglichkeiten, die sich ihm dafür in Bremen eröffneten: „Ein besonderes Potenzial in Forschung und Lehre.“ Er sei sehr beeindruckt von der Uni, dem BIBA sowie der Weltoffenheit und Aufgeschlossenheit der Menschen in der Hansestadt. Neugierig und gespannt starte er in den neuen Lebensabschnitt.
Prof. Dr. sc. ETH Julian Ferchow
Vor seinem Maschinenbau-Studium mit dem Schwerpunkt Produktentwicklung und Konstruktion am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT) absolvierte Julian Ferchow eine Industriemechaniker-Ausbildung und erlangte danach auf dem Zweiten Bildungsweg die Allgemeine Hochschulreife. Nach dem Studium forschte er als Wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter bei der Inspire AG und promovierte an der Eidgenössischen Technischen Hochschule Zürich (ETH Zürich) im Maschinenbau zu dem Thema „Industrialisierung der Additiven Fertigungsverfahren“.
Anschließend hatte Ferchow die Gruppenleitung Design for New Technologies bei der Inspire AG und der ETH Zürich in dem Bereich Industrialisierung von neuen Technologien in der Konstruktion und Fertigung inne und arbeitete als Dozent an der ETH Zürich. Durch seine 10-jährige Arbeit an der Schnittstelle zwischen Forschung und Industrie bringt er auch eine vielfältige Erfahrung und Expertise im Transfer in das BIBA und in den Uni-Fachbereich Produktionstechnik ein.

Blut abnehmen, ins Labor schicken, auf Ergebnisse warten: Wer wissen will, wie es um seinen Stoffwechsel steht, braucht häufig aufwendige Untersuchungen. Zwei Masterstudenten der Universität Duisburg-Essen wollen das ändern: Mit ihrem Projekt VitaMetis entwickeln sie ein tragbares Sensorsystem, das künftig mehrere Stoffwechselwerte kontinuierlich und ohne Eingriff in den Körper erfassen soll. Mit dieser Idee haben sich Abdulmohaimen Algamoudi und Abdullah Osman Gwela für den bundesweiten COSIMA-Wettbewerb qualifiziert. Am 12. und 13. November stellen sie ihr Projekt auf der Elektronikmesse electronica in München vor.
Harnstoff, Vitamine oder sogar Hormone: Solche Stoffwechselwerte sollen sich eines Tages genauso einfach beobachten lassen wie heute schon Puls oder Bewegung mit einer Smartwatch. Daran arbeiten Abdulmohaimen Algamoudi (27) und Abdullah Osman Gwela (28) von der Universität Duisburg-Essen (UDE), die im Master Elektrotechnik studieren. ‚Wenn der Körper spricht und die Technologie zuhört‘ – dieser Gedanke steckt hinter ihrem Projekt VitaMetis, an dem sie seit über einem Jahr tüfteln. In München werden sie nun einen funktionsfähigen Demonstrator vorstellen.
So soll VitaMetis funktionieren: Ein kleiner Sensor-Patch auf der Haut misst kontinuierlich verschiedene Stoffwechselwerte. Dafür nutzt er ein optisches Verfahren, das bestimmte Substanzen im Schweiß erkennt und ihre Konzentration bestimmt. Möglich macht das eine Sensortechnologie mit winzigen Kohlenstoffröhrchen, sogenannten Carbon Nanotubes (CNTs), die am Duisburger Fraunhofer IMS zur Anwendungsreife gebracht wurde. Mit einer Art Handscanner lassen sich die Daten dann aus dem Patch auslesen – ganz ohne Blutabnahme oder sonstigen Eingriff in den Körper.
Bis zur Marktreife ist es noch ein weiter Weg. Doch die beiden Studenten haben ein klares Ziel: „Wir möchten eine Technologie entwickeln, die möglichst vielen Menschen zugutekommt. Das können gesunde Menschen, Sportler:innen, Schwangere, aber auch Nierenpatient:innen sein“; erklärt Abdulmohaimen Algamoudi. „In Ländern mit schlechter Gesundheitsversorgung wie Libyen, wo wir herkommen, wäre ein tragbares Sensorsystem wie VitaMetis ein Segen“, ergänzt Abdullah Osman Gwela.
Für die Umsetzung konnten die Studenten bereits Sponsoren gewinnen. Auch von der Universität und ihrem Betreuer Prof. Dr. Karsten Seidl aus dem Fachgebiet Elektronische Bauelemente und Schaltungen erhalten sie Unterstützung. Und das Ziel für München steht fest: „Wir fahren nach München“, betont Algamoudi, „um COSIMA zu gewinnen!“
COSIMA als Sprungbrett
Der vom Verband der Elektrotechnik, Elektronik und Informationstechnik (VDE) ausgerichtete COSIMA-Wettbewerb richtet sich an studentische Teams, die innovative Anwendungen der Mikrosystemtechnik entwickeln. Den drei bestplatzierten Teams winkt u.a. die Qualifikation für einen internationalen Wettbewerb.

Räume erleben, bevor sie gebaut sind
Neues IEQ-Lab am Hermann-Rietschel-Institut der TU Berlin verbindet Klimaraum und Virtual Reality und erforscht, wie sich Energieeffizienz, Gesundheit und Komfort in Gebäuden zusammenbringen lassen
Wie warm soll ein Raum sein, wie viel Licht brauchen wir und wann empfinden wir die Luft als angenehm? Im neuen IEQ-Lab des Hermann-Rietschel-Instituts (HRI) der TU Berlin können solche Fragen unter genau kontrollierten und zugleich realitätsnahen Bedingungen untersucht werden. Das Labor verbindet dafür einen hochflexiblen Klimaraum mit Virtual Reality. Temperatur, Luft, Licht und die visuelle Gestaltung eines Raumes lassen sich gezielt verändern und miteinander kombinieren. So können Forscher*innen untersuchen, wie unterschiedliche Bedingungen auf Gesundheit, Wohlbefinden und Leistungsfähigkeit wirken – und wie Gebäude künftig zugleich komfortabel, gesund und energieeffizient geplant werden können.
Virtuelle Räume, reales Klima
Die Besonderheit des Labors liegt in der engen Kopplung von Virtual Reality und real erzeugten Raumbedingungen. Versuchspersonen sehen durch eine VR-Brille beispielsweise einen Büroraum mit bestimmten Fenstern, Lichtverhältnissen oder Raumgeometrien. Gleichzeitig erzeugt der Klimaraum genau die dazu passenden thermischen Bedingungen. Öffnet eine Versuchsperson in der virtuellen Realität beispielsweise ein Fenster, spürt sie unmittelbar den damit einhergehenden Luftzug – und zwar aus genau der Richtung, aus der er auch im virtuellen Raum kommt.
54 einzeln regelbare Oberflächenmodule an Wänden und Decke können dafür geheizt oder gekühlt werden. Elektrische Heiztextilien und wassergeführte Kapillarrohrmatten ermöglichen schnelle Temperaturänderungen. Innerhalb von nur 30 Sekunden können sich die Oberflächentemperaturen um bis zu fünf Kelvin verändern. Eine leistungsfähige Klimaanlage erlaubt darüber hinaus die präzise Einstellung von Lufttemperatur, Luftfeuchtigkeit und Luftströmung. Auch unterschiedliche Lüftungsformen wie Misch- und Quelllüftung können nachgebildet werden.
Parallel dazu erfassen zahlreiche Sensoren unter anderem Luft- und operative Temperatur, Luftfeuchtigkeit, CO₂-Konzentration und Beleuchtungsstärke. Auf diese Weise können thermische, visuelle und lufthygienische Einflüsse sowohl einzeln als auch in ihrem Zusammenspiel untersucht und mit der Wahrnehmung der Proband*innen verknüpft werden.
„Der große Vorteil des IEQ-Labs ist, dass wir Innenräume unter genau kontrollierten Bedingungen realitätsnah untersuchen können. Thermische, visuelle und akustische Bedingungen sowie die Luftqualität lassen sich gezielt und reproduzierbar verändern – und mit ganz unterschiedlichen virtuellen Raumkonzepten kombinieren. Das ist in Feldstudien nur eingeschränkt möglich. So können wir systematisch untersuchen, wie verschiedene Raumkonzepte auf den Menschen wirken und wie sich dabei zugleich die Energieeffizienz optimieren lässt“, sagt Lukas Schmitt.
Wann ist ein Raum wirklich gut?
Das Labor ist Teil eines grundlegenderen Forschungsansatzes des Projekts EnOB: GEnEff (Neuartige Bewertung der Gebäudeenergieeffizienz). Bislang wird die Energieeffizienz eines Gebäudes vor allem daran gemessen, wie viel Energie es im Betrieb benötigt. Welchen Komfort und welche Innenraumqualität dieser Energieeinsatz für die Menschen tatsächlich erzeugt, wird dagegen nur eingeschränkt berücksichtigt. Das Forschungsteam am HRI hat deshalb einen Ansatz entwickelt, der beide Seiten miteinander verbindet. Die sogenannte GEnEff-Kennzahl setzt die Wahrscheinlichkeit, dass Nutzer*innen das Innenraumklima akzeptieren, ins Verhältnis zum dafür notwendigen spezifischen Energiebedarf.
Energieeffizienz soll damit nicht mehr allein anhand des Verbrauchs beurteilt werden, sondern auch anhand des tatsächlich erzielten Nutzens für die Menschen im Gebäude.
Wie wichtig diese Perspektive ist, zeigte bereits eine Befragung in zwei nachhaltig zertifizierten Bürogebäuden. Zwischen dokumentierten Zertifizierungswerten und der tatsächlichen Wahrnehmung der Nutzer*innen fanden die Forschenden teilweise Abweichungen von bis zu 50 Prozent – insbesondere bei der Raumluftqualität und den Möglichkeiten, das Raumklima selbst zu beeinflussen.
Temperatur verändert auch die Wahrnehmung der Luft
Im IEQ-Lab wurde der neue Ansatz bereits in einer Studie mit Proband*innen erprobt. Dabei kombinierten die Forschenden unterschiedliche operative Temperaturen zwischen 20 und 28 Grad Celsius mit verschiedenen Beleuchtungsstärken, während Luftqualität und Akustik konstant gehalten wurden.
Die Ergebnisse zeigen, wie eng die einzelnen Faktoren der Innenraumqualität miteinander verbunden sind. So wurden warme Räume von den Versuchspersonen als Räume mit schlechterer Luftqualität wahrgenommen – unabhängig davon, wie hoch der tatsächliche CO₂-Gehalt war. In der Untersuchung hatte die thermische Behaglichkeit mit 33 Prozent den größten Einfluss auf die Gesamtbewertung des Raums. Es folgten die wahrgenommene Raumluftqualität mit 26 Prozent, die visuelle Behaglichkeit mit 23 Prozent und die Akustik mit 18 Prozent.
Eine anschließende Feldstudie an 16 Arbeits- und Wohnorten bestätigte, dass sich die im Labor gewonnenen Erkenntnisse auch auf reale Gebäude übertragen lassen. Die im IEQ-Lab entwickelte Komfortfunktion sagte die Bewertung der Innenraumqualität in 81 Prozent der untersuchten Fälle richtig voraus.
Energie sparen, ohne an Raumqualität zu verlieren
Mit dem IEQ-Lab steht der TU Berlin nun eine Forschungsinfrastruktur zur Verfügung, mit der sich das Zusammenspiel von Mensch, Gebäude und Energieverbrauch wesentlich differenzierter untersuchen lässt. Künftig können weitere Einflussgrößen der Innenraumqualität integriert und unterschiedliche Gebäudekonzepte bereits unter Laborbedingungen erprobt werden.
Die Forschung ist insbesondere mit Blick auf Klimawandel und steigende Anforderungen an die Energieeffizienz von Gebäuden relevant. Denn ein möglichst niedriger Energiebedarf allein macht noch kein gutes Gebäude. Entscheidend ist vielmehr, mit möglichst wenig Energie eine hohe Qualität des Innenraums zu erreichen. Die im Projekt entwickelten Methoden könnten deshalb langfristig auch für Zertifizierungsverfahren, Normen und Richtlinien interessant werden. Ziel ist eine Gebäudeplanung, bei der Energieeinsparungen nicht zulasten von Gesundheit, Komfort und Zufriedenheit der Nutzer*innen gehen.
Auch über das GEnEff-Projekt hinaus soll das IEQ-Lab für Forschungs- und Entwicklungsprojekte sowie in der universitären Lehre eingesetzt werden. Es schafft damit neue Möglichkeiten, die Gebäude der Zukunft aus der Perspektive der Menschen zu entwickeln, die sich täglich in ihnen aufhalten.
Das IEQ-Lab ist im Forschungsprojekt „EnOB: GEnEff“ entstanden, das vom Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie (BMWE) gefördert wurde. Beteiligt war neben dem Hermann-Rietschel-Institut der TU Berlin das Fachgebiet Versorgungsplanung und Versorgungstechnik der Universität der Künste Berlin unter Leitung von Prof. Dr. Christoph Nytsch-Geusen.

ATHENE Startup Award UP26@itsa auf in Nürnberg verliehen
1. Platz: Fuzzware – Sicherheitstests für eingebettete Software
2. Platz: Complioty – CRA-Compliance für Maschinenbau
3. Platz: RedCastle - SOC für den Mittelstand
Nürnberg/Darmstadt, 28. Oktober 2026 – Fuzzware ist Sieger des ATHENE Startup Awards UP26@it-sa. Das Startup aus Bochum gewann am Mittwochnachmittag beim Live-Pitch-Event auf der it-sa Expo&Congress den 1. Platz und sicherte sich damit ein Preisgeld von 7.500 Euro. Das Unternehmen überzeugte mit einer innovativen Lösung zur Testung von eingebetteten Systemen. Complioty aus München belegte den 2. Platz und erhielt 5.000 Euro für eine CRA-Compliance-Lösung. Der 3. Platz ging an Redcastle aus Heubach. Für sein Mittelstands-SOC erhielt das junge Unternehmen ein Preisgeld von 2.500 Euro.
Die besten Cybersecurity Startups der DACH-Region
Am 28. Oktober 2026 wurde der ATHENE Startup Award zum neunten Mal im Rahmen der it-sa Expo&Congress verliehen. Auf der großen Messe-Bühne pitchten die fünf Startup-Finalisten vor Fachpublikum und Jury um den Sieg. Nach jedem Pitch stellte die Jury kritische Fragen, bevor diese zur finalen Abstimmung schritt. Am Ende gab es folgende Gewinner:
1. Platz: Fuzzware – Sicherheitstests für eingebettete Software
Fuzzware verbessert die Sicherheit eingebetteter Systeme: Das Tool ermöglicht Fuzzing kompletter Firmware-Systeme ohne physische Hardware und setzt dabei auf eine gründliche Analyse allein auf Basis des Binärcodes.
2. Platz: Complioty – CRA-Compliance für Maschinenbau
Complioty macht Product Security für den Maschinenbau zum laufenden Prozess statt zum Einmalprojekt. Ihre Plattform erstellt automatisiert Software-Stücklisten, überwacht sie kontinuierlich auf Schwachstellen und unterstützt den gesamten Weg bis zur Compliance mit dem Cyber Resilience Act ab, der ab Dezember 2027 zur Pflicht wird.
3. Platz: RedCastle - SOC für den Mittelstand
RedCastle betreibt ein KI-gestütztes Security Operations Center für den Mittelstand – mit eigenen Analysten, eigener Forensik und Betrieb in Deutschland. Ein Monitoring-Dienst analysiert die Angriffsfläche mittelständischer Unternehmen, bewertet diese mit Hilfe von KI und gibt IT-Sicherheitsempfehlungen.
„In diesem Jahr haben beide erstplatzierten Startups eine laufende StartUpSecure Förderung des Bundesforschungsministeriums erhalten. Das beweist: Hochinnovative Gründungen aus der Forschung überzeugen durch ihre Marktfähigkeit.“ sagt Clara Pfeuffer, Leiterin des ATHENE Digital Hub Cybersecurity. „Unser Award schafft Sichtbarkeit für die Innovationspower in Deutschland und der DACH-Region.“
Über den ATHENE Startup Award UP@it-sa
Der ATHENE Startup Award UP@it-sa würdigt erfolgreiche Neugründungen und aussichtsreiche junge Unternehmen im Bereich IT-Sicherheit und Datenschutz. Innovative Produkte und attraktive Geschäftsmodelle stehen dabei im Mittelpunkt. Der Preis ist eine Initiative des nationalen Forschungszentrums für angewandte Cybersicherheit ATHENE bzw. des ATHENE Digital Hub Cybersecurity und der it-sa. Der Award wird seit 2018 auf Europas führender IT-Sicherheitsfachmesse it-sa Expo&Congress vergeben.
