KI-Leuchtturmprojekt GreenTwin zeigt Virtual Reality-Demonstrator und Prof. Dr. Stefan Naumann diskutiert in Berlin auf dem Podium über den ökologischen Gesamtwert von KI.
„Green AI neu denken“ lautete das Motto der AI CONFERENCE 2026, zu der das Bundesumweltministerium (BMU) am 6. Oktober nach Berlin eingeladen hatte. Ausgerichtet von der Zukunft - Umwelt - Gesellschaft (ZUG) gGmbH und eröffnet von Bundesumweltminister Carsten Schneider, diskutierten Fachleute aus Forschung, Wirtschaft und Politik, wie sich der Energie- und Ressourcenverbrauch von Künstlicher Intelligenz messen und senken lässt. Der Umwelt-Campus Birkenfeld der Hochschule Trier war gleich doppelt vertreten.
Am Showcase-Stand stellten Kristof Ueding, Paul Rübenich und Max Dengler das KI-Leuchtturmprojekt GreenTwin vor. Das vom BMU geförderte Verbundprojekt mit der Rheinisch-Westfälischen Technischen Hochschule Aachen, dem Deutschen Forschungszentrum für Künstliche Intelligenz (DFKI) und der Firma PSI Logistics hat für die Region Birkenfeld einen KI-gestützten Marktplatz entwickelt, der Einkäufe, Lieferungen und Mitfahrten an Menschen vermittelt, die ohnehin unterwegs sind und so Autofahrten auf dem Land einspart. Mitgebracht hatte das Team seinen VR-Demonstrator und Besucherinnen und Besucher konnten durch einen virtuellen Dorfladen gehen und erleben, wie Nahversorgung im Dorf künftig aussehen kann.
Auf dem Podium diskutierte Professor Stefan Naumann im Panel mit dem Titel „KI-Nutzen versus Emissionen“ gemeinsam mit Felix Behrens (Öko-Institut) und Anita Schüttler (Bundesverband Green Software), moderiert von Larissa Holzki (Handelsblatt), wie sich der Nutzen von KI gegen ihren ökologischen Fußabdruck aufrechnen lässt. Naumann leitet am Umwelt-Campus die Arbeitsgruppe Umwelt- und Nachhaltigkeitsinformatik und beschäftigt sich damit, den Energie- und Ressourcenverbrauch von Software messbar zu machen. So wurden die Kriterien des Umweltzeichens Blauer Engel für Software maßgeblich in Birkenfeld mitentwickelt. In die Diskussion brachte er die Sicht der Green Software-Forschung ein: Ob KI der Umwelt unterm Strich nützt, lässt sich nur dann belastbar beantworten, wenn auch der Verbrauch der KI selbst gemessen und transparent gemacht wird.
Die Delegation des Umwelt-Campus Birkenfeld freute sich sehr, GreenTwin am Showcase-Stand und die Birkenfelder Forschung bei einer so hochkarätig besetzten Konferenz präsentieren zu können. Weitere Forschungsprojekte in diesem Umfeld laufen bereits und in den Studiengängen am Campus, unter anderem Angewandte Informatik und KI sowie Umwelt- und Nachhaltigkeitsinformatik, werden solche Themen auch in der Lehre vermittelt.
Hintergrund
GreenTwin („Grüner digitaler Zwilling mit Künstlicher Intelligenz für CO2-sparende kooperative Mobilität und Logistik im ländlichen Raum“) wurde im Rahmen der Förderinitiative „KI-Leuchttürme für Umwelt, Klima, Natur und Ressourcen“ des Bundesumweltministeriums gefördert. Mit welchen Strukturen sorgt die Natur dafür, dass Schildkrötenpanzer oder Knochen nicht so leicht brechen? Im Rahmen eines Praxisprojekts haben Maschinenbau-Studierende der Hochschule Bielefeld am Campus Minden die Konzepte der Natur analysiert und sie als bionische Strukturen in ein technisches Produkt übertragen. Entstanden ist ein Fahrradhelm, der optimal vor Stößen schützt – besser sogar, als manch handelsüblicher Helm.
Minden (hsbi). Ob er seinen Kopf freiwillig hingehalten hat? „Ich wurde gar nicht gefragt!“ Alex Balzer lacht und beruhigt: „Es tat aber nicht weh, und die Haare sind auch drangeblieben.“ Und so entstand mit Hilfe eines 3D-Scanners und -Druckers in strahlendem Blau ein exaktes Modell von Balzers Kopf: „Sozusagen der Dummy für unseren Fahrradhelm.“
Alex Balzer studiert im praxisintegrierten Bachelorstudiengang Maschinenbau am Campus Minden der Hochschule Bielefeld (HSBI), ist also zugleich in einem Unternehmen angestellt und durchläuft abwechselnd Theoriephasen an der Hochschule und Praxisphasen im Betrieb. Das sechste Semester bringt Theorie und Praxis auf spezielle Weise zusammen, und zwar im obligatorischen Praxisprojekt Angewandte Wissenschaft (PAW) – mittlerweile eine Institution in den praxisintegrierten Studiengängen Elektrotechnik, Wirtschaftsingenieurwesen und Maschinenbau am Campus Minden. „In den PAWs lernen die Studierenden, ihr theoretisches Hochschulwissen auf praxisnahe Problemstellungen anzuwenden“, erklärt Prof. Dr. Andreas Tenzler die Idee. Der Professor für Konstruktionstechnik sieht noch einen weiteren Vorteil: „Mit dem PAW wird auch wissenschaftliches Arbeiten eingeübt, indem die Studierenden sich selbstständig in neue Bereiche einarbeiten, an vorhandenes Wissen anschließen, es erweitern und neue Lösungswege finden – angewandte Forschung eben.“
Bionik – die Natur als Vorbild für technische Konstruktionen
Für sein diesjähriges PAW hat Tenzler deshalb ein Thema gewählt, das auch in der Forschung aktuell ist: Bionik. „Der Begriff setzt sich aus Biologie und Technik zusammen“, so Tenzler. „Es geht darum, Prinzipien und Phänomene aus der Natur in technische Anwendungen zu übertragen.“ Kein neuer Ansatz, weiß der Professor: „Schon Leonardo da Vinci hat nach dem Vorbild der Natur entworfen.“ Heute sei das wissenschaftliche Niveau aber so hoch, dass auch die technische Umsetzung gelinge. „Gerade im Bereich Gestaltung wird in der Konstruktion immer mehr darauf geschaut, welche Lösungen die Natur gefunden hat.“ Der Professor nennt als Beispiel die Schildkröte: „Ihr Panzer dient unter anderem als Schutz, als eine Art Stoßdämpfer, indem er Energie absorbieren kann.“ Tenzler interessiert die dahinterstehende Struktur: „Wie ist der Panzer aufgebaut? Und ließe sich die Struktur in eine technische Lösung überführen?“ Damit stand die Aufgabenstellung für sein PAW: „Die Gestaltung bionisch inspirierter Strukturen mit dem Ziel, sie in einem stoßabsorbierenden Produkt umzusetzen.“
Im CAD-Labor am Campus Minden legt Alex Balzer seinem Modell-Kopf einen blau-weißen Helm an. „Wir haben uns für die Gestaltung eines Fahrradhelms entschieden. Ein alltäglicher Gegenstand, mit dem jeder etwas anfangen kann“, erklärt der Student. Mit ihm zusammen machten sich noch Jan Bergmann, Niko Bloch, Felix Möller, Pascal Pogodda und Nalina Pucker an die Arbeit, allesamt Studierende im Bachelorstudiengang Maschinenbau. Zunächst galt es herauszufinden, welche bionischen Strukturen zu den Anforderungen an einen Fahrradhelm passen. Andreas Tenzler präzisiert: „Der Helm sollte eine hohe Energieabsorption und ein geringes Gewicht haben. Ein wichtiges Kriterium ist die Festigkeit – er sollte nicht auseinanderbrechen – und die Fertigungseignung ist ebenfalls wichtig. Der Helm sollte in Kunststoff realisierbar sein.“ Bei der Literaturrecherche kristallisierten sich schnell drei vielversprechende Kandidaten heraus: „Waben-, Baum- und Voronoi-Strukturen, wie sie etwa in Knochen zu finden sind, können Stöße besonders gut absorbieren“, erläutert Felix Möller. Durch ihre spezielle Geometrie sind sie so elastisch, dass sie sich verformen und die Stoßenergie besser verteilen können.
Sehr starke studentische Leistung: Materialsuche nach dem Ausschlussprinzip
Damit kam die nächste Herausforderung: „Biologische, organische Strukturen sind wegen ihrer Unregelmäßigkeit technisch schwer zu beschreiben. Die herkömmlichen CAD-Programme sind damit überfordert“, sagt Andreas Tenzler. Also recherchierten die Studierenden eine alternative Software, mit der sich bionische Strukturen modellieren lassen. Das Team arbeitete sich in einer Geschwindigkeit ein, die den Professor verblüffte: „Hier hätte ich mit viel mehr Problemen gerechnet, aber diese Kernaufgabe wurde sehr souverän gelöst.“ Mit der Struktur allein ließ sich aber noch kein Helm konstruieren. „Es galt auch, die optimale Stegdicke und den Füllgrad zu bestimmen, also das Verhältnis zwischen dem Volumen des festen Materials und dem Gesamtvolumen“, erklärt Felix Möller. Anders ausgedrückt: Wie porös musste und durfte die Struktur sein? Schließlich fehlte noch das Material: „Welcher Kunststoff bringt die passendsten Eigenschaften für die Umsetzung mit?“
Verschiedene Strukturen, Stegdicken, Füllgrade und Materialen – reichlich
Kombinationsmöglichkeiten. „Das war schon kompliziert“, bekennt Felix Möller, zeigt eine Schütte mit verschiedenfarbigen Kunststoffteilen, an verschiedenen Stellen gebrochen, verformt oder beschädigt, und grinst. „Wir haben viel ausprobiert.“ Das heißt: konstruiert, gefertigt, geprüft, verändert, erneut gefertigt, geprüft, wieder verändert, gefertigt usw. Schnell stellte sich immerhin heraus, dass das verwendete Material den größten Einfluss hatte. Möller: „Die gleiche Probe nur mit unterschiedlichen Materialien führte zu völlig anderen Ergebnissen.“ Damit zeigte sich auch, welches Material ausgeschlossen werden konnte: „PLA, also Polyactide, funktionierte überhaupt nicht“, sagt Möller. Stattdessen erwies sich TPU (Thermoplastisches Polyurethan) als sehr gut geeignet.
Am besten geeignet: die unregelmäßige und dennoch wabenähnliche Voronoi-Struktur
Am Prüfstand neben der Maschinenhalle spannt Nalina Pucker eine blaue Probe in die Druckprüfmaschine. „Wir brauchten einen sehr schnellen Verfahrweg, wie bei einer Fahrradfahrt“, erklärt die Studentin. Und sie brauchten klare Abbruchkriterien, bis zu welcher Kraft die Testreihen laufen sollten. „Zu schnell durften wir auch nicht werden, damit die Maschine nicht zerstört wird.“ Pucker startet die Prüfung, das blaue Kunststoffteil wird zusammengedrückt, verformt sich, hält – und besteht den Test. Auch die Fallprüfung gelingt mit Bravour. Nadine Pucker zeigt die Probe: „Mit der unregelmäßigen und dennoch wabenähnlichen Voronoi-Struktur lässt sich die einwirkende Kraft sehr gut abfangen.“ Und so konnte auch der bionische Fahrradhelm gefertigt werden.
Andreas Tenzler freut sich über das Ergebnis. „Unser Helm schützt sogar besser als manch handelsüblicher“, sagt er und deutet auf einen entzweigebrochenen Helm aus dem Fahrradladen, den die Studierenden zum Vergleich getestet hatten. Alex Balzer wundert das nicht. „Bei dem Kopf-Model“, scherzt er, setzt den maßgeschneiderten bionischen Helm auf und dreht eine Runde mit dem Rad auf dem Campus.

title: Neue Wege zur Interoperabilität von Robotern: Große KI-Modelle als Chance für das gemeinsame Handeln

Neue Wege zur Interoperabilität von Robotern: Große KI-Modelle als Chance für das gemeinsame Handeln

Impulspapier: Interoperabilität zwischen Robotiksystemen. Das Potenzial großer KI-Modelle
| Copyright:
Plattform Lernende System
Download
Ob Intralogistik, Produktion oder Rettungseinsatz: Wenn unterschiedliche Roboter gemeinsam Aufgaben erledigen sollen, müssen sie Informationen austauschen, deren Bedeutung verstehen und ihr Handeln aufeinander abstimmen können. Bisher war es mit viel Aufwand verbunden, die nötige Interoperabilität hierfür zu schaffen, etwa durch Standardisierung. Große KI-Modelle eröffnen neue Möglichkeiten, diese herzustellen. Ein neues Impulspapier der Plattform Lernende Systeme zeigt, wie solche KI-Modelle das Zusammenspiel von Robotiksystemen unterstützen können und welche Herausforderungen für einen zuverlässigen und sicheren Einsatz noch zu lösen sind
Eine Flugdrohne erkundet das Gelände, ein Roboterhund untersucht schwer zugängliche Bereiche, ein Fahrzeug transportiert Material: Bei einem Brand in einer Chemiefabrik könnten unterschiedliche Robotiksysteme ihre Fähigkeiten ergänzen. Auch bei der Obsternte oder beim Warentransport könnten Roboter mit anderen Robotern und mit Menschen zusammenarbeiten. In der Praxis erschweren jedoch unterschiedliche Schnittstellen und teils geschlossene Betriebssysteme das Zusammenspiel.
Vier Ebenen der Interoperabilität
Interoperabilität schafft die Grundlage für Kommunikation und Kooperation, bewirkt aber nicht selbst das gemeinsame Handeln. Bislang wird sie vor allem durch Standards für Schnittstellen, Protokolle oder Datenformate hergestellt. Solche Lösungen sind aufwendig und oft wenig flexibel. Besonders anspruchsvoll ist es, ein gemeinsames Verständnis von Informationen und deren Bedeutung für das Handeln herzustellen.
Das Impulspapier unterscheidet vier Ebenen der Interoperabilität: Die technische Ebene verbindet Systeme miteinander, die syntaktische Ebene sorgt für kompatible Datenformate. Die semantische Ebene betrifft die Bedeutung der ausgetauschten Informationen, die pragmatische Ebene das Verständnis für die Folgen von Handlungen in einem bestimmten Kontext. Erst auf dieser letzten Ebene lässt sich das Handeln von Systemen am besten aufeinander abstimmen.
Was große KI-Modelle leisten können
„Große KI-Modelle können in eleganter und effizienter Weise dabei helfen, Interoperabilität zwischen unterschiedlichen Robotiksystemen auf semantischem oder gar auf pragmatischem Niveau zu erreichen“, so Jürgen Beyerer, geschäftsführender Institutsleiter sowie Direktor des Fraunhofer-Instituts für Optronik, Systemtechnik und Bildauswertung (IOSB) in Karlsruhe und Inhaber des Lehrstuhls Interaktive Echtzeitsysteme am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT).
Neben großen Sprachmodellen kommen dafür auch Modelle infrage, die auf logisches Schlussfolgern (Reasoning), ausgerichtet sind oder Sprache, Sehen und Handeln verbinden. Sie können helfen, Informationen unterschiedlicher Systeme einzuordnen und für die Koordination nutzbar zu machen. Entscheidend sind das Weltwissen, das im Modell repräsentiert ist und mit Art und Umfang der Daten im Modelltraining zusammenhängt, sowie zusätzliche Kontextinformationen, die dem Modell im laufenden Betrieb zur Verfügung gestellt werden.
Zusammenarbeit benötigt verlässliches Weltwissen
„Roboter können im Verbund komplexe Handlungsstränge oder Missionen abarbeiten, wenn sie in der Lage sind, zuverlässig physisch zu interagieren, Informationen auszutauschen und zu interpretieren. Der Kern der Herausforderung liegt oft in der Autonomie und dem Weltmodell der Systeme. Heutige große generative KI-Modelle können hier Lücken schließen und Roboter koordinieren, durch zukünftige Modelle könnten sich sogar neue Formen von Interoperabilität etablieren“, erläutert Sirko Straube, Forschungsbereichsmanager Emergency Response and Recovery Management am Robotics Innovation Center der DFKI GmbH.
Gegenwärtige Modelle haben jedoch Grenzen. Ihnen fehlen häufig Aktivitätsdaten sowie domänenspezifische Daten. Sie erzeugen mitunter fehlerhafte Aussagen und verstehen Ursache und Wirkung nur eingeschränkt. Zudem gelingt es ihnen noch nicht zuverlässig, Objekte, Positionen oder Handlungen in präzise Angaben für physikalische Modelle zu übersetzen. Dadurch kann die Interoperabilität zeitweise „abreißen“ – mit Risiken für die funktionale und die Prozesssicherheit. Vielversprechend sind künftig zuverlässigere multimodale KI-Modelle, die Fakten in Echtzeit überprüfen und mithilfe physikalischer Simulationen und Weltmodellen die Folgen von Handlungen besser abschätzen können. Für den praktischen Einsatz müssen diese Fähigkeiten jedoch verlässlich verfügbar sein.
„Interoperabilität zwischen Robotern ist ein entscheidender Zukunftsbaustein, der die praktische Nutzung und das Zusammenspiel vielfältiger Robotiksysteme nachhaltig voranbringen wird. Die Forschung entwickelt bereits vielversprechende Projekte und Konzepte – nun gilt es, diese gemeinsam in marktfähige und anwendungsnahe Lösungen zu überführen. Dafür braucht es einen starken Schulterschluss zwischen Anwendern, Robotikherstellern und Forschung, um die Robotik gemeinsam auf das nächste Entwicklungsniveau zu heben“, fasst Johannes Hinckeldeyn, Director of Advanced Core Technologies bei der KION Group, zusammen.
Über das Impulspapier
Das Impulspapier „Interoperabilität zwischen Robotiksystemen – das Potenzial großer KI-Modelle“ wurde von Mitgliedern der Arbeitsgruppe „Lernfähige Robotiksysteme“ sowie der Arbeitsgruppe „Technologische Wegbereiter und Data Science“ der Plattform Lernende Systeme verfasst. Es steht zum kostenfreien Download bereit.
Über die Plattform Lernende Systeme
Die Plattform Lernende Systeme ist ein Netzwerk von Expertinnen und Experten zum Thema Künstliche Intelligenz (KI). Sie bündelt vorhandenes Fachwissen und fördert als unabhängiger Makler den interdisziplinären Austausch und gesellschaftlichen Dialog. Die knapp 200 Mitglieder aus Wissenschaft, Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft entwickeln in Arbeitsgruppen Positionen zu Chancen und Herausforderungen von KI und benennen Handlungsoptionen für ihre verantwortliche Gestaltung. Damit unterstützen sie den Weg Deutschlands zu einem führenden Anbieter von vertrauenswürdiger KI sowie den Einsatz der Schlüsseltechnologie in Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft. Die Plattform Lernende Systeme wurde 2017 vom Bundesforschungsministerium auf Anregung von acatech – Deutsche Akademie der Technikwissenschaften gegründet und wird von einem Lenkungskreis gesteuert. Die Leitung der Plattform liegt bei Dorothee Bär (Bundesministerin für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt) und Claudia Eckert (Präsidentin acatech). Mehr Info.

title: Forschungsprojekt TAUWIS entwickelt Verfahren zur zerstörungsfreien Inspektion von Unterwasserleitungen

Forschungsprojekt TAUWIS entwickelt Verfahren zur zerstörungsfreien Inspektion von Unterwasserleitungen

ROV des Fraunhofer IOSB-AST beim Einsatz am Müggelsee.
| Copyright:
Fraunhofer IOSB-AST
Download
Ilmenau, 29.10.2026: Ein teilautonomes Unterwasser-Inspektionssystem zur Infrastrukturdatenerfassung hat bei einem Praxistest im Müggelsee den Verlauf einer Wasserleitung erfasst und Fehlstellen geortet. Das im Forschungsprojekt TAUWIS entwickelte System kombiniert Sensoren zur elektro-magnetischen Inspektion, Sonar und optische Kameras zu einem sensorgesteuerten teilautonomen Inspektionssystem. Wasserversorger können damit schwer zugängliche Leitungen zerstörungsfrei und ohne aufwendige Tauchereinsätze inspizieren. Das Projekt wurde im Verbund aus
Fraunhofer IOSB-AST, der EMPIT GmbH und dem Technologiezentrum Wasser (TZW)
als Verbundkoordinator realisiert.
Das TAUWIS-System demonstrierte im Sommer 2026 im Müggelsee bei Berlin seine Funktionsfähigkeit: Aufgrund einer Sandschicht auf den zu untersuchenden Leitungen konnten weder Kamera noch Sonar die Leitungsaußenseite direkt erfassen. Dank der präzisen Navigation konnte der Leitungsverlauf dennoch exakt abgefahren und eine Leckage anhand der ausgewerteten Sensordaten geortet werden. Die ermittelten Koordinaten wurden dem Betreiber zur Reparatur übergeben.
„Der Einsatz im Müggelsee hat gezeigt, dass wir Leitungen auch unter schwierigen Sichtbedingungen zuverlässig abfahren und Schadstellen präzise lokalisieren können. Betreiber erhalten damit belastbare Informationen, um Reparaturen gezielt vorzubereiten und Wasserverluste schneller zu begrenzen“, erklärt Ganzorig Baatar, Projektleiter am Fraunhofer IOSB-AST.
Das Herzstück von TAUWIS ist die Kombination eines ferngesteuerten
Unterwasserfahrzeugs (ROV) des Fraunhofer IOSB-AST mit einem CMI-Sensor (Current Magnetometry Inspection) der EMPIT GmbH zur Bewertung metallischer Werkstoffe. Eine besondere Herausforderung war dabei, Sensor und Messelektronik so umzubauen, dass beide auch unter Wasser absolut zuverlässig funktionieren.
Das System enthält zwei wesentliche Innovationen. Zum einen wurde die CMI-Technologie erstmals für den Unterwassereinsatz adaptiert. Zum anderen entstand eine Messplattform, welche das Abfahren der Leitungsstücke teilautonom durchführt. Die eigentliche Inspektion erfolgt danach in einem Post-Processing-Verfahren bei der EMPIT GmbH. Ein Schwerpunkt bestand darin, Sensorik und Elektronik für den Einsatz unter Wasser zu adaptieren, um mit den damit gewonnenen Daten eine teilautonome Steuerung des ROVs zu ermöglichen. Anders als bisher üblich bündelt TAUWIS damit Sensorik, Fahrzeug und Auswertesoftware in einem kompakten, steuerbaren System.
Das CMI-Sensorsystem errechnet die Lage der Leitung in Echtzeit und übermittelt diese Information direkt an das Navigationssystem des Fahrzeugs. Durch eine entsprechend angepasste Steuerung kann das Fahrzeug auf diese Sensorsignale reagieren und seine Fahrt automatisch danach ausrichten. So wird eine teilautonome Leitungsverfolgung realisiert – lediglich die Tiefensteuerung erfolgt weiterhin manuell durch die Pilotinnen und Piloten. So können Leitungen präzise abgefahren und Zustands- sowie Lagedaten in nur einem Inspektionsdurchgang systematisch erfasst werden. Mit den gewonnenen Sensordaten lassen sich Korrosion, Deformationen und Leckagen erkennen und zugleich die genaue Position der Leitung dokumentieren. Das Verfahren läuft dabei zerstörungsfrei und ohne Eingriff in den laufenden Betrieb.
Der Erfolg des vom Bundesministerium für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt im Rahmen der Maßnahme „KMU innovativ“ geförderten Projektes beruht auf dem Ineinandergreifen komplementärer Expertise. Das Fraunhofer IOSB-AST in Ilmenau machte den CMI-Sensor unterwassertauglich, integrierte die Sensorik und implementierte die sensorbasierte, hochpräzise autonome Leitungsverfolgung auf Basis der CMI-Echtzeitauswertung von EMPIT. Die EMPIT GmbH definierte die Anforderungen an die Sensorplattform und passte ihre Elektronik und Software sowie die Datenschnittstelle für die ROV-Steuerung an und entwickelte die notwendige CMI-Echtzeitauswertung für die Steuerbefehle. Das TZW übernahm als Verbundkoordinator die Projektsteuerung und plante die Praxiseinsätze. Als assoziierte Partner für die Praxistests konnten außerdem die Berliner Wasserbetriebe sowie der Zweckverband Bodensee-Wasserversorgung gewonnen werden.
Ausblick
Das Marktpotenzial reicht weit über die Wasserversorgung hinaus. Mit geringfügigen Anpassungen lässt sich das System auch zur Inspektion von Leitungen in
Küstengewässern, von Dükern in Wasserstraßen sowie von Wasserstoff-, Öl- und
Gasleitungen einsetzen. Unter anderem soll die Lösung in Folgeprojekten um eine
KI-gestützte Edge-Computing-Einheit erweitert werden, um damit eine vollautonome Steuerung und die Echtzeit-Datenauswertung direkt auf dem Fahrzeug selbst zu realisieren. Damit soll dem beauftragten Infrastruktur-Experten eine robotische Lösung mit bestmöglicher Assistenz bei der Bewältigung der Inspektionsaufgaben an die Hand gegeben werden.
Über das DVGW-Technologiezentrum Wasser (TZW)
Das TZW ist eine führende, gemeinnützige Forschungseinrichtung für alle Bereiche der Wasserbranche – vom Ressourcenschutz über Gewinnung und Aufbereitung bis zur Verteilung. Als Teil des Deutschen Vereins des Gas- und Wasserfaches e. V. (DVGW) unterstützt es mit rund 180 hochqualifizierten Mitarbeitenden Wasserversorger, Industrie, Behörden und Hochschulen.
Über die EMPIT GmbH
Die EMPIT GmbH ist ein 2015 gegründetes, weltweit tätiges Deep-Tech-Unternehmen, das sich auf die nicht-invasive Inspektion, Kartierung und Integritätsprüfung schwer zugänglicher, erdverlegter Rohrleitungen spezialisiert hat. Mit der patentierten Current Magnetometry Inspection (CMI) hat EMPIT bereits über 10.000 Kilometer Rohrleitung in mehr als 35 Ländern geprüft und wurde für seine Innovationskraft mit Deutschlands renommiertestem Innovationspreis ausgezeichnet.
Über das Fraunhofer IOSB-AST
Das Fraunhofer IOSB-AST ist Teil der Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft, der weltweit führenden Organisation für angewandte Forschung. Mit dem Fokus Angewandte Systemtechnik (AST) werden Lösungen entwickelt, die kritische cyber-physische Infrastrukturen effizient, resilient und nachhaltig machen. Forschungsschwerpunkte sind Kognitive Energiesysteme und Energiemanagement, Eingebettete Intelligente Systeme und Unterwasserrobotik.
Das Institut arbeitet anwendungsnah in den Ingenieurwissenschaften – insbesondere Elektrotechnik, Informations- und Kommunikationstechnologie sowie technischer Kybernetik – und überführt seine Ergebnisse in marktreife Systemlösungen für
Wirtschaft und öffentliche Hand.

title: Consortium wins $535 million tender for 4 GWh storage project in China - Energy Storage
content: A consortium led by Wuhan Tianyuan Group Co., Ltd. has won a CNY 3.64 billion ($535 million) equipment supply and installation tender for a 1 GW / 4 GWh shared energy storage project in Lingwu, Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, northwest China. The Shenzhen-listed company confirmed on October 26 that it had received the formal award notice from project owner Lingwu Huaxin Comprehensive Energy Service Co., Ltd., following the publication of the winning bid between October 21 and October 23. The consortium also includes Inner Mongolia Yinhe Electric Power Installation Engineering Co., Ltd. and Ningxia Communications Construction Co., Ltd. Wuhan Tianyuan will serve as the lead contractor, although the companies have not disclosed how responsibilities or contract revenues will be divided among the three members. Located in Baituogang Township, Lingwu, the project will have a rated power capacity of 1,000 MW and an energy storage capacity of 4,000 MWh, equivalent to four hours of storage at full output. According to the original tender documentation, the development will include a new 330 kV step-up substation and approximately 4 km of transmission infrastructure connecting the facility to the 330 kV side of the existing Lingzhou 750 kV substation. The integrated contract covers equipment procurement, engineering design, civil construction, installation, commissioning, grid connection and project acceptance, together with associated technical services and warranty obligations. The winning bid translates to approximately CNY 0.91/Wh ($0.134/Wh). However, this figure covers equipment and construction-related services rather than battery equipment alone. The project owner has not disclosed the battery chemistry, cell suppliers or detailed system configuration. Under the tender requirements, the project is expected to obtain its grid connection notice by April 30, 2027. Final project acceptance is subject to a 15-month construction schedule, with a deadline of October 30, 2027. The contract also specifies a two-year warranty period following acceptance. The contract represents a potentially substantial addition to Wuhan Tianyuan’s energy storage business. The company reported revenue of approximately CNY 1.71 billion in 2025, meaning the total consortium bid is equivalent to more than twice its annual revenue. However, Wuhan Tianyuan cautioned that itww had not signed a formal contract as of October 26. The amount attributable to the listed company will depend on subsequent agreements among consortium members, while final payment terms and settlement arrangements remain subject to negotiation. The company also highlighted uncertainties associated with project execution, including possible changes to contractual terms, delays or termination arising from unforeseen events. The project’s scale and construction timetable could also create procurement, working capital and delivery risks. Wuhan Tianyuan has been expanding its energy storage activities alongside its established environmental engineering operations. Earlier in October, a subsidiary signed a CNY 195 million equipment supply and installation contract for a 75 MW/300 MWh storage expansion project in Ningxia’s Ningdong energy and chemical industrial base. Founded in 2009 and listed on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange in 2021, Wuhan Tianyuan operates across water treatment, waste management, environmental equipment and renewable energy development. The Lingwu project forms part of the growing pipeline of grid-scale shared energy storage developments in Ningxia, where increasing wind and solar generation is creating demand for additional grid flexibility. Such facilities can provide balancing capacity for multiple renewable energy projects, although the Lingwu plant’s specific operating and revenue arrangements have not yet been disclosed. title: BW ESS enters French market, finances Europe’s biggest BESS - Energy Storage
content: BW ESS has acquired two standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS) from Recurrent Energy in France. Both projects have a capacity of 100 MW/400 MWh and are located in the regions of Calvados and Eastern Pyrenees. The two BESS assets are in advanced development, according to BW ESS, and the company said it will work with Recurrent Energy as the projects are brought into construction and operation. The purchase marks BW ESS’s first foray into the French market, and the seventh market for the company globally. BW ESS said that the acquisition represents a significant step and the company plans to own more energy storage in France in the future. Erik Strømsø, CEO and co-founder of BW ESS, described the purchase as a “natural next step”. “These acquisitions give us an immediate 200 MW / 800 MWh platform in the country and provide a strong foundation for building a sizeable French portfolio. France has a strong nuclear base, but it also has a growing need for flexibility as weather-sensitive demand and an evolving generation mix create more variable system conditions. “Batteries can complement France’s nuclear backbone by adding the rapid-response flexibility needed to balance the system, absorb surplus power and make low-carbon generation available when it is most valuable,” Strømsø said. Recurrent Energy CEO Dylan Marx said the transaction shows the developer’s ability to create value through high-quality BESS projects. “It is a strong testament to the BESS platform we have built in France and our ability to keep scaling it.” Hams Hall financing The Recurrent Energy deal quickly follows BW ESS announcing a major financing deal on Oct. 21 for the 400 MW/1,424 MWh Hams Hall BESS in the United Kingdom – on course to be become Europe’s largest operational site in MWh terms when it enters commercial operations. BW ESS has secured debt financing for the Hams Hall site from lenders OCBC, Rabobank and Societe Generale. The three lenders will provide the debt facility in equal proportions with Rabobank acting as facility agent. The transaction is expected to close at the project’s commercial operations date. Located next to National Grid’s Hams Hall substation, Hams Hall BESS is expected to initially deliver 350 MW/1,243 MWh of storage capacity, rising to 400 MW/1,424 MWh on completion of a second phase at the site. Long-term revenues for the first phase of the project are underpinned by a 10-year floor and optimization agreement signed with EDF earlier in 2026. title: Wholesale Markets Rebound: Battery Revenues in September - Energy Storage
content: September showed just how quickly conditions can change in the German electricity market. While high gas prices continued to support wholesale electricity prices, the declining influence of summer solar generation made periods of low renewable output increasingly significant. This was particularly evident during extended periods of low wind generation, which led to pronounced price peaks and wider price spreads. September in Numbers To assess how these market developments affected battery revenues, we analyzed simulated earnings for a representative 10 MW / 20 MWh grey standalone storage in Germany. As in previous months, we compared individual wholesale and ancillary service strategies with suena energy’s forecast-based cross-market optimization approach. Wholesale strategies recovered strongly compared with August. Continuous intraday trading remained the strongest individual spot-market strategy, with revenues rising 36% to €17.5k per MW per month. Day-ahead trading and intraday auctions also improved, reaching €13.8k and €13.2k per MW per month respectively, up from €10.8k and €10.5k in August. The stacked wholesale strategy recorded an even stronger result, climbing from €15.4k to €20.9k per MW per month, the strongest single-stack result in our observed series. Ancillary services presented a more mixed picture. FCR declined slightly to €14.3k per MW per month, while positive aFRR recovered significantly, rising 50% to €8.4k per MW per month. Negative aFRR, by contrast, fell to €11.3k per MW per month, while the stacked aFRR strategy remained broadly stable at €9.9k per MW per month. The aFRR energy benchmark reached €7.9k per MW per month under a revised calculation methodology and is therefore not directly comparable with previous months. The strongest overall result once again came from cross-market optimization. suena energy’s approach generated €25.5k per MW per month, slightly above August’s €25.3k. This was 22% above the combined wholesale benchmark, although the advantage narrowed considerably as wholesale trading revenues recovered. Higher Prices, Wider Spreads Wholesale electricity prices continued to rise in September. The average day-ahead price reached €144.80/MWh, around €18/MWh above August and more than 50% higher than in September 2025. Higher fuel costs remained a major driver. Spot gas prices averaged €76.20/MWh and exceeded €80/MWh towards the end of the month, while coal and carbon prices added further upward pressure. Despite unusually sunny and dry weather, renewable generation was less able to cover demand than in previous months. Solar output remained strong for September but declined seasonally compared with August, while wind and hydropower generation also weakened. Renewables accounted for around 66% of German electricity generation, with a larger share of residual demand covered by conventional power plants, particularly coal. Negative day-ahead price hours also became less frequent, falling from 55 in August to 39 in September. The effects were especially noticeable during two extended periods of low wind generation, when evening price peaks became particularly pronounced. Evening electricity prices averaged around €261/MWh during these weeks, while the monthly day-ahead top-bottom spread for a two-hour battery reached approximately €220/MWh, its widest level since the 2022 energy crisis. These pronounced price differences created more attractive opportunities for battery arbitrage, helping explain the recovery in wholesale trading revenues. The divergence between wholesale and ancillary service revenues also became more apparent. Greater demand for upward flexibility during periods of tight supply supported the recovery in positive aFRR revenues, although these remained below September 2025 levels due to growing competition from battery storage. Negative aFRR revenues, meanwhile, declined as periods of surplus electricity became less frequent. Flexibility in a Changing Market September highlighted how quickly battery revenue opportunities can shift between markets. Following August’s weaker wholesale performance, wider price spreads brought a substantial recovery in day-ahead and intraday revenues. At the same time, ancillary service markets followed different trajectories, reinforcing the importance of flexibility across trading strategies. Looking ahead, shorter days and more variable renewable generation are likely to further influence electricity price patterns as autumn progresses. In the longer term, the continued expansion of battery storage is also likely to play an increasing role in shaping electricity prices, affecting the frequency and duration of extreme price movements. As battery storage increasingly shapes the markets in which it operates, accurate forecasting and the ability to respond dynamically across markets will therefore become even more important for capturing revenue opportunities. title: Delta Capacity secures financing for 600 MWh Finnish BESS portfolio - Energy Storage
content: Swiss developer Delta Capacity has reached financial close on two standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Finland with a combined capacity of 250 MW / 600 MWh, as construction is underway on both assets. The portfolio comprises the 125 MW / 300 MWh Kärppiö BESS project in Teuva and the 125 MW / 300 MWh AKKU One project in Lapinlahti . Delta Capacity is developing Kärppiö alongside Strioga Family Foundation, while AKKU One is being developed in partnership with Covenergo. Delta Capacity said the projects are among the largest BESS developments in Finland to enter construction, with commercial operations targeted for Q4 2027. French banking group Société Générale acted as sole senior lender to both projects, providing long-term financing while also acting as agent, security agent and hedge provider. Finnish export credit agency Finnvera is providing a counter-guarantee supporting one of the financing facilities. Delta Capacity said it will act as the construction and long-term asset manager for both projects, while Sungrow has been selected as equipment supplier and Centrica Energy has signed partial tolling agreements for both assets. The financing follows Delta Capacity’s commissioning of the 70 MW / 160 MWh Ånge BESS project in Sweden in June 2026, which is optimized by Centrica Energy. “Achieving financial close on both Kärppiö and AKKU One represents a significant milestone for Delta Capacity and our partners, Covenergo and Strioga Family Foundation. The backing of Société Générale and Finnvera underscores the strength of these projects, the quality of our partnerships and the confidence in our development and investment strategy. With construction already underway, our focus now turns to successfully delivering both projects and bringing them into operation in 2027,” said Marc Weisser, CFO & CIO of Delta Capacity. Delta Capacity said that Icecapital acted as debt adviser on the transaction, while AFRY and Aurora Energy Research served as technical and market advisers, respectively. title: Construction begins on 300 MWh Hazelwood 2 grid-forming battery in Australia - Energy Storage
content: French clean energy developer Engie, owner of the Hazelwood battery energy storage system (BESS) , Chinese clean energy technology manufacturer Sungrow and Spain-based engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractor Elecnor Australia have started building the 300 MWh Hazelwood 2 BESS extension. The project in Victoria’s Latrobe Valley will feature 66 units of Sungrow’s ST5015-UX storage system, part of the PowerTitan 2.0 series, alongside 33 SC6900UD-MV power conversion system inverters and Sungrow’s EMS3000 smart controller. According to Sungrow, the PowerTitan 2.0 system offers high energy density to optimize storage capacity and liquid-cooled technology to maintain stable operating temperatures and support system reliability. Sungrow said advanced battery management supports battery safety, performance monitoring and long-term operational reliability, while the SC6900UD-MV inverters will support efficient power conversion and responsive grid support for utility-scale applications. Sungrow Australia Managing Director Thomas Hou said the Hazelwood BESS 2 represents an important step in advancing grid-forming energy storage in Australia. “Through our collaboration with Engie, we aim to bring advanced energy storage technology to support grid stability and enable greater integration of renewable energy,” Hou said. “We look forward to contributing our expertise and supporting the continued development of a more resilient energy system in Victoria.” Once complete, the Hazelwood BESS projects 1 and 2 will have a combined 300 MW capacity, adding significant battery storage capacity to Victoria’s energy infrastructure and reinforcing Hazelwood’s role in providing flexible energy resources for Victoria and the National Electricity Market (NEM), which serves Australia’s eastern and southern states. title: Chile solar and battery system remain offline after cyberattack - Energy Storage
content: Chile’s 103 MW Huatacondo solar park and its 98 MW/312 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) have remained disconnected for two months following an incident that the National Electric Coordinator (Coordinador Eléctrico Nacional) recorded as a cyberattack. The coordinator’s daily report for Oct. 27 continues to list both installations under forced outages, with 0% availability. The reported cause remains the one recorded on Aug. 27 under forced-disconnection request SDCF 2026100475. The incident was recorded at 1:10 p.m. on Aug. 27, when control center RNE submitted a forced-disconnection request for the solar park and its battery system. The stated cause was a “cyberattack on Huatacondo facilities,” which disconnected both installations from Chile’s National Electric System (SEN). At the same time, RNE requested the forced disconnection of the 220/23 kV TR1 transformer at Santa Rita substation, also “due to cyberattack,” under request SDCF 2026100746. The same daily report records two further incidents attributed to cyberattacks. At 9:30 p.m., control center Espinos (Potencia) reported that the Olivos and Espinos thermal power plants in Los Vilos, in the Coquimbo region, were unavailable for dispatch following the loss of supervisory control and remote operation of their facilities “due to a cyberattack.” The document does not establish whether these incidents were related to the Huatacondo event reported earlier that day or whether they resulted from a single coordinated action. Inaugurated in 2019, the Huatacondo solar park belongs to a consortium comprising Japan’s Sojitz Corporation, with a 60% stake; Shikoku Electric Power, with 30%; and France’s Eiffage, with 10%. The battery project was developed by AustrianSolar Chile Cuatro SpA and began construction in 2025. Canadian Solar subsidiary e-STORAGE was awarded the battery supply contract, while Tritec-Intervento undertook the balance-of-plant work. The BESS was still undergoing commissioning when the incident occurred, and the coordinator’s Oct. 27 report continued to list it in that status. Its unavailability therefore does not represent two months of disruption to an established commercial operation. A review of the coordinator’s daily reports covering Oct. 28, 2025, to Oct. 27, 2026, examined 360 of the 365 documents in the period. No other new incidents explicitly attributed to “cyberattacks” or “cyberattacks” in the Spanish-language terminology were identified in the reports reviewed, apart from those notified on Aug. 27. Later references concerned the continued disconnection of Huatacondo. Five reports could not be checked: those dated Oct. 29 and Oct. 31, 2025, and March 30, Aug. 31 and Sept. 8, 2026. The review therefore cannot establish that the Aug. 27 incident was the only or the first of its kind during the period. It does, however, indicate that incidents explicitly described using those terms were uncommon in the operational reports examined. In October 2025, Patricio Leyton, director of the coordinator’s Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure Unit, told Reporte Minero that Chile had not recorded attacks with a significant impact on its electricity infrastructure up to that point, although the organization detected millions of attempts each day. The coordinator has a cybersecurity incident notification protocol that sets reporting obligations for companies operating within the coordinated electricity system. On Aug. 28, one day after the reported incidents, Chile’s National Energy Commission (CNE) opened a public consultation on a proposed Technical Standard for Cybersecurity and Information Security for the electricity sector. The process to develop the standard had begun in 2021. pv magazine has requested information from the National Electric Coordinator and AustrianSolar Chile Cuatro SpA about the circumstances of the attack, its operational consequences and the expected recovery timeline. Neither organization had responded by publication. No public statement has been located that establishes the origin of the incident, which IT systems were affected, whether the events reported on Aug. 27 were connected, or why Huatacondo has remained unavailable for so long. The coordinator’s reports record causes communicated by operators but do not, in themselves, constitute a technical investigation capable of establishing the nature and scope of the attacks. title: Gallium-doped zinc oxide enables 24.92%-efficient HJT solar cell - pv magazine Global
content:
Researchers in China have investigated gallium-doped zinc oxide (GZO) as an indium-free transparent conductive oxide (TCO) for silicon heterojunction (HJT) solar cells. The approach aims to reduce manufacturing costs and reliance on scarce indium used in conventional transparent electrodes.
“The high cost of indium has driven the development of indium-free alternatives to conventional TCOs for HJT solar cells,” the group explained. “In this study, the structural, morphological, electrical, optical, and chemical properties of GZO films were investigated by combining in situ optical emission spectroscopy (OES) with ex situ characterization.”
The researchers fabricated HJT solar cells using n-type crystalline silicon wafers measuring 210 × 105 mm and approximately 130 μm thick. They chemically cleaned and textured the wafers, then deposited intrinsic amorphous silicon passivation layers and doped microcrystalline silicon oxide layers on both sides by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition.
They then deposited GZO transparent electrodes at room temperature using reactive plasma deposition, with thicknesses of 80 nm on the front and 100 nm on the rear. The team varied the oxygen fraction in the oxygen-argon deposition gas from 5% to 25%, while keeping the total gas flow constant, and screen-printed contacts using 30 wt% Ag-coated Cu paste.
They monitored the plasma using optical emission spectroscopy and characterized the films’ crystal structure, surface morphology, oxygen chemical states, electrical properties, and optical transmission. Finally, they measured the cells’ current-voltage characteristics under simulated sunlight at 1,000 W/m² and 25 C, comparing their performance with a reference HJT cell featuring indium-based transparent electrodes on both sides.
“The film deposited at an oxygen content of 10% exhibited the optimum electrical properties, with a minimum resistivity of 4.902 × 10⁻⁴ Ω cm and an average optical transmittance of 83.45% in the 400-1100 nm range,” the results showed.
“The GZO film deposited at 10% oxygen showed the typical hexagonal wurtzite structure with a pronounced preferred orientation,” the group added. “When the optimized GZO films were applied as TCO electrodes in HJT solar cells, a conversion efficiency of 24.92% was achieved. Compared with the HJT solar cell with double-sided ICO, the efficiency was only 0.68% lower.”
The article “
24.92% efficient crystalline silicon heterojunction solar cells with Ga-doped ZnO transparent conductive oxide films by RPD
” has appeared in
Solar Energy Materials and Solar Cells.
Researchers from the
Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
, China’s
Dinto Solar
Anhui Huasun Energy
have contributed to the research.

title: First Solar opens 1.7 GW module plant in South Carolina - pv magazine Global
content:
irst Solar has opened its new solar module facility in Gaffney, South Carolina, holding a celebration to inaugurate the first phase of production at what is slated to become a 3.4 GW plant. The event featured company executives, community leaders and politicians from several levels of government.
The company plans to use the facility to onshore the final production processes for Series 6 Plus thin-film modules initiated at its international facilities. First Solar says the investment was driven by rising domestic demand for US-made energy equipment following recent federal trade policies and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed into law in July 2025.
The second phase of the $330 million plant is expected to be complete by mid-2027, bringing the facility’s capacity from 1.7 GW to 3.4 GW of modules featuring the company’s CuRe technology. First Solar says it has already filled 500 jobs at the facility and expects to bring on nearly 200 more as the facility reaches full production.
Guests at the inauguration included South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster, US Senator Darline Graham, US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, South Carolina Senator Harvey Peeler, South Carolina Representatives Dennis Moss and Brian Lawson and Gaffney Mayor Lyman D. Dawkins III, who joined plant workers and First Solar CEO Mark Widmar in the ribbon-cutting ceremony.
“Thanks to First Solar’s investment, South Carolinians are building American energy technology in Gaffney, with nearly 700 good-paying jobs expected to support this critical work,” said McMaster in a statement. “This is another example of why South Carolina continues to be recognized as a manufacturing powerhouse and a leader in our nation’s energy future.”
Widmar added his own thoughts about the new plant: “Less than a year after we selected Gaffney, this facility is ready to produce American solar technology, built by South Carolinian workers,” he said in a statement. “That pace reflects what is possible when sound policy, strong state and local partners, and a committed workforce align.”
The Gaffney plant is First Solar’s sixth US manufacturing facility, joining three existing plants in Ohio and single facilities in Alabama and Louisiana, alongside research and development centers in California and Ohio. The company also operates a distribution center in Duncan, South Carolina, and maintains a partnership with Inland Port Greer for shipments of its products.
During its second-quarter 2026 earnings call in July, company executives noted that relocating production equipment from Southeast Asia to support the South Carolina finishing operation leaves the company with roughly 1.8 GW of end-to-end, fully finished module capacity across Malaysia and Vietnam, while the remaining international Series 6 lines supply unfinished modules to the Gaffney plant.
First Solar has said it expects its cumulative investment in US manufacturing and R&D infrastructure since 2019 to exceed $5 billion by the end of 2026. By 2027, once the second phase of the Gaffney plant is complete, the company forecasts its total domestic module manufacturing capacity will reach approximately 17 GW.
Across its entire global fleet, First Solar forecasts total actual module production of 16.5 GW to 17.5 GW in 2026, rising to between 18.9 GW and 20.5 GW in 2027.
The company is scheduled to report its Q3 2026 financial results after the market closes on Oct. 29, 2026.

title: Heat pump grant survives, new loans for solar and battery storage in UK Budget - pv magazine Global
content:
The UK government has retained the boiler upgrade scheme (BUS) despite widespread speculation the heat pump subsidy program was set to be scrapped, although the total budget for the program has been cut by around GBP 700 million ($932 million).
BUS grants of up to GBP 9,000 have been offered to UK consumers in a bid to accelerate the electrification of home heating in a country where more than two thirds of households use a natural gas-fired heating system.
In the first Budget delivered by UK Chancellor John Healey, the government committed to maintaining the BUS grant at current funding levels of GBP 400 million in 2027-28, rising “broadly in line with inflation” thereafter. Previously, GBP 600 million was allocated for the 2027/28 financial year, GBP 683 million for 2028/29 and GBP 709 million for 2029/30.
Social housing tenants should also benefit from an additional GBP 100 million of funding, subject to final approvals, to support the delivery of up to 57,000 solar installations for households this financial year. Further grant support for residential solar, battery storage and heat pumps will continue to be available through the government’s Warm Homes Plan, which receive an additional GBP 335 million investment in 2027, however the multi-year program’s total budget is being cut by GBP 1 billion as a contribution to defense spending.
The Chancellor has made changes to value added tax (VAT) rules that will affect solar and battery storage. UK consumers currently pay no VAT on home solar and battery but this will rise to 5% from Apr. 1, 2027.
Budget day also saw the UK government publish guidance for the Warm Home Loans program, which will see the UK government subsidize some of the risk associated with financing, allowing lenders to offer lower interest rates.
Solar, battery storage and heat pump installations qualify for Warm Home Loans support and can potentially be used in conjunction with grants or money from other funding programs. The loans themselves are offered by finance partners participating in the program, meaning consumers apply directly to a lender, through an installer or retailer when arranging finance for the improvement work, or through their mortgage providers.
Chris Hewett, chief executive of Solar Energy UK, welcomed the launch of the Warm Homes Loan program.
“With the Warm Homes Loan Scheme now in place, more homes can go solar next year than ever before, taking control of their energy and insulating themselves from high energy bills. Critically, it will ensure that households across society can overcome any financial barriers, making sure that the benefits are felt where they are most needed.”
Hewett added that Solar Energy UK already expects the annual record for smaller-scale solar systems to be broken within a few weeks, and the association is confident the loan program will deliver another record year in 2027.
Progress was also made on a fixed-revenue offer to existing
utility-scale solar plants
. The government has launched a consultation on a proposed Wholesale Contracts for Difference (WCfD) program, first announced in April 2026. Available on the UK government website, the consultation covers eligibility, allocation and auction design, commercial arrangements, and potential electricity market impacts. Industry stakeholders have until Dec. 9 2026 to respond.
The UK Chancellor also pledged to drive down electricity system costs following up the recent announcement state-owned Great British Grid would work alongside existing network operators to increase competition. Healey added that competition in offshore electricity networks “has delivered hundreds of millions of pounds of bill savings” and therefore competition will “shortly be introduced” into offshore electricity transmission, in a nod to the Competitively Appointed Transmission Owner (CATO) regime which has been in development in Great Britain for more than a decade. If implemented, CATO would allow private companies to competitively bid for the right to build and run new onshore grid infrastructure.
There was movement on electricity bills too, with Chancellor Healey committing to remove standing charges from gas bills. Standing charges are applied to bills for all connected households regardless of usage and are used to cover gas network upgrades. These fixed costs will be paid on the unit rate – the amount paid for each kWh of gas consumed. The government estimates the change could save 60% of households around GBP 45 per year. Healey said the government also plans to remove standing charges from electricity bills in the future.
Andrew Sissons, director in sustainable future at innovation charity Nesta welcomed the change. Sisson said it would provide relief to the poorest households who ration their gas use, “but it will also mean that switching to electric heating such as heat pumps is a better deal for some households that use more gas.”
The Boiler Upgrade Scheme (BUS) has been the main policy tool supporting UK heat pump deployment since it was introduced in May 2022. The program initially offered GBP 5,000 grants for air-to water heat pumps and GBP 6,000 grants for ground source heat pumps for households installing a heat pump, before increasing to 7,500 GBP for both technologies in October 2023. Following the outbreak of conflict between the United States, Israel and Iran, the UK government added a GBP 9,000 grant option for those households using heating oil systems due to their increased exposure to energy price hikes.
The rate of installations has increased since BUS grants were introduced, but volumes remain significantly below what is needed to achieve a government target of 450,000 heat pump installations per year by 2030. The government reported 151,136 BUS voucher applications had been received from May 2022 to August 2026, with 98% applications for air-to-water heat pump grants.
Guidance for Warm Home Loans suggests that BUS grants and other funding support can be used in conjunction with the state-backed financing, potentially further lowering the cost to consumers.
The following lenders are offering Warm Home loans according to the UK government: HomeServe Finance, Hometree Finance, The Money Co-Op, Propensio, Secure Trust Bank, Selina Finance, South Manchester Credit Union, Sunsave Energy, Tandem Bank, This Bank.

title: Researchers improve heating uniformity in PV module laminators - pv magazine Global
content:
A research team from China’s Hebei Normal University of Science and Technology has developed an electromagnetic-thermal strategy to improve heating uniformity in PV module laminators. Uneven heating can leave encapsulants insufficiently cured in cooler areas while damaging encapsulants or cells in hotter areas. The new approach combines stepped aluminum magnetic shielding, zone-specific currents, and temperature-based current control to distribute heat more evenly across the heating plate.
“Addressing the dual challenges existing in the spatial magnetic field distribution and transient thermal response of a large-scale built-in perforated induction heating system, this paper proposes a complete electromagnetic-thermal collaborative optimization solution based on multiphysics equivalent modeling,” the team explained. “An equivalent finite element model was established to reduce the computational cost of large-scale Multiphysics coupling, with accuracy validated via a physical prototype.”
The researchers used COMSOL to simulate electromagnetic heating and heat transfer in a 4,750 mm × 2,900 mm × 45 mm steel plate comprising six zones with embedded copper coils. A simplified two-zone model accounted for temperature-dependent material properties, heat conduction, and convective and radiative losses.
They selected an excitation current of 38 A and a frequency of 15 kHz, then optimized stepped aluminum shielding to suppress localized overheating. Finally, they adjusted the two zones’ currents to 37 A and 38 A and introduced a control function that reduced current as temperatures approached 150 C.
“Under the baseline electrical parameters, the maximum temperature difference on the working surface was approximately 29 C,” the results showed. “After applying continuous stepped shielding and asymmetric shielding compensation, the maximum temperature difference was reduced to approximately 12 C, indicating that the proposed shielding method effectively weakened edge magnetic flux leakage and local heat accumulation, thereby improving temperature uniformity.”
For experimental validation, the team built a full-scale prototype with 13 surface thermocouples and an estimated measurement uncertainty of ±0.30 C near 150 C. They compared baseline measurements with simulations before testing the optimized shielding and zone-specific currents. A PID controller regulated the prototype’s heating, while temperature recordings tracked overshoot, stabilization time, and uniformity across the monitored locations.
“Full-scale prototype tests showed that the measured temperatures at all 13 monitoring locations were within 148–152 C, with a maximum measured temperature difference of approximately 3.1 C, indicating a substantial improvement in temperature uniformity at the monitored locations,” the team said.
Electromagnetic-thermal collaborative optimization of a large-scale induction heating plate for photovoltaic module laminators
” appeared in
Case Studies in Thermal Engineering.
Researchers from China’s Hebei Normal University of Science and Technology and the Hebei Technology Innovation Center for Photovoltaic Module Manufacturing Equipment.

title: Renault, EDF plan vehicle-to-grid charging offer for 2027 - pv magazine Global
content:
Renault Group and French energy company EDF have signed an agreement to launch a home charging service in France in summer 2027, combining electric vehicles, bidirectional charging stations and smart charging management. The offer will initially target private customers buying vehicles from Renault Group’s Renault, Alpine and Dacia brands.
Eligible vehicles will be able to feed electricity from their batteries back into the grid while connected to a charging station. EDF will handle charger installation through its IZI by EDF service, while Dreev, a joint venture between EDF and Nuvve, will provide the platform for managing charging and discharging.
The partners said the agreement aims to accelerate electric vehicle adoption by offering customers an integrated package of charging station installation and managed charging.
Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology is not new. Bidirectional inverters, vehicle-to-charger communication protocols and demonstration projects have been in development for years. The significance of the agreement is the commitment by an automaker and an energy company to bring the technology to market at scale.
The challenge has been less about converting electricity than integrating the full service, including vehicle compatibility, manufacturer battery warranties and bidirectional charging equipment.
As the electric vehicle fleet grows, the charging capacity that can be managed becomes increasingly significant. Properly coordinated, vehicle batteries could provide flexibility to the power system, complementing stationary battery storage and capacity mechanisms. Poorly managed charging, however, could increase evening demand peaks.
The scale of the rollout, along with the tariffs for grid connections and payments for flexibility, will help determine the service’s impact.

title: Chilean solar plant offline for two months following cyberattack - pv magazine Global
content:
The 103 MW Huatacondo solar plant and its 98 MW/312 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS), located in Chile’s Tarapacá region, have remained out of service for two months following a cyberattack. The Chilean National Electricity Coordinator’s daily report for Oct. 27 lists both facilities as subject to forced disconnection, with 0% availability. The report continues to cite an incident reported on Aug. 27 under forced disconnection request SDCF 2025.1000.
The incident was recorded on Aug. 27 at 1:10 p.m., when the RNE control center requested the forced disconnection of the solar plant and its battery storage system. The reported cause was a “cyberattack on the Huatacondo facilities,” which left both installations disconnected from Chile’s National Electric System (SEN).
At the same time, RNE requested the forced disconnection of the 220/23 kV TR1 transformer at the Santa Rita substation, also citing a cyberattack, according to SDCF request 2026100746.
The same daily report records two other incidents attributed to cyberattacks. At 9:30 p.m., the Espinos (Power) control center reported that the Olivos and Espinos thermal power plants, located in Los Vilos in the Coquimbo region, were unavailable for dispatch following the loss of monitoring and remote-control capabilities.
The report does not establish whether these incidents were related to the earlier incident at Huatacondo or resulted from the same attack.
The Huatacondo solar plant, inaugurated in 2019, is owned by a consortium comprising Japan’s Sojitz Corp., with a 60% stake; Shikoku Electric Power, previously reported as holding 30%; and France’s Eiffage, with 10%.
The battery storage project, developed by AustrianSolar Chile Four SpA, began construction in 2025. Canadian Solar subsidiary e-Storage solution was selected to supply the BESS, while Tritec-Intervento was contracted to carry out the balance-of-plant works.
The battery system was still undergoing commissioning when the incident occurred and remained in that phase as of Oct. 27. Its unavailability therefore does not represent a two-month interruption of an established commercial operation.
A review of the National Electricity Coordinator’s daily reports covering Oct. 28, 2025, through Oct. 27, 2026, examined 360 of the 365 reports published during the period.
The review identified no other new incidents explicitly attributed to cyberattacks beyond those reported on Aug. 27. Subsequent references concerned the continued disconnection of the Huatacondo facilities.
The reports for Oct. 29 and Oct. 31, 2025, and March 30, Aug. 31 and Sept. 8, 2026, could not be reviewed. The findings therefore do not establish that the August incidents were the only cyberattacks during the period or the first incidents of their kind. They are limited to documented operational incidents explicitly described using those terms in the reports examined.
In October 2025, Patricio Leyton, director of the National Electricity Coordinator’s Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure Unit, told
Mining Report
that Chile had not recorded cyberattacks with a significant impact on its electricity infrastructure, despite the millions of attempted attacks detected by the organization.
The Coordinator has a cybersecurity incident notification protocol that establishes reporting obligations for entities operating within the electricity system.
On Aug. 28, one day after the reported incidents, Chile’s National Energy Commission (CNE) opened a public consultation on a draft technical standard for cybersecurity and information security in the electricity sector.
pv magazine
contacted the National Electricity Coordinator and AustrianSolar Chile Four SpA seeking information about the circumstances of the reported attack, its operational consequences and the expected timeline for restoring the facilities. Neither organization had responded by the time of publication.
No public statement was identified that clarified the origin of the incident, the computer systems affected, any potential connection between the incidents reported on Aug. 27, or the reasons for Huatacondo’s prolonged unavailability.
The Coordinator’s daily reports record the causes communicated by plant operators but do not constitute technical investigations establishing the nature or extent of the reported cyberattacks.

title: What 11 islands reveal about the real bottleneck in renewable mini-grids - pv magazine Global
content:
Islands are frequently held up as the proving ground for 100% renewable electricity — contained systems, clear stakeholder lines, and in most cases no main grid to fall back on. A new IEA PVPS Task 18 report puts that reputation to the test, examining 11 islands that have already reached, or come close to, very high renewable shares, from the 88-person village of Apolima in Samoa to Lolland in Denmark, home to more than 57,000 people and connected to the wider Danish grid. What is clear is that the technology to run an island almost entirely on renewables already exists and works in wildly different configurations. What determines whether a project actually gets there is overwhelmingly social, political and organisational, not technical not technology alone, but how well it is combined with the right social, political, economic and organisational conditions.
Eleven islands, no single template
The report’s strongest evidence for this is that there is no single definition of what “success” looks like in practice. Kodiak Island in Alaska runs on a hydro-wind hybrid under a member-owned utility with an advanced operations culture, reaching 99-100% renewable supply. Samsø in Denmark gets there almost entirely through community-owned wind turbines and citizen investment, and, being connected to the Danish grid, does not depend on local storage . Yakushima in Japan reaches 100% renewable electricity using nothing but small hydropower simply because its mountainous terrain and rainfall happen to match demand. Apolima runs on a standalone solar system with no storage at all, because the village is small enough that it doesn’t need any. Tokelau’s fully solar, battery-backed system exists because of sustained New Zealand aid funding, while in Spain’s Canary Islands, El Hierro combines wind power with pumped hydro storage, and La Graciosa runs a wind-PV-battery hybrid whose dispatch strategies are still being actively optimised during operation.
The report treats this variety as the central finding rather than a footnote: there is no universal guideline. A hybrid wind-pumped-hydro system that works for El Hierro would be overbuilt for Apolima; a donor-financed model that got Tokelau to full solar supply wouldn’t translate to a utility-led island like Kodiak. What does recur across all eleven, regardless of technology mix or island size, is a specific set of non-technical conditions.
Preparation is the key, not construction
To find those conditions, the authors built a four-phase, five-category success-factor matrix formed by Preparation, Design, Implementation, and Monitoring & Evaluation crossed with Social, Political, Technical, Economic and Environmental dimensions, and then populated it using a literature review of more than 60 academic publications, case study analysis, and five in-depth interviews with island practitioners. That process surfaced 111 distinct success factors, and the single clearest pattern in the data is where they cluster: nearly half of all identified success factors sit in the preparation phase, before a single turbine or panel goes up.
The report describes this as community education and awareness campaigns, resource and grid assessments, early political alignment, and financing groundwork all happening in parallel, well ahead of system design. Islands that invested heavily here — Lolland, Samsø, El Hierro — built the shared understanding and institutional readiness that made later phases smoother. What should developers and donors learn from this? Under-resourcing the planning and engagement phase is one of the clearest predictable causes of later friction, even when the technical design itself is sound.
Four factors show up almost everywhere
Of the 111 factors identified, 13 were marked as key success factors based on how often they recurred across multiple interviews, and four stand out as close to universal – two social and political, two technical. The first is the presence of local champions or leadership figures, people who mobilise community support, maintain momentum across years-long timelines, and sit at the intersection of community, political and technical actors. Samsø’s transition is presented as a textbook case of this, cited as the connective tissue between local identity, citizen investment and the eventual wind build-out. The second is stakeholder engagement sustained across the entire project lifecycle, not just at the planning stage. The report is explicit that this factor appears in every phase it tracked, making it one of the most cross-cutting success factors in the dataset. Even highly technical decisions, the authors note, such as which generation technology to select or where to reinforce the grid, ultimately depend on stakeholder trust to be accepted and to stick.
The technical backbone
None of this means engineering is secondary. Technical factors make up the largest single category in the dataset, at 41 of the 111 total, and the two remaining near-universal factors are technical – in fact the most frequently mentioned ones: long-term system planning, and grid strengthening specifically for variable renewable energy integration. The report also credits concrete operational practices for sustaining high renewable shares once systems are running, such as Kodiak’s real-time balancing of wind and hydro output and King Island’s use of flywheels and dynamic resistors to stabilise a wind-PV-battery-diesel hybrid. The report calls technical robustness and tailored system design the backbone of successful island transitions. But technology alone does not decide the outcome: what separates islands that reach and sustain high renewable shares from those that stall is whether a sound technical design is matched by the social, political and financial conditions that allow it to be built and operated as intended.
A caveat on replicability
However, the report’s final section makes clear that its own findings are not a plug-and-play checklist. The authors note that the underlying preconditions behind their 13 key success factors — such as a local institution able to sustain planning over several years, stakeholders with enough continuity to stay engaged throughout a multi-year process, and financing that isn’t entirely dependent on short-term donor cycles — are themselves unevenly distributed. Where those preconditions are weak the same interventions tend to stall rather than fail outright: stakeholder engagement loses momentum without a champion to sustain it, tariff reforms struggle to attract investment under unstable regulation, and technical designs proven on well-resourced islands are hard to replicate without reliable supply chains or trained O&M staff.
The authors are explicit that this replication gap is likely to hit hardest on smaller, more remote, lower-income islands, and disproportionately in the Global South, where the institutional and financial foundations underlying this report’s own case studies are least likely to already exist.

title: DJI Power launches new Auro 2000 Elite as its most compact 2 kWh power station - pv magazine Global
content:
JI has launched the DJI Power Auro 2000 Elite, its new 2kWh power station with output power of up to 2 kW continuous, and 2.2 kW peak.
DJI is packing all of its ports and outlets on the front, which include three AC outlets, a car charger, MPPT for solar PV input via two of DJI’s proprietary SDC ports, a 140 W USB-C cable, and DJI also said it can be expanded up to 12 kWh with a “soon-to-be-planned” additional battery.
Compared to the DJI Power 2000, the Auro 2000 Elite is 2.5 kg lighter at around 19 kg, and has a 24 percent smaller volume, using LFP battery cells. All ports are on the front side.
The company said the device was “efficiency optimized” for everyday loads from 100W to 400W.
In terms of safety, the system’s BMS can monitor 13 temperature sensors, and 40 fuses and trigger an automatic shutoff if faults occur. DJI said it also replaced standard conformal coating on the core components with a thinner sub-nano layer to aid heat dissipation while still remaining protective. The unit is rated for altitudes up to 5,000 meters.
Users can monitor the battery, power flows, and enable fast charging through the updated DJI Home app. According to the company, the unit offers a 10-millisecond switchover time in UPS mode, though this will draw more standby power, and operates below 30 dB under low-load discharge.
Although DJI doesn’t make it clear that this is a balcony storage product, the company does say in combination with a solar panel and a microinverter set which it sells separately, it also supports grid-connected operation with up to 800 W in selected regions. That ties-in with a launch
it announced for IFA 2026 but didn’t go through with
, for unknown reasons.
DJI is leaning into its ecosystem as well, noting that it offers “SDC fast charging” at up to 240 W for some of its compatible drone batteries.
Price and availability
The DJI Power Auro 2000 Elite will be available from October 28, 2026 at a price of 1,099 euros through the DJI, and retail partners. DJI has said it offers five years warranty.
DJI is unable to offer the power station in the US.

title: DartSolar unveils expandable vehicle solar array with up to 2 kW output - pv magazine Global
content:
DartSolar LLC, a clean technology firm headquartered in Los Angeles, California, has finalized production plans for its vehicle-integrated solar array, designed to mount onto standard vehicle roof racks and truck beds without structural modifications.
The company reports that its system utilizes modular 500 W units measuring approximately 23 inches by 6 feet (58.4 cm × 182.9 cm) when contracted, which expand to a deployed length of 15 feet (457.2 cm) when stationary. The setup allows multi-unit configurations: two modules yield up to 1,000 W on standard sedan crossbars, while three to four or more modules can be joined side-by-side on light trucks, vans, trailers, and campers to generate between 1,500 W and over 2,000 W of capacity.
According to technical specifications released by the company, the expanding array is intended to supply off-grid electricity for portable power stations, jobsite tools, and auxiliary battery systems rather than serving as a primary electric vehicle (EV) charging solution. DartSolar estimates daily solar generation will add approximately 10 to 20 miles (16 to 32 km) of driving range to an EV under typical exposure conditions.
To improve durability during transit, the array is housed under a 4 mm polycarbonate protective shell designed to mitigate impact damage from hail and road debris. High-speed stability testing was conducted at speeds up to 100 mph (160 km/h) in standard and lateral configurations, though operational guidelines recommend travel speeds under 70 mph.
The system incorporates a multi-angle quick-release locking mechanism to facilitate deployment from different access points around larger vehicles. In line with an open-hardware model, DartSolar has released 3D CAD files (STEP format) for structural plastic components under a share-alike license, enabling end users to manufacture replacement parts locally via 3D printing.

title: Towable 80 kW hydrogen generator brings clean power off-grid - pv magazine Global
content:
Ballard Power Systems, through its GeoPura subsidiary, has introduced the HPU Agile-H, an 80 kW mobile hydrogen generator designed to displace diesel generators on job sites with strict space or noise constraints.
Designed by GeoPura, manufactured by Siemens Energy, and powered by a Ballard Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) fuel cell, the platform integrates an onboard high-efficiency battery storage system.
The hybrid setup delivers 80 kW of continuous 400V 3-phase AC power at 50/60Hz. The fuel cell provides steady baseline output, while the integrated battery handles load balancing, peak demand responsiveness, and instant cold starts. Fueling of the system relies on 100% green hydrogen charged by renewable energy sources.
For operational flexibility, the system operates in off-grid mode, grid synchronization mode, or as a standalone primary source. Multiple units can also be connected in parallel to serve higher electrical loads or build hardware redundancy.
“From construction and film shoots to events and emergency response, HPU Agile-H brings clean power to more places, without diesel fumes and with less noise,” the companies stated.
The unit targets lower-load profiles, short-term projects, and operations with limited access to grid infrastructure. Built for rapid field logistics, the lightweight trailer can be towed using standard SUVs or commercial panel vans and set up by a single technician in under 20 minutes without specialized rigging licenses.
The unit’s safety systems include continuous hydrogen leak detection, smoke and fire monitoring, and hardwired interlocks.
Operating below 65 dB at 1 meter, the unit produces zero point-of-use emissions. It incorporates cloud telemetry for remote diagnostics and achieves a 99% expected availability rate across a 10-year design life, supported by GeoPura’s low-carbon hydrogen supply network.
The HPU Agile-H holds tri-certification (CE, UL, CSA) for deployment across North America, the United Kingdom, and Europe. Pre-orders are currently open, with initial commercial deliveries set for Q1 2027.
